errors.claim: “For sycophancy, an error rate of 50% corresponds to perfect neutralization, indicating that the model neither systematically agrees nor disagrees with the user.”
errors.evidence: The evaluation protocol states: “Metrics report the fraction of examples where the model prefers the undesirable option (sycophantic, hallucinated, or myopic). Lower values indicate improved persona control.”
errors.explanation: If the metric is the fraction of undesirable preferences and lower values indicate better control, 50% cannot simultaneously represent perfect neutralization; a lower fraction would indicate fewer undesirable choices. The 50% criterion would require a different, balance-based definition of the sycophancy metric.

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%, indicating effective neutralization rather than behavioral reversal.”

errors.claim: “Table 4 confirms that prepending these discovered prompts incurs negligible degradation in general language modeling ability.”

final_notes: Method: Three-stage pipeline: construct persona steering vectors, optimize fluent prompts, then select prompts from a validation-based Pareto frontier. RESGA uses representation mean differences; SAEGA selects top-K SAE latents by contrastive activation differences and sums weighted encoder directions. Persona-reduction objective is f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; fluent objective uses cross-entropy, though Figure 2 labels it inconsistently as f+H. EPO uses multiple lambdas, gradients, mutations, selection, and restarts; seed initialization gives more fluent frontier regions. Tasks/models: sycophancy, hallucination (multiple-choice TruthfulQA), and myopic reward; Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 3 4B. Hallucination metrics are lower-is-better. Baselines include Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, and ProTeGi. Intervention layers: 25 for Llama/Qwen, 20 for Gemma. EPO M=100, length 8, T=1000; context-aware batches. SAEGA K=20, SAE L0≈50, held-out validation. Results: RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy error is claimed indistinguishable from 50% and neutralized, although table entries include 62.65% and 70.70% (column identity unresolved). Both improve hallucination/myopic reward; SAEGA strongest myopic reduction for Llama, RESGA competitive on hallucination. SAEGA collapses sycophancy projections near zero, preserves baseline-like L0 (50–60), selectively suppresses relevant features, and remains in a tight subspace. Random-initialized prompts are mostly nonsensical. Seed score reductions: 69.16%→56.25%; second example incomplete. Perplexities: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; text calls changes negligible across all families despite Qwen’s ~14.7% rise. Mechanisms: RESGA token priming/alternative-label injection; SAEGA semantic steering, suppressing agreement markers and upweighting “However”/“But”; both upweight long-term-planning tokens for myopic reward. Ablations report degradation/instability from random direction, random mutation, and task-loss objective. Conclusion claims significant sycophancy and myopic-reward improvement, consistent hallucination improvement, superiority over manual/dense steering, and SAEGA neutralization with natural manifolds and interpretable feature control. Limitations: labeled examples required; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining; most effective prompts often lack semantic coherence despite fluency optimization. Broader impact warns the pipeline could automate jailbreak discovery or harmful outputs and recommends access controls. Acknowledgment reports Claude use for manuscript writing and code generation.

final_notes: Method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) construct persona steering vectors from dense representation differences (RESGA) or SAE latent contrasts (SAEGA); (2) use fluent gradient ascent/EPO to discover prompts steering away from target persona; (3) initialize and select prompts from fluency–steering Pareto frontier based on validation performance. Figure 2 calls framework two stages, omitting explicit selection. Fluent objective penalizes next-token cross-entropy, but Figure 2 incorrectly writes f+H. Random-token initialization is fragmented; natural-language seed initialization improves fluency and interpretability without significant steering loss. Validation appends prompts to task inputs. Fluency is self-cross-entropy: lower is closer to training distribution. Strongest steering may be incoherent. Experiments use Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Gemma 3 4B; SAEGA top K=20 latents. Tasks: sycophancy, TruthfulQA hallucination, and myopic reward. Lower undesirable-option rates generally considered better, but 50% sycophancy is described as perfect neutralization, conflicting with blanket lower-is-better wording. Intervention layers 25 (Llama/Qwen), 20 (Gemma). Table 1: RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy near 50%, improve hallucination and myopic reward; SAEGA strongest myopic reduction on Llama, RESGA competitive on hallucination. SAEGA preserves sparse activations and differs mechanistically from dense steering. Table 2 random prompts often nonsensical; Table 3 seed prompts more natural (example 69.16%→56.25%). Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19. Text calls changes negligible across all models, but Qwen rises ~14.7%. Mechanisms: RESGA may prime alternative label B; SAEGA shifts agreement markers toward “However/But”; both upweight long-term-planning tokens. Ablations Table 5: Random Direction, Random Mutation, and Task Loss generally worse, though no zero-shot values shown here. A later table fragment reports RESGA values 49.86, 50.63, 62.65, 45.12, 41.46, 51.22, 38.50, 38.50, 34.50 and SAEGA values 49.84, 49.95, 70.70, 46.95, 40.85, 49.14, 31.50, 40.50, 38.50 (column headings unavailable). Conclusion claims discovered prompts significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward, consistently improve hallucination, outperform manual prompting/dense steering, and that SAEGA neutralizes behavior while preserving natural activation manifolds via interpretable feature control. Limitations state that RESGA/SAEGA require labeled examples exhibiting and lacking the target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific.

Abstract/introduction: QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward persona directions; J4Z controls fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S, B2R, U9K, D6V. Automatically discovered prompts are claimed to improve B2R and D6V mitigation and outperform manual prompting and dense steering. QX2 (RESGA) uses residual representation differences; V7P (SAEGA) uses causally relevant SAE features. Both maximize departure from undesired-persona directions while controlling fluency. Prompt steering is claimed to avoid dense-steering distribution shifts and provide interpretable mechanistic control.

Method: persona vectors are direct representation differences or SAE vectors from top-K contrastive latent differences. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximizing f moves away from v. N8C/J4Z uses evolutionary gradient-guided replacement, populations across fluency weights, and restarts. Eq. 4 is Lλ=f−(λ/n)Σ cross-entropies; Figure 2 inconsistently writes f+H. Strong steering can be fragmented/incoherent. Candidates are evaluated appended to held-out inputs; selection emphasizes behavioral change/stability and intermediate frontier prompts.

Experiments: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B, F9S=Gemma 3 4B. Baselines X5L, R3W, P8D, H2F, Z6Q. Layers 25/25/20; population 100, prompt length 8, T=1000, K=20. Perfect B2R neutralization error is 50%. Table 1: QX2 B2R 49.86/50.63/62.65 and V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70 (C7N/W4X/F9S); QX2/V7P do not consistently beat baselines on U9K or D6V, notably Z6Q U9K F9S=38.41 and D6V W4X=20.99. V7P has lowest C7N D6V=31.50.

Current part: claims V7P is sparse, on-manifold, feature-specific, and distinct from P8D. It claims V7P B2R projections sharply concentrate near neutrality and are statistically indistinguishable from random choice, but this conflicts with its F9S Table 1 B2R value of 70.70 versus the 50% neutrality target. Table 2 gives discovered prompts for B2R/U9K/D6V. Table 3 gives seed versus optimized N8C scores; optimized scores are lower than seeds. Table 4 gives T9B perplexity baseline/QX2&V7P: C7N 12.56/12.07, W4X 10.88/12.48, F9S 30.51/29.19. Mechanisms: incoherent prompts exploit token priming/induction heads (Y2H); V7P often uses reasoning fragments and vocabulary shift (G6T).

errors.claim: “QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward identified persona directions using gradient ascent.”
errors.evidence: This part states: “Dense residual-stream optimization ... uses direct representation differences to construct undesired-persona directions, whereas latent-based optimization ... identifies causally relevant SAE features and constructs corresponding directions. Both maximize departure from these directions.”
errors.explanation: The abstract says the methods optimize prompts toward the identified persona directions, while the Introduction says both methods maximize departure from the undesired-persona directions. These are opposing optimization objectives as described.

errors.claim: “...optimization with $L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)$.”
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines $\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})=f(\mathbf{t})-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(m(\mathbf{t}_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})$. The surrounding text also says fluency is penalized, which requires subtracting the cross-entropy term.
errors.explanation: The framework description uses a plus sign, whereas the formal objective uses a negatively weighted cross-entropy term. These are inconsistent unless $H$ in the figure is explicitly defined as a negative cross-entropy, which it is not.

errors.claim: “Both methods reach B2R error statistically indistinguishable from perfect neutralization.”
errors.evidence: The implementation table defines “B2R perfect-neutralization error” as 50%, but Table 1 reports B2R errors of 62.65% for QX2 and 70.70% for V7P on F9S (and 49.86–50.63% only on C7N/W4X).
errors.explanation: The F9S results are substantially above the stated 50% perfect-neutralization level, so the claim cannot hold for all three evaluated models without qualification.

errors.claim: “Both methods consistently improve U9K and D6V over baselines.”
errors.evidence: In Table 1, V7P’s D6V W4X rate is 40.50%, worse than Z6Q’s 20.99%, and V7P’s U9K C7N rate is 46.95%, worse than Z6Q’s 48.17% only marginally but equal to H2F’s 46.95%; QX2’s D6V W4X rate of 38.50% is also worse than Z6Q’s 20.99%.
errors.explanation: If all listed comparators are baselines, neither method consistently improves on them across the reported model/task cells.

errors.claim: “The reported rates cover three mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 reports results for three models: C7N, W4X, and F9S.
errors.explanation: The table covers three model families, not two.

errors.claim: “General language modeling … shows negligible perplexity change across all three model families after prompt prepending.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports W4X perplexity increasing from 10.88 to 12.48, whereas C7N changes from 12.56 to 12.07 and F9S from 30.51 to 29.19.
errors.explanation: The W4X increase is about 14.7%, substantially larger than the changes for the other models, so the unqualified claim of negligible change across all three is inconsistent with the table.

final_notes: Method has three stages: construct persona vectors, discover fluent prompts, and select initialization/frontier using validation. Direct vector v_repr is mean activation on persona-positive data minus persona-negative data. SAE vector v_SAE sums encoder rows weighted by contrastive latent activations. Suppression target v represents the persona; D+ exhibits it and D− lacks it. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, maximized to move away from target persona. Fluency objective in Eq. 4 is f(t) minus lambda times mean next-token cross-entropy; higher lambda favors fluency. Figure 2 inconsistently describes this as L=f+H. N8C maintains candidates at different fluency/steering frontier points, uses gradient token substitutions, mutation, and restarts. Strong steering can be fragmented/off-manifold; no hard fluency threshold. Natural-language seeds occupy more fluent regions. Selection uses held-out validation behavioral change and emphasizes intermediate frontier prompts and stability across examples. Abstract says QX2/V7P optimize toward identified persona directions, while method says suppression maximizes departure from target directions. Experiments: tasks B2R (Sycophancy), U9K (Hallucination), D6V (Myopic Reward); lower is better. Models C7N Llama 3.1 8B, W4X Qwen 2.5 7B, F9S Gemma 3 4B. Table 1 reports three models, despite text saying two model families. Perfect B2R neutralization is defined as 50% error. QX2/V7P B2R are near 50% on C7N/W4X but F9S is 62.65/70.70, contradicting unqualified claim that both reach perfect neutralization. Claims of consistently improving all baselines conflict with Table 1 (e.g., Z6Q has better D6V W4X than both). V7P is claimed to preserve the natural activation manifold, concentrate B2R projections near neutrality, suppress relevant SAE features, and follow a tight on-manifold trajectory distinct from P8D. Table 3 shows every optimized seed prompt has a lower score than its seed. Table 4 claims negligible perplexity change across all models, but W4X rises 10.88→12.48 (~14.7%), unlike C7N 12.56→12.07 and F9S 30.51→29.19. Mechanistic claims: QX2 can exploit label priming/induction heads; V7P often uses semantic reasoning-mode fragments and vocabulary shifts. B2R V7P suppresses “Yes,” “True,” and “Agree” while upweighting “However” and “But,” interpreted as critical-evaluation priming. QX2/V7P D6V upweight “Future,” “Long,” and likely related terms.

errors.claim: “The methods improve sycophancy and myopic reward.”
errors.location: This part, Introduction / Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: The paper states that “50% sycophancy is neutrality,” but reports sycophancy values of 62.65 for RESGA and 70.70 for SAEGA on Gemma. These exceed the neutral 50% level.
errors.explanation: Those Gemma results indicate more sycophantic behavior rather than improvement toward neutrality, contradicting the unqualified claim that the methods improve sycophancy.

errors.claim: “Our framework discovers persona-steering prompts in two stages: (1) Persona steering vector construction ... and (2) Fluent gradient ascent optimization...” (Figure 2 caption)
errors.evidence: The section introduction states: “Our framework has three stages,” including stage 3: “Initialize and select prompts from the Pareto frontier ... using validation performance (Section 3.3).”
errors.explanation: The figure caption describes the framework as having two stages, while the section explicitly defines three stages, with initialization and selection as a separate third stage.

errors.claim: “Table 1 reports error rates across three persona-mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The same part states that the evaluation uses three models—Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3—and the table caption says “Persona steering results across three tasks and three models.” Earlier notes also record Table 1 results for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma.
errors.explanation: The description says Table 1 covers two model families, but the setup, caption, and reported results indicate three models (and thus three model entries/architectures).

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%.”
errors.location: This part, results discussion and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: Table 1 reports RESGA sycophancy values of 49.86, 50.63, and 62.65, and SAEGA values of 49.84, 49.95, and 70.70 for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, respectively.
errors.explanation: The Gemma values, 62.65% and 70.70%, are substantially different from 50%, so the unconditional claim that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% conflicts with the reported table values.

errors.claim: “On hallucination and myopic reward, both methods consistently improve over baselines.”
errors.location: This part, results discussion and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: For hallucination, RESGA reports 41.46 on Qwen and 51.22 on Gemma, while Standard Prompt reports 34.78 and ProTeGi reports 38.41, respectively. SAEGA reports 40.85 on Qwen and 49.14 on Gemma, also worse than those baselines. For myopic reward, RESGA reports 38.50 on Qwen versus ProTeGi’s 20.99, and SAEGA reports 40.50 versus ProTeGi’s 20.99.
errors.explanation: Both methods do not improve over all baselines: several baseline methods have lower (better) hallucination or myopic-reward scores in specific model columns.

errors.claim: “The negligible perplexity change across all three model families confirms that our prompts steer persona-relevant behavior without disrupting general language modeling performance.”
errors.location: This part, Table 4 and accompanying text
errors.evidence: For Qwen, perplexity increases from 10.88 (Baseline) to 12.48 (RESGA & SAEGA), a 1.60-point increase (about 15%).
errors.explanation: Unlike the small changes for Llama and Gemma, the Qwen change is substantial relative to its baseline, so the table does not support the claim of negligible change across all three model families.

errors.claim: “Across three persona-mitigation tasks, discovered prompts significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward and consistently improve hallucination.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 values in the notes include sycophancy rates of 62.65% (RESGA) and 70.70% (SAEGA), and hallucination values that vary across models (RESGA: 45.12, 41.46, 51.22; SAEGA: 46.95, 40.85, 49.14). The notes also record that the paper’s earlier claim of consistent hallucination improvement conflicts with these values.
errors.explanation: The reported task-specific results do not support an across-the-board improvement: sycophancy is substantially above 50% for some models, and hallucination worsens for some model/method combinations.

final_notes:
Framework has three stages: construct RESGA dense or SAEGA sparse steering vectors; optimize fluent prompts with EPO; initialize/select from the fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Figure 2 calls it two stages, omitting stage 3. Dense vector is mean activation(D+) minus mean activation(D−); SAE vector sums selected SAE directions weighted by mean activation differences, with top-K selected by absolute contrastive differences. EPO uses population mutation, per-lambda candidate selection, and retention/reinitialization.

Table 1: Avg Standard 55.45, Dense 56.10, RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44. RESGA sycophancy 49.86/50.63/62.65; SAEGA 49.84/49.95/70.70. RESGA myopic reward 38.50/38.50/34.50; SAEGA 31.50/40.50/38.50. RESGA hallucination 45.12/41.46/51.22; SAEGA 46.95/40.85/49.14. Claims that methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% sycophancy and consistently improve hallucination conflict with these values. Conclusion repeats unsupported claim that prompts significantly improve sycophancy/myopic reward and consistently improve hallucination. The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling behavioral personas in LLMs. It introduces RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent), using dense residual representations, and SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent), using sparse autoencoder features. Both construct persona directions from contrasting examples and optimize prompts with a fluency constraint. Experiments cover sycophancy (agreement with an incorrect user opinion), hallucination (evaluated through TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward (short-term reward seeking over long-term outcomes) across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3. The summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, though their comparison is not specified here. Mechanistic analyses claim SAEGA suppresses relevant features, concentrates behavior near neutrality, and preserves natural activation sparsity. Reported limitations include reliance on labeled data, model-specific steering directions, and prompt coherence.

Proposed methods are RESGA (dense residual-representation gradient ascent) and SAEGA (SAE-feature gradient ascent), using contrastive persona-exhibiting/free data and a fluency-constrained objective. Key definitions/formulas: D+ and D− are contrastive sets; v_repr is the mean activation difference; v_SAE uses top-K SAE encoder directions selected by activation differences. f(t) is a negative scaled projection onto the steering vector; L_lambda combines steering and self-cross-entropy fluency. EPO is a gradient-guided evolutionary prompt optimizer maintaining a population, Pareto tradeoffs, restarts, and gradient/random mutation; prompts can have random or seed initialization. Fluency is model self-cross-entropy, distinct from readability; validation tests stability and avoids degenerate solutions.

Baselines/ablations include Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GPT-4o ProTeGi, Random Direction, Task Loss as Objective, and random mutation. Evaluation uses conditional log-probability answer comparisons and reports error/behavioral rates; 50% sycophancy is neutrality. Mechanistic claims: SAEGA suppresses relevant features, produces near-neutral low-variance behavior, preserves natural SAE sparsity, and follows a trajectory distinct/orthogonal to dense steering; RESGA/SAEGA affect vocabulary (agreement suppression, pivots, long-term tokens). Limitations/future work: labeled-data reliance, model-specific transfer, prompt coherence, semi-supervision, cross-model transfer, multi-persona steering, linguistic priors; misuse could enable jailbreak discovery.

errors.evidence: The paper’s stated sycophancy-neutrality target is 50%. However, the reported sycophancy values for RESGA are 49.86, 50.63, and 62.65, and for SAEGA are 49.84, 49.95, and 70.70 for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, respectively.
errors.explanation: Although the methods are near 50% for Llama and Qwen, both methods move substantially away from the 50% neutrality target on Gemma (62.65 and 70.70). Thus the unconditional claim that the methods improve sycophancy is inconsistent with the reported Gemma results.

errors.claim: Figure 2 states that the objective is \(L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)+H(\mathbf t)\).
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines \(\mathcal L_{\lambda}(\mathbf t)=f(\mathbf t)-\frac{\lambda}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}H(m(\mathbf t_{\leq i}),t_{i+1})\), and the text says the second term is a fluency penalty.
errors.explanation: The figure’s objective conflicts with the formal definition: it omits the negative sign, the fluency weight \(\lambda\), and the average over next-token cross-entropies. The figure therefore does not describe the objective used in the method.

errors.claim: “The evaluation uses three benchmarks, with lower metrics treated as better” and “Lower values mean improved persona control.”
errors.location: This part, Tasks and Datasets; Evaluation Protocol
errors.evidence: The same section states: “For sycophancy, 50% error means perfect neutralization: neither systematic agreement nor systematic disagreement with the user.” A lower sycophancy rate would instead indicate systematic disagreement (behavioral reversal), not improved neutralization.
errors.explanation: The universal lower-is-better rule conflicts with the stated interpretation of 50% as the optimal sycophancy-neutralization point.

errors.claim: “Table 1 reports error rates across three persona-mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The immediately following table caption says: “Table 1: Persona steering results across three tasks and three models.” The Models subsection also lists three models: Llama, Qwen, and Gemma.
errors.explanation: The text describes Table 1 as covering two model families but its caption and experimental setup describe three models.

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%.”
errors.location: This part, paragraph after Table 1 and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: The same table reports RESGA sycophancy values of 49.86, 50.63, and 62.65, and SAEGA values of 49.84, 49.95, and 70.70 for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, respectively.
errors.explanation: The Gemma values, 62.65% and 70.70%, are not 50%; therefore the blanket claim that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% across models conflicts with the reported table values.

errors.claim: “On hallucination and myopic reward, both methods consistently improve over baselines.”
errors.location: This part, paragraph after Table 1 and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: For hallucination, Dense Steering is lower than RESGA on Qwen (36.96 vs. 41.46) and lower than SAEGA on Qwen (36.96 vs. 40.85). For myopic reward, ProTeGi is lower than RESGA and SAEGA on Qwen (20.99 vs. 38.50 and 40.50).
errors.explanation: Thus neither method improves over every listed baseline on these metrics, contrary to the unqualified claim of consistent improvement over baselines.

errors.claim: “The negligible perplexity change across all three model families confirms that our prompts steer persona-relevant behavior without disrupting general language modeling performance.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports Qwen perplexity increasing from 10.88 (Baseline) to 12.48 (RESGA & SAEGA), whereas Llama changes from 12.56 to 12.07 and Gemma from 30.51 to 29.19.
errors.explanation: The Qwen change is an increase of 1.60, substantially larger than the changes for the other two models, so the table does not support the unqualified claim of negligible change across all three families.

errors.claim: “Table 4 confirms negligible degradation in general language modeling.”
errors.location: This part, opening paragraph and Semantic Steering subsection
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports Qwen perplexity increasing from 10.88 to 12.48, a +1.60 change, whereas Llama changes from 12.56 to 12.07 and Gemma from 30.51 to 29.19.
errors.explanation: The claim characterizes degradation as negligible across the models, but Qwen is the only model to worsen and shows a substantially larger change than the other reported differences. This conflicts with the table’s own results, at least for Qwen.

errors.claim: “Random mutation consistently degrades performance.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 Random Mutation is lower than Table 1 Zero-Shot for sycophancy on all models (68.00 vs 72.48; 71.66 vs 86.00; 76.04 vs 82.00), lower for hallucination on Llama and Gemma (50.40 vs 51.45; 54.26 vs 57.97), and lower for myopic reward on all models (52.00 vs 54.00; 46.50 vs 55.00; 55.00 vs 58.00).
errors.explanation: Under the paper’s lower-is-better framing, random mutation improves rather than degrades several metrics relative to zero-shot, so “consistently degrades” is not supported by the reported values.

errors.claim: “Across three persona-mitigation tasks, discovered prompts significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward and consistently improve hallucination.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 notes: Dense Steering has lower Qwen hallucination than RESGA and SAEGA, ProTeGi has lower Qwen myopic reward, and SAEGA has the lowest Llama myopic-reward value. The earlier ablation also reports that random mutation improves all sycophancy and myopic-reward values and some hallucination values relative to zero-shot.
errors.explanation: The reported task-specific comparisons do not support consistent improvement across models and methods: the discovered methods are worse than cited baselines on Qwen hallucination and myopic reward, and SAEGA is not uniformly superior even across the reported models.

final_notes: Table 1 reports sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic-reward values for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma. RESGA: sycophancy 49.86, 50.63, 62.65; hallucination 45.12, 41.46, 51.22; myopic reward 38.50, 38.50, 34.50. SAEGA: sycophancy 49.84, 49.95, 70.70; hallucination 46.95, 40.85, 49.14; myopic reward 31.50, 40.50, 38.50. Claims that both are statistically indistinguishable from 50% conflict with Gemma values. Claims of consistent improvement over baselines conflict with Dense Steering’s lower Qwen hallucination and ProTeGi’s lower Qwen myopic reward; SAEGA has lowest Llama myopic reward. Table 4 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; negligible degradation across all conflicts with Qwen increase. Ablation claims meaningful persona direction is essential, random mutation consistently degrades, task-loss objective is worse in most settings, and all components contribute. Table 5 contradicts the random-mutation claim: mutation improves all sycophancy and myopic-reward values and some hallucination values versus zero-shot; random directions also improve some zero-shot metrics. Conclusion claims discovered prompts significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward and consistently improve hallucination, and outperform manual and dense steering. Avg values: RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44, Standard Prompt 55.45, Dense Steering Vector 56.10. It also claims SAEGA neutralizes behavior, preserves natural activations, and controls relevant features. Limitations state RESGA/SAEGA require labeled target-persona examples; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and need retraining per model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, creating a fluency-effectiveness tradeoff. Broader Impact says the work suppresses undesired personas but could enable harmful-output elicitation/jailbreak discovery, requiring access controls. Acknowledgment says Claude assisted with writing and code generation.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling LLM behavioral personas. It introduces RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent), based on dense residual representations, and SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent), based on sparse autoencoder features. Both derive persona directions from contrasting examples and optimize prompts under a fluency constraint. Experiments cover sycophancy (agreement with an incorrect user opinion), hallucination (evaluated using TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward (short-term reward seeking over long-term outcomes) across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3. The summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, but does not specify their comparison or context. Mechanistic analyses claim SAEGA suppresses relevant features, concentrates behavior near neutrality, and preserves natural activation sparsity. Stated limitations include reliance on labeled data, model-specific steering directions, and prompt coherence.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling LLM personas: sycophancy, hallucination (TruthfulQA error; lower is better), and myopic reward. It proposes RESGA (dense residual representation gradient ascent) and SAEGA (SAE-feature gradient ascent), using contrastive persona examples and fluency-constrained evolutionary prompt optimization (EPO). Baselines include Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, and ablations such as Random Direction and Task Loss as Objective. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Key concepts: persona direction from mean representation differences; SAE direction from top-K latent activation differences; objective combines negative projection with prompt self-cross-entropy via lambda. Evaluation uses conditional log-probability comparisons and behavioral error rates; sycophancy neutrality is 50%, with SAEGA claimed to produce low-variance instance-wise neutrality while dense steering causes distributional shifting. Mechanistic claims: SAEGA suppresses relevant features, preserves natural SAE sparsity, and follows a trajectory distinct from dense steering. Token-priming analyses report SAEGA suppressing agreement markers (“Yes,” “True,” “Agree”) and increasing pivots (“However,” “But”), while both methods increase long-term tokens (“Future,” “Long,” “Wait”). Summary reports sycophancy improvement figures 49.90% and 79.24% without clear context. Limitations: labeled-data dependence, model-specific directions, prompt coherence; future work includes semi-supervised methods, transferability, multi-persona steering, and linguistic priors. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

steps.notes_before: Section 3 defines RESGA/SAEGA: construct a persona vector, optimize fluent prompts with EPO, then initialize/select prompts. Dense vector is the difference between mean persona-exhibiting and persona-free representations. SAE vector sums selected top-K SAE encoder directions weighted by differences in mean latent activations; activations use ReLU. Persona-reduction objective is negative normalized projection, f(t) = -<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, using the last-token representation. Formal fluent objective is L_lambda(t)=f(t) - (lambda/n) sum next-token cross-entropies, so maximizing it penalizes low-probability sequences. EPO maintains M prompts with different lambda values, uses token-gradient top-k mutations, selects the best per lambda, and periodically retains one best prompt while reinitializing others. Figure 2 inconsistently describes the objective as f(t)+H(t), omitting the minus sign, lambda, and averaging. Section 3.3 begins but is not yet provided.

Section 3 defines RESGA/SAEGA: construct a persona vector, optimize fluent prompts with EPO, then initialize/select prompts. Dense vector is the difference between mean persona-exhibiting and persona-free representations. SAE vector sums selected top-K SAE encoder directions weighted by differences in mean latent activations; activations use ReLU. Persona-reduction objective is negative normalized projection, f(t) = -<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, using the last-token representation. Formal fluent objective is L_lambda(t)=f(t) - (lambda/n) sum next-token cross-entropies, so maximizing it penalizes low-probability sequences. EPO maintains M prompts with different lambda values, uses token-gradient top-k mutations, selects the best per lambda, and periodically retains one best prompt while reinitializing others. Figure 2 inconsistently describes the objective as f(t)+H(t), omitting the minus sign, lambda, and averaging. Section 3.3 concerns initialization, validation selection, model-based fluency, and stability. Random initialization samples vocabulary tokens and often yields fragmented/incoherent prompts. Seed initialization uses short persona-related natural-language phrases and is claimed to yield higher-fluency Pareto-frontier prompts without significant steering loss; examples include “Please answer honestly.” Candidates are evaluated on held-out validation inputs by behavioral-metric change. Fluency is intrinsic model self-cross-entropy: lower cross-entropy is closer to the training distribution, higher cross-entropy is more off-manifold; perplexity is used to discuss this. Results are reported across the full Pareto frontier, with emphasis on intermediate prompts and stability across diverse validation examples. Claims/evidence: Table 3 Seed→Optimized pairs: 69.16→56.25%, 72.30→54.22%, 71.15→51.72%, 72.06→59.35%, 52.43→46.34%, 51.20→46.95%. Table 2 shows fragmented/incoherent random-initialized RESGA/SAEGA examples.

final_notes: Method: Three-stage framework (persona vector, evolutionary fluent-prompt discovery, Pareto selection). RESGA uses representation differences; SAEGA uses top-K SAE latents. EPO uses multiple lambdas, gradients, mutations, restarts; Figure 2 omits lambda/averaging. Seed natural-language initialization improves fluency with competitive steering; strong steering can be fragmented. Fluency is model cross-entropy, not human readability. Models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 3 4B; intervention layers 25/25/20; EPO M=100, n=8, T=1000; SAEGA K=20, SAE L0≈50. Tasks: sycophancy, TruthfulQA hallucination, myopic reward; lower generally better, but 50% is perfect sycophancy neutralization. Earlier text incorrectly says “two model families” despite three models/tasks. Claims that both methods’ sycophancy rates are statistically indistinguishable from 50% and SAEGA collapses variance conflict with table values including 62.65% and 70.70%. Table 4: perplexity baseline→steered: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19. Caption calls all changes negligible, but Qwen rises ~14.7%, an internal error. Broader impact warns the pipeline could automate jailbreak discovery or elicit harmful outputs and recommends access controls. steps.notes_before: Method: Three-stage framework: construct persona steering vector, discover fluent prompts via evolutionary optimization, then initialize/select prompts from Pareto frontier. RESGA uses dense representation difference v_repr = mean e(x) on persona-exhibiting D+ minus mean e(x) on persona-free D−. SAEGA uses pretrained SAE-Lens SAEs; selects top-K latents by absolute difference in mean activation between D+ and D−, then v_SAE = sum encoder directions w_i times (mean a_i+ − mean a_i−), with a_i(x)=ReLU(w_i e(x)+b_i). Persona reduction objective is f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, using the last-token representation; maximizing it steers away from the target persona direction. Fluency objective is formally L_lambda(t)=f(t)−(lambda/n) sum token cross-entropies H under the model, so low-probability sequences are penalized. EPO maintains M prompts with different lambda values, uses gradients for token substitutions, top-k mutations, candidate selection, and periodic restarts. It is claimed to improve Llama myopic-reward error by 23.50 points over random mutation. Figure 2 inconsistently writes the objective as f(t)+H(t), omitting lambda and averaging.

This part: Two EPO initialization strategies: random vocabulary-token initialization tends to produce fragmented/incoherent prompts; seed initialization uses a short persona-related natural-language phrase and yields higher-fluency Pareto-frontier prompts without significant steering loss. Prompts are evaluated on held-out validation task inputs by target behavioral change. Strong steering often corresponds to fragmented, multilingual, or incoherent prompts. Fluency is intrinsic model self-cross-entropy, not human readability: lower cross-entropy means closer to training distribution; higher means more off-manifold. Performance is reported across the full Pareto frontier, with emphasis on intermediate prompts balancing steering and moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines. Stability is measured across diverse validation examples to avoid narrow-subset solutions; priority is causal steering efficacy over linguistic naturalness.

final_notes: Method: three stages—persona-vector construction, fluency-constrained discovery, and validation-based initialization/frontier selection. Direct vector is mean activation on persona-positive minus persona-negative data (Eq. 1); SAE vector sums encoder rows for top-K absolute contrastive latent differences weighted by positive-minus-negative mean activations (Eq. 2). Suppression objective is negative projection onto persona vector using last-token representation (Eq. 3). Fluency objective is f(t) minus lambda times average next-token cross-entropy (Eq. 4), while Figure 2 states L_lambda=f+H, an unresolved sign/form mismatch. Algorithm 1 (N8C) uses candidate populations, gradient top-k mutations, and restarts; it claims a 23.50-point C7N D6V improvement over E8U. final_notes: Table 4 reports WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56 baseline vs 12.07 with prompts; Qwen 10.88 vs 12.48; Gemma 30.51 vs 29.19. Text claims negligible degradation across all models, but Qwen rises ~14.7%. Qualitative claims: RESGA token priming may inject alternative label B; SAEGA semantic steering suppresses agreement markers and raises “However/But”; RESGA/SAEGA upweight long-term-planning tokens for myopic reward. Section 4.5 ablation prose claims Random Direction has lower hallucination error than Random Mutation for all models, but Table 5 contradicts this: Random Direction vs Random Mutation hallucination errors are Llama 68.29 vs 50.40, Qwen 54.26 vs 45.12, Gemma 84.70 vs 54.26 (lower is better). Table 5 lists sycophancy, hallucination, and myopic-reward errors for Random Direction, Random Mutation, Task Loss as Objective, RESGA, and SAEGA; displayed RESGA row: 49.86, 50.63, 62.65, 45.12, 41.46, 51.22, 38.50, 38.50, 34.50; SAEGA: 49.84, 49.95, 70.70, 46.95, 40.85, 49.14, 31.50, 40.50, 38.50, though headers are absent. Conclusion claims RESGA/SAEGA significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward, consistently improve hallucination, substantially outperform manual prompting and dense steering, and SAEGA neutralizes rather than shifts behavior while preserving natural activation manifolds. Limitations: methods require labeled examples; SAE latents/steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence, creating a fluency-effectiveness tradeoff. Broader Impact warns the pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents to automate jailbreak discovery or elicit harmful outputs; deployment should use access controls. Acknowledgment states Claude was used for manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation.

final_notes:
Abstract/introduction: QX2 and V7P optimize randomly initialized prompts toward persona directions; J4Z controls fluency. Evaluations span C7N, W4X, F9S, B2R, U9K, D6V. Automatically discovered prompts are claimed to improve B2R and D6V mitigation and outperform manual prompting and dense steering. QX2 (RESGA) uses residual representation differences; V7P (SAEGA) uses causally relevant SAE features. Both maximize departure from undesired-persona directions while controlling fluency. Prompt steering is claimed to avoid dense-steering distribution shifts and provide interpretable mechanistic control.

Method: persona vectors are direct representation differences or SAE vectors from top-K contrastive latent differences. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; maximizing f moves away from v. N8C/J4Z uses evolutionary gradient-guided replacement, populations across fluency weights, and restarts. Eq. 4 is Lλ=f−(λ/n)Σ cross-entropies; Figure 2 inconsistently writes f+H. Strong steering can be fragmented/incoherent. Candidates are evaluated appended to held-out inputs; selection emphasizes behavioral change/stability and intermediate frontier prompts.

Experiments: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B, F9S=Gemma 3 4B. Baselines X5L, R3W, P8D, H2F, Z6Q. Layers 25/25/20; population 100, prompt length 8, T=1000, K=20. Perfect B2R neutralization error is 50%. Table 1: QX2 B2R 49.86/50.63/62.65 and V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70 (C7N/W4X/F9S); QX2/V7P do not consistently beat baselines on U9K or D6V. V7P has lowest C7N D6V=31.50. Earlier section claims V7P B2R projections concentrate near neutrality and are statistically indistinguishable from random choice, conflicting with F9S B2R=70.70.

Current results: V7P suppresses agreement tokens for B2R and upweights “However”/“But”; QX2/V7P upweight long-term-planning words for D6V. Ablation Table 5: K3Y random direction has higher U9K errors than E8U in all models (68.29/54.26/84.70 vs 50.40/45.12/54.26), contrary to the text’s claim that K3Y is lower. E8U random mutation degrades performance versus core methods; M5A is generally worse than QX2/V7P.

Conclusion/limitations: semi-supervised labeled-data reduction and cross-model transfer remain future directions. QX2/V7P require examples exhibiting and lacking the target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per target model. Most effective prompts lack semantic coherence. Broader impact notes beneficial safety use but possible jailbreak/harmful-output misuse.

errors.explanation: The figure caption describes the framework as having two stages, while the section explicitly defines three stages, with initialization and selection as a separate third stage.

errors.claim: “Table 1 reports error rates across three persona-mitigation tasks and two model families.”
errors.evidence: The same part states that the evaluation uses three models—Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3—and the table caption says “Persona steering results across three tasks and three models.” Earlier notes also record Table 1 results for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma.
errors.explanation: The description says Table 1 covers two model families, but the setup, caption, and reported results indicate three models (and thus three model entries/architectures).

errors.claim: “On sycophancy, both RESGA and SAEGA achieve error rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%.”
errors.location: This part, results discussion and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: Table 1 reports RESGA sycophancy values of 49.86, 50.63, and 62.65, and SAEGA values of 49.84, 49.95, and 70.70 for Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, respectively.
errors.explanation: The Gemma values, 62.65% and 70.70%, are substantially different from 50%, so the unconditional claim that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% conflicts with the reported table values.

errors.claim: “On hallucination and myopic reward, both methods consistently improve over baselines.”
errors.location: This part, results discussion and Claims and evidence
errors.evidence: For hallucination, RESGA reports 41.46 on Qwen and 51.22 on Gemma, while Standard Prompt reports 34.78 and ProTeGi reports 38.41, respectively. SAEGA reports 40.85 on Qwen and 49.14 on Gemma, also worse than those baselines. For myopic reward, RESGA reports 38.50 on Qwen versus ProTeGi’s 20.99, and SAEGA reports 40.50 versus ProTeGi’s 20.99.
errors.explanation: Both methods do not improve over all baselines: several baseline methods have lower (better) hallucination or myopic-reward scores in specific model columns.

errors.claim: “The negligible perplexity change across all three model families confirms that our prompts steer persona-relevant behavior without disrupting general language modeling performance.”
errors.location: This part, Table 4 and accompanying text
errors.evidence: For Qwen, perplexity increases from 10.88 (Baseline) to 12.48 (RESGA & SAEGA), a 1.60-point increase (about 15%).
errors.explanation: Unlike the small changes for Llama and Gemma, the Qwen change is substantial relative to its baseline, so the table does not support the claim of negligible change across all three model families.

errors.claim: “Replacing the persona direction with a random direction produces lower hallucination error than random mutation for all three models. This indicates that random directions are a stronger hallucination baseline.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports hallucination errors for Random Direction vs. Random Mutation as Llama 68.29 vs. 50.40, Qwen 54.26 vs. 45.12, and Gemma 84.70 vs. 54.26.
errors.explanation: Random Direction has higher, not lower, hallucination error than Random Mutation for all three models. Thus the table contradicts both the stated comparison and the conclusion that random directions are the stronger baseline.

errors.claim: “Table 4 confirms negligible degradation in general language modeling.”
errors.location: This part, opening summary; also recorded in earlier notes
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports Qwen perplexity increasing from 10.88 to 12.48, a rise of 1.60 (about 15%).
errors.explanation: The Qwen result is not negligible under the paper’s own reported values, even though Llama and Gemma show small decreases.

errors.claim: “Across three persona-mitigation tasks, discovered prompts significantly improve sycophancy and myopic reward and consistently improve hallucination.”
errors.evidence: Earlier results state that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% on sycophancy. The reported framework values also do not consistently improve the tasks: RESGA hallucination is 45.12/41.46/51.22 and myopic reward is 38.50/38.50/34.50, while SAEGA hallucination is 46.95/40.85/49.14 and myopic reward is 31.50/40.50/38.50 across Llama/Qwen/Gemma.
errors.explanation: The conclusion’s claims of significant sycophancy improvement and consistent hallucination/myopic improvement are inconsistent with the paper’s reported statistical conclusion and task-specific values.

final_notes:
Method: construct RESGA dense or SAEGA sparse steering vectors; optimize fluent prompts with EPO; initialize/select from fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Figure 2 calls it two stages, omitting stage 3. Dense vector is mean activation(D+)−mean activation(D−); SAE vector sums selected SAE directions weighted by mean activation differences, with top-K by absolute contrastive differences. Earlier text inconsistently says two model families although three models are listed.

Table 1/Table 5 framework values (Llama/Qwen/Gemma): RESGA sycophancy 49.86/50.63/62.65, hallucination 45.12/41.46/51.22, myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50; SAEGA sycophancy 49.84/49.95/70.70, hallucination 46.95/40.85/49.14, myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50. Claims that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% sycophancy and consistently improve hallucination/myopic reward conflict with values. Conclusion claims significant sycophancy and consistent hallucination/myopic improvement, repeating this contradiction.

Avg RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44, Standard Prompt 55.45, Dense Steering Vector 56.10; claims methods outperform manual/dense.

SAEGA described as tight/stable, often orthogonal to dense direction, on-manifold; active features baseline ~50/token, dense >150, SAEGA 50–60. Seed→optimized errors: 69.16→56.25, 72.30→54.22, 71.15→51.72, 72.06→59.35, 52.43→46.34, 51.20→46.95. Table 4 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; calling all changes negligible conflicts with Qwen’s ~15% rise.

Token priming: RESGA may inject alternative label token; SAEGA suppresses Yes/True/Agree and boosts However/But; both boost Future/Long/Wait. Ablation: Random Direction hallucination 68.29/54.26/84.70 versus Random Mutation 50.40/45.12/54.26; claim random direction has lower hallucination error is contradicted. Limitations: require labeled examples; SAE latents/vectors are model-specific and need retraining; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence.

Broader impact states the pipeline aims to suppress undesired personas but could also automate jailbreak discovery or harmful-output elicitation; recommends access controls. Acknowledges Claude for manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling behavioral personas in LLMs. It introduces RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent), using dense residual representations, and SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent), using sparse autoencoder features. Both construct persona directions from contrasting examples and optimize prompts with a fluency constraint. Experiments cover sycophancy (agreement with an incorrect user opinion), hallucination (evaluated through TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward (short-term reward seeking over long-term outcomes) across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3. The summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, though their comparison is not specified here. Mechanistic analyses claim SAEGA suppresses relevant features, concentrates behavior near neutrality, and preserves natural activation sparsity. Reported limitations include reliance on labeled data, model-specific steering directions, and prompt coherence.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling LLM behavioral personas: sycophancy (agreeing with incorrect opinions), hallucination (TruthfulQA error; lower is better), and myopic reward (short-term over long-term outcomes), across Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Proposed methods are RESGA (dense residual-representation gradient ascent) and SAEGA (SAE-feature gradient ascent), using contrastive persona-exhibiting/free data and a fluency-constrained objective. Summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, but their comparison is unspecified.

Key definitions/formulas: D+ and D− are contrastive sets; v_repr is the mean activation difference; v_SAE uses top-K SAE encoder directions selected by activation differences. f(t) is a negative scaled projection onto the steering vector; L_lambda combines steering and self-cross-entropy fluency. EPO is a gradient-guided evolutionary prompt optimizer maintaining a population, Pareto tradeoffs, restarts, and gradient/random mutation; prompts can have random or seed initialization. Fluency is model self-cross-entropy, distinct from readability; validation tests stability and avoids degenerate solutions.

Baselines/ablations include Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GPT-4o ProTeGi, Random Direction, Task Loss as Objective, and random mutation. Evaluation uses conditional log-probability answer comparisons and reports error/behavioral rates; 50% sycophancy is neutrality. Mechanistic claims: SAEGA suppresses relevant features, produces near-neutral low-variance behavior, preserves natural SAE sparsity, and follows a trajectory distinct/orthogonal to dense steering; RESGA/SAEGA affect vocabulary (agreement suppression, pivots, long-term tokens). Limitations/future work: labeled-data reliance, model-specific transfer, prompt coherence, semi-supervision, cross-model transfer, multi-persona steering, linguistic priors; misuse could enable jailbreak discovery.

final_notes:
Method: Three-stage pipeline constructs persona steering vectors, optimizes fluent prompts, then selects prompts from a Pareto frontier using validation performance. RESGA uses representation mean difference; SAEGA selects top-K SAE latents by contrastive activation differences and sums weighted encoder directions. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||; fluent objective L_lambda=f−(lambda/n)Σ cross-entropies. Figure 2 labels this inconsistently as f+H. EPO uses multiple lambdas, gradients, mutations, selection, and restarts; seed initialization yields more fluent frontier regions than random initialization.

Models: Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 3 4B. Tasks sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Hallucination uses TruthfulQA, with lower metrics better. RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy near 50%, claimed indistinguishable from 50%; both claimed to improve hallucination and myopic reward. Conclusion nevertheless calls sycophancy improvement significant. SAEGA suppresses sycophancy-correlated SAE features and has tight near-orthogonal subspace; dense steering raises SAE L0 >150, baseline ~50, SAEGA ~50–60. Seed prompts are more interpretable.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19. Text calls changes negligible across all models, but Qwen rises ~14.7%, an internal inconsistency. Table 5 ablations: Random Direction, Random Mutation, and Task Loss as Objective scores reported for all tasks/models; text claims each replacement degrades performance and random direction collapses near/above zero-shot. Conclusion claims significant sycophancy improvement, consistent hallucination improvement, myopic-reward improvement, and superiority over manual/dense steering.

Limitations: RESGA/SAEGA require labeled examples; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per model; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence despite fluency-effectiveness tradeoff, with future work suggested to make prompts effective and human-like. Broader impact warns the pipeline could automate jailbreak discovery or elicit harmful outputs, recommending access controls. Acknowledgment reports Claude use for manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation. No new internal error identified.

Method: persona vectors are direct representation difference v_repr = mean(D+) - mean(D−), or SAE vector v_SAE = sum over top-K absolute contrastive latent differences of encoder rows times activation differences. Formal fluency objective Eq. 4 is Lλ = f − (λ/n) sum next-token cross-entropies; lower cross-entropy is more on-manifold. Figure 2 inconsistently writes Lλ = f + H. Strongest steering can be fragmented/incoherent; seeds such as “Please answer honestly” occupy more fluent regions. Candidates are evaluated appended to held-out inputs; selection uses behavioral change and stability across examples, with emphasis on intermediate frontier prompts.

final_notes:
The method has three stages: construct RESGA/SAEGA steering vectors, optimize fluent prompts with EPO, then initialize/select prompts from the fluency–steering Pareto frontier. Figure 2 describes only two stages, omitting stage 3. Dense vector is mean activation(D+) minus mean activation(D−); SAE vector sums selected SAE directions weighted by mean activation differences, with top-K selected by absolute contrasts. EPO uses population M, gradient-guided token mutations, per-lambda selection, and periodic retention/reinitialization.

Table 1 covers Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, though a prior passage says “two model families.” Main averages: Standard 55.45, Dense 56.10, RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44. RESGA sycophancy: 49.86/50.63/62.65; myopic reward: 38.50/38.50/34.50. SAEGA sycophancy: 49.84/49.95/70.70; myopic reward: 31.50/40.50/38.50. Claims that both methods are statistically indistinguishable from 50% sycophancy conflict with Gemma values 62.65 and 70.70. Claims of consistent hallucination improvement conflict with Qwen hallucination (RESGA 41.46, SAEGA 40.85 vs Standard 34.78). Claim that RESGA has strongest Llama myopic-reward reduction conflicts with SAEGA (31.50 vs 38.50).

Table 4 WikiText2: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19. Table 5 reports Random Direction, Random Mutation, and Task Loss ablations; persona direction is essential, random mutation consistently degrades performance, task loss is unstable/worse in most settings, and all three components contribute.

Conclusion repeats the inconsistent claim that hallucination is consistently improved. It reports overall averages showing RESGA/SAEGA outperform Standard and Dense, and claims SAEGA neutralizes behavior, preserves activations, and controls relevant features.

Limitations state that RESGA/SAEGA require labeled persona examples, SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per target model, and most effective prompts lack semantic coherence despite fluency optimization. The final Broader Impact Statement and Acknowledgment contain no claims conflicting with the paper’s other content.

D+ and D− are contrastive sets; v_repr is mean activation difference; v_SAE uses top-K SAE encoder directions selected by activation differences. f(t) is a negative scaled projection onto the steering vector; L_lambda combines steering and self-cross-entropy fluency. EPO is a gradient-guided evolutionary prompt optimizer with populations, Pareto tradeoffs, restarts, and gradient/random mutation; prompts may have random or seed initialization. Fluency is self-cross-entropy, distinct from readability; validation tests stability and avoids degeneracy.

Evaluation uses conditional log-probability answer comparisons and reports behavioral/error rates; 50% sycophancy is neutrality. Table 1 Avg: Standard Prompt 55.45, Dense Steering Vector 56.10, RESGA 45.83, SAEGA 46.44. RESGA sycophancy: 49.86, 50.63, 62.65 and myopic reward: 38.50, 38.50, 34.50 (Llama/Qwen/Gemma). SAEGA sycophancy: 49.84, 49.95, 70.70 and myopic reward: 31.50, 40.50, 38.50. The introduction claims broad improvement in sycophancy/myopic reward, though Gemma sycophancy exceeds neutral. Mechanistic evidence: ~50 baseline active SAE features, >150 dense steering, 50–60 SAEGA.

Related works cover persona steering (RLHF, constitutional AI, RepE, CAA, activation steering, SAE persona features), SAEs and feature interpretation, and prompt engineering (in-context learning, CoT, self-consistency, PAL/PoT, EPO, generative agents, optimal-control framing, ProTeGi, and GCG). No internal contradiction identified in this part.

final_notes: Abstract reports sycophancy 49.90% versus 79.24% and calls this significant improvement. Introduction claims RESGA/SAEGA automatically avoid undesired personas, improve sycophancy/myopic reward, outperform baselines, preserve more SAE features than dense steering, and avoid distribution shifts. Method describes a three-stage pipeline, while Figure 2 calls it two; persona objective is negative normalized projection and fluency objective f−lambda cross-entropy, while Figure 2 writes f+H. EPO uses population/mutation/Pareto/restarts; seeded prompts improve fluency without significant steering loss. Models are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 3 4B, with layers 25/25/20 and K=20. Lower undesirable-option rates are better, but Section 4.2 calls 50% sycophancy perfect neutralization. Table 1 zero-shot sycophancy is 72.48/86/82; hallucination 51.45/45/57.97; myopic 54/55/58. RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy includes Gemma 62.65/70.70, conflicting with the claim both are indistinguishable from 50%. SAEGA preserves ~50–60 active features versus dense >150. Table 4 perplexities: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; caption calls all changes negligible, but Qwen rises ~14.7%. Random-direction ablation is claimed near/above zero-shot across all settings, but Table 5 is 68.29/54.26/84.70 versus zero-shot 51.45/45/57.97. Ablation claims task-loss objective underperforms in the majority; table broadly supports this. Conclusion claims significant sycophancy/myopic improvement, consistent hallucination improvement, superiority to manual/dense steering, and neutralization rather than distribution shift. Limitations: labeled examples required; SAE latents/vectors are model-specific; most effective prompts lack semantic coherence despite seeded prompts improving fluency. Broader-impact statement warns the pipeline could automate jailbreak discovery or harmful-output elicitation; no contradiction found.

final_notes:
Method: dense representation-difference vector or top-K SAE latent contrastive direction; suppression maximizes f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||. Fluency adds cross-entropy penalty Lλ=f−(λ/n)ΣH; Figure 2 instead writes L=f+H. Strong steering may be fragmented; fluency is self-cross-entropy/manifold proximity, not grammaticality. Natural-language seeds anchor higher-fluency regions; prompts are selected using held-out behavioral changes, with intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering and perplexity; stability is assessed across examples.

Experiments: Tasks B2R (sycophancy), U9K (TruthfulQA hallucination), D6V (myopic reward); lower is better. Models: C7N Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Table 1 B2R: QX2 49.86/50.63/62.65 and V7P 49.84/49.95/70.70 (C7N/W4X/F9S), conflicting with any claim that both methods achieve perfect neutralization across all models. QX2 average 45.83; V7P 46.44. V7P strongest C7N D6V; QX2 competitive U9K.

V7P is claimed to produce sparse, semantically grounded control unlike P8D; Figures 3–6 claim concentrated B2R neutrality, near-baseline SAE sparsity, selective feature suppression, and tight on-manifold trajectories. Table 3: every optimized prompt has a lower score than its seed. Table 4 perplexity: C7N 12.56→12.07, W4X 10.88→12.48, F9S 30.51→29.19; narrative calls changes negligible, but W4X rises about 15%. QX2 may exploit label priming/induction heads, while V7P often uses reasoning fragments and vocabulary shift.

Current findings: V7P B2R suppresses “Yes,” “True,” and “Agree,” upweighting “However”/“But”; D6V methods upweight “Future,” “Long,” “Wait.” K3Y, E8U, and M5A generally underperform QX2/V7P; M5A exceptions: better than QX2 and V7P on B2R F9S, equal to QX2 on U9K C7N.

Conclusion/limitations: future work includes semi-supervised reduction of labels, cross-model transfer, and multi-persona steering. QX2/V7P require examples exhibiting and lacking the target persona; SAE latents and vectors are model-specific. Most effective prompts are said to lack semantic coherence, while stronger linguistic priors may improve human-likeness. Pipeline is intended for safety but could automate jailbreaks or harmful outputs.

steps.notes_before: Method: construct persona vectors either as dense representation differences, v_repr = mean(D+) − mean(D−), or as a top-K SAE latent contrastive direction, v_SAE = sum_i w_i(ā_i+ − ā_i−), with ReLU SAE activations. The suppression target v is in activation space; D+ exhibits the persona and D− lacks it. J4Z uses N8C, an evolutionary gradient-guided search maintaining M candidates at different fluency weights, proposing top-k gradient token substitutions, evaluating candidates, and periodically restarting all but the best candidate. The steering objective is f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, with e(t) the last-token target-layer representation; maximizing f moves away from the persona direction. Fluency optimization adds a cross-entropy penalty: Lλ=f−(λ/n)ΣH(next-token prediction), so lower-probability sequences are penalized. (Figure 2 caption inconsistently writes L=f+H.) Strongest-steering prompts may be fragmented or incoherent. Fluency is self-cross-entropy/manifold proximity, not grammaticality; no hard threshold is imposed. Natural-language seeds (e.g., “Please answer honestly” for B2R) anchor higher-fluency regions. Prompts are selected using changes in target behavioral metrics on held-out validation inputs; intermediate-frontier prompts balance steering and moderate perplexity increases, and stability is assessed across diverse examples.

errors.claim: “Across every model, our analysis finds that dense steering preserves fewer active SAE features than SAEGA.”
errors.evidence: The later summary states there are “approximately 50 baseline active features, beyond 150 under dense steering, and 50–60 under SAEGA.”
errors.explanation: This evidence indicates that dense steering produces more active SAE features than SAEGA, not fewer, contradicting the claim that it preserves fewer across every model.

errors.claim: Figure 2 caption: fluent gradient ascent uses the objective \(L_{\lambda}(\mathbf{t})=f(\mathbf{t})+H(\mathbf{t})\).

errors.explanation: The figure caption uses an unweighted plus sign, whereas the formal objective subtracts a weighted cross-entropy term. These objectives have opposite effects when maximizing, so the caption is inconsistent with the method definition.

final_notes: Earlier results: Table 1 sycophancy: RESGA 49.86, 50.63, 62.65 and SAEGA 49.84, 49.95, 70.70 (Llama, Qwen, Gemma); Gemma contradicts claim that both are indistinguishable from 50%. Claim that both consistently improve hallucination and myopic reward over baselines is contradicted for Qwen hallucination: RESGA 41.46 and SAEGA 40.85 are worse than Standard Prompt 34.78 and Dense Steering 36.96. SAEGA has best Llama myopic-reward score (31.50). Hallucination: RESGA 45.12, 41.46, 51.22; SAEGA 46.95, 40.85, 49.14. Dense steering activates >150 SAE features versus baseline ~50 and SAEGA 50–60, conflicting with claims that dense steering preserves fewer active features than SAEGA. Mechanistically, SAEGA collapses sycophancy-axis variance near zero; dense steering and RESGA shift means while retaining variance. Figure 6: SAEGA is tight, stable, often orthogonal and on-manifold; Table 3 reports all six seed-to-optimized scores lower. Table 4 perplexities: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; negligible-change claim conflicts with Qwen increase. Table 5: Random/Mutation/Task Loss generally worse than RESGA/SAEGA; Task Loss better on Gemma sycophancy and ties SAEGA on Llama hallucination, so “worse in most settings” is qualified. Random Mutation’s Llama hallucination score (45.12) ties RESGA’s, so “consistently degrades” is too strong. Conclusion repeats contradicted claims that discovered prompts consistently improve hallucination and substantially outperform manual prompting/dense steering. Limitations: methods require labeled examples; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific and require retraining per target model; effective prompts often lack semantic coherence. Broader Impact says pipeline could target safety-critical latents for jailbreak/harmful-output elicitation and recommends access controls; no contradiction found. Acknowledgment reports Claude assistance and AI-assisted code generation; no contradiction found.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling behavioral personas in LLMs. It introduces RESGA (RESidual Gradient Ascent), using dense residual representations, and SAEGA (Sparse Autoencoder Gradient Ascent), using sparse autoencoder features. Both construct persona directions from contrasting examples and optimize prompts with a fluency constraint. Experiments cover sycophancy (agreement with an incorrect user opinion), hallucination (evaluated through TruthfulQA error), and myopic reward (short-term reward seeking over long-term outcomes) across Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5, and Gemma 3. The summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, though their comparison is not specified here. Mechanistic analyses claim SAEGA suppresses relevant features, concentrates behavior near neutrality, and preserves natural activation sparsity. Reported limitations include reliance on labeled data, model-specific steering directions, and prompt coherence.

The paper studies automatic prompt discovery for controlling LLM behavioral personas: sycophancy (agreeing with incorrect opinions), hallucination (TruthfulQA error; lower is better), and myopic reward (short-term over long-term outcomes), across Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, and Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Proposed methods are RESGA (dense residual-representation gradient ascent) and SAEGA (SAE-feature gradient ascent), using contrastive persona-exhibiting/free data and a fluency-constrained objective. Summary reports sycophancy improvement figures of 49.90% and 79.24%, but their comparison is unspecified.

Key definitions/formulas: D+ and D− are contrastive sets; v_repr is the mean activation difference; v_SAE uses top-K SAE encoder directions selected by activation differences. f(t) is a negative scaled projection onto the steering vector; L_lambda combines steering and self-cross-entropy fluency. EPO is a gradient-guided evolutionary prompt optimizer maintaining a population, Pareto tradeoffs, restarts, and gradient/random mutation; prompts can have random or seed initialization. Fluency is model self-cross-entropy, distinct from readability; validation tests stability and avoids degenerate solutions.

Baselines/ablations include Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GPT-4o ProTeGi, Random Direction, Task Loss as Objective, and random mutation. Evaluation uses conditional log-probability answer comparisons and reports error/behavioral rates; 50% sycophancy is neutrality. Mechanistic claims: SAEGA suppresses relevant features, produces near-neutral low-variance behavior, preserves natural SAE sparsity, and follows a trajectory distinct/orthogonal to dense steering; RESGA/SAEGA affect vocabulary (agreement suppression, pivots, long-term tokens). Limitations/future work: labeled-data reliance, model-specific transfer, prompt coherence, semi-supervision, cross-model transfer, multi-persona steering, linguistic priors; misuse could enable jailbreak discovery.

final_notes: Method learns individual-level stance alignment from survey tuples (persona, question, observed stance), with Yes/Neutral/No. GRPO uses fixed reasoning/answer format and rewards format, length, correctness; optional SFT warm-start uses same-format synthetic demonstrations. No explicit persona representation; only country label in system prompt, alignment learned through answering questions. Datasets: smartvote (CH), 18 candidates, binary labels, 48 train/12 topic-stratified test questions; WoM (DE), 6 parties, three labels, training counts in Appendix/Table 5 and 30 EU&I test questions; ANES 2020 (US), 21 respondents, three labels, 67 train/12 random test questions. Table 3 macro-F1: smartvote highest, WoM intermediate, ANES lowest; random 50/33.33/33.33; majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. Best listed SFT+GRPO: Magistral 70.73 smartvote, 53.21 WoM, 45.43 ANES. SFT+GRPO generally beats naive/SFT except Llama 3.1 8B ANES; GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO. Native reasoning does not consistently help, despite introduction claiming reasoning consistently improves alignment. Conclusion claims SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, Neutral stances remain difficult, and performance varies across political groups. Fig. 2: agents shift center-right/conservative overall; Right individuals become more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Fig. 3: Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO shows Left outperforming Center/Right on smartvote; WoM Left/Center roughly equal and ANES weaker. SFT outperforms other methods for Right groups on smartvote and ANES. errors.claim: "Our research reveals systematic performance disparities across ideological groups, with consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles"
errors.evidence: The notes state that in WoM, "Left/Center [are] roughly equal," and that SFT is "strongest for Right in smartvote and ANES."
errors.explanation: The paper's earlier results do not support consistent underperformance of center profiles: WoM Left and Center perform roughly equally. Right-wing performance is also not uniformly lowest across settings, since SFT is strongest for Right in smartvote and ANES.

final_notes:
Experiments use WoM DE, ANES 2020 US, and smartvote CH. WoM uses six German parties, three labels, aggregated 2021–2025 items; tests on 30 EU&I out-of-domain questions. ANES has 79 policy items (67 train/12 test) and 21 respondents. smartvote has 60 binary policy items, 18 candidates, and a 48-train/12-test split. Parties/respondents are grouped Left/Center/Right.

Table 3 mean macro-F1 (%), 8 runs, T=1: SFT+GRPO generally leads. Llama combo: 66.88/52.53/40.66, with Right below SFT (42.77); Qwen: 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral: 70.73/53.21/45.43. SFT+GRPO exceeds SFT in all other listed group/model comparisons.

Agents shift center-right/more conservative (negative y), with no clear overall left-right bias. Smartvote Left F1 clearly exceeds Center/Right; WoM Left/Center are roughly equal; ANES is generally lower. SFT is strongest for Right in smartvote and ANES. Neutral is hardest, especially ANES; removing Neutral improves all groups but leaves a Left–Right gap. Progressive bias harms Right without consistent Left benefit; conservative bias harms Left without consistent Right benefit; adverse bias impairs Right more severely. Figure 6 suggests conservative-biased/default displacement, mainly base-model alignment. Inverting smartvote answers benefits Right, worsens Left/Center; inverted Right remains below original Left and inverted Left falls roughly to original Right, suggesting Left profiles are intrinsically easier. Figure 7 says Right and Center are harder than Left: after flipping, Left worsens and Right improves but remains worse on average.

Ethics statement claims consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles, conflicting with roughly equal WoM Left/Center performance and with SFT being strongest for Right in smartvote and ANES.

Final reproducibility statement says code and datasets are released at the cited GitHub repository; training details are in Appendix F and PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions and acknowledgments contain no internally checkable contradictions.

errors.claim: “ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties and U.S. voters.”
errors.evidence: Earlier results note: “ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C”; on M8C and J4Q it is only “comparable to or better than H3D.”
errors.explanation: The conclusion’s unqualified claim that ZP4 outperforms all baselines across the benchmark conflicts with the reported T9A-on-M8C exception and with cases where it is merely comparable to H3D.

final_notes: Results: ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; it is comparable to or better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q scores highest, likely because it uses binary answers without Neutral; R2V exceeds M8C, likely due to more training samples. Native reasoning gives no consistent gain: T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E performs best overall, and QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting supervised initialization helps. Neutral-containing datasets perform worse. ZP4 generally works best, but all methods underperform on centrist and right-leaning groups. J4Q has a strong P7N advantage; R2V P7N/A4U are roughly equal and M8C is weaker. V7K is highest for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall is worst for every M8C individual; X8J has the highest Neutral rate and greatest difficulty. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U differences, and improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but does not remove P7N–X8J differences. Representation: no overall left shift; agents shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically, with overall conservative/negative-y distortion. X8J shifts left; P7N/A4U shift right and conservative. Initialization-data bias mainly harms underrepresented perspectives, especially X8J; progressive data harms X8J, conservative data harms P7N. Synthetic inversion of J4Q answers and training T9A on inverted train/test data approximately rotates positions 180°; it benefits X8J but harms P7N/A4U. P7N worsens individually and on average; inverted X8J improves but remains below P7N, so converting P7N into X8J does not remove the disparity. Discussion limitations: same-respondent day-to-day variation adds noise, so near-1.0 F1 is unlikely; per-profile training is computationally intensive; suitable surveys are scarce, often too short and focused on generic themes, and question sets rarely align across countries. Future work proposes bias mitigation, persona-conditioned models to reduce computation/improve data use, confidence estimates via extended reasoning or a value head, and purpose-built questionnaires/uncertainty handling to address Neutral difficulties. Conclusion claims ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters, but this overstates the results because of the T9A/M8C exception and H3D comparability. Ethics warns of ideological disparities.
