steps.notes_before: Results: ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K baselines across datasets except T9A on M8C; it is comparable to or better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q scores highest, likely because it uses binary answers without Neutral; R2V exceeds M8C, likely due to more training samples. Native reasoning gives no consistent gain: T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E performs best overall, and QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting supervised initialization helps. Neutral-containing datasets perform worse. ZP4 generally works best, but all methods underperform on centrist and right-leaning groups. J4Q has a strong P7N advantage; R2V P7N/A4U are roughly equal and M8C is weaker. V7K is highest for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall is worst for every M8C individual; X8J has the highest Neutral rate and greatest difficulty. Removing Neutral improves all groups, narrows P7N–A4U differences, and improves ZP4 relative to H3D, but does not remove P7N–X8J differences. Representation: no overall left shift; agents shift center-right horizontally and centerward vertically, with overall conservative/negative-y distortion. X8J shifts left; P7N/A4U shift right and conservative. Initialization-data bias mainly harms underrepresented perspectives, especially X8J; progressive data harms X8J, conservative data harms P7N. Synthetic inversion of J4Q answers and training T9A on inverted train/test data approximately rotates positions 180°; it benefits X8J but harms P7N/A4U. P7N worsens individually and on average; inverted X8J improves but remains below P7N, so converting P7N into X8J does not remove the disparity. Discussion limitations: same-respondent day-to-day variation adds noise, so near-1.0 F1 is unlikely; per-profile training is computationally intensive; suitable surveys are scarce, often too short and focused on generic themes, and question sets rarely align across countries. final_notes: Method: individual-level survey stance prediction using GRPO with formatted reasoning/answer outputs. Rewards: format (max 4), length penalty, correctness; weights alpha1=.25, alpha2=.01, alpha3=1. Optional SFT warm starts precede GRPO. Datasets: smartvote CH (18 candidates, 48 train/12 topic-stratified test policy questions); WoM DE (6 parties, Yes/Neutral/No, 30 EU&I OOD test); ANES 2020 (79 items, 67 train/12 test, 21 respondents, conservative/aggressive 3-class recodings). Table 3 macro-F1: Magistral SFT+GRPO smartvote/WoM/ANES 70.73/53.21/45.43; Llama 66.88/52.53/40.66; Qwen 65.11/49.38/38.44. SFT+GRPO generally best, except Llama ANES where SFT is higher (42.77(1.23) vs 40.66). Warm start beats GRPO alone. Smartvote highest, ANES lowest; neutral-class datasets harder. PCA groups Left/Center/Right. Left exceeds Center/Right clearly on smartvote; weaker elsewhere. Neutral recall is worst for every ANES individual; Right has highest Neutral base rate. Removing Neutral improves F1 but not Left–Right gap; alternative recoding makes Center and Right nearly identical. F1/accuracy negatively correlate with Neutral base rate; removing Neutral narrows Left–Center gap but preserves Left–Right gap. Results use Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. Figures 2 and 6: Right individuals shift leftward more strongly; Left/Center shift rightward and conservative; no overall left shift. Bias mainly harms underrepresented groups. Conservative-biased/default SFT patterns are similar. Section 4.9/Figure 7: flipping all smartvote answers approximately rotates positions 180 degrees; worsens Left, improves Right, but Right still has lower average F1 than Left. Right positions may be intrinsically harder to learn; disparity is not removed by converting Left to Right. The left-most Right candidate is correctly placed. Conclusion: structured reasoning improves alignment, but Neutral and ideological disparities remain; SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with explicit Llama ANES SFT exception. Ethics statement cautions against deployment until ideological fairness problems are resolved, citing underperformance on center/right profiles and difficulty modeling neutral positions. Reproducibility statement claims code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation details are publicly available via the project GitHub repository, with training details in Appendix F and PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions and acknowledgments contain no claims that conflict with recorded content.

The paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. Group-relative policy optimization rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start. Experiments involve Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. Models generate a reasoning trace and final stance; GRPO rewards formatting, desired reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers, while SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data harms the underrepresented perspective. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 Time Series (79 U.S. policy items; respondent models), German Wahl-O-Mat (six parties: CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), EU&I 2024 as German out-of-domain test, and Swiss smartvote 2023 (candidate models; topic-stratified split). Labels are Yes/Neutral/No; Swiss four-point responses are collapsed to Yes/No. Metrics include per-unit macro-F1, accuracy, recall, and standard deviations across eight runs.

Methods/backbones: GRPO is PPO-related and normalizes rewards within groups without a learned value function; SFT+GRPO is the warm-start method. Evaluated open-weight backbones are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization for training. Synthetic arguments use Llama 3.1 70B by default and Llama 3.3 70B for progressive/conservative bias tests.

Key analyses include PCA of candidate/agent positions, counterfactual answer inversion (approximately 180° rotation), demographic/persona prompting, and political distortion. Reward notation: R_format, R_length = negative absolute length error, R_correct, total R(r_i,y_i*); x_i is reasoning trace, y_i predicted answer, y_i* ground truth.

Datasets include ANES (U.S.), German Wahl-O-Mat party profiles, EU&I 2024 out-of-domain testing, and Swiss smartvote candidate profiles. GRPO rewards formatted reasoning, desired length, and agreement with survey answers; SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally improves alignment, but not consistently: the paper explicitly acknowledges a Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception. It claims reasoning improves alignment overall, with evidence in Table 3, while ideological effects and answer inversion are analyzed in Figures 3 and 7. The method trains an agent to produce a rationale and final choice matching respondent answers on unseen questions. Contributions claim benchmarking German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates, and analysis of ideological effects via inverted survey answers. Models include Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B; synthetic data generally uses Llama 3.1 70B.

Related work distinguishes demographic, character, and individualized personas. Demographic methods use affiliations, demographics, demonstrations, and preference optimization, but face representativeness, steerability, consistency, subgroup accuracy, and prompt-sensitivity limitations. Few studies model individualized profiles: Park et al. use interview transcripts; Haller et al. use in-context respondent QA pairs mainly for bias identification. Table 1 gives a Llama 3.1 8B ANES Right-group example: before training the answer is No; after SFT+GRPO the answer is Yes, with reasoning invoking inevitable inequality, incentives, and basic opportunities. The paper describes reasoning via prompting, search, and RL, and explains GRPO as group-normalized PPO without a value function. Prior opinion-alignment reasoning work (Yu et al.) uses persona-based chain-of-thought prompting calibrated with ANES for aggregate voting prediction.

Related work distinguishes demographic, character, and individualized personas. Demographic methods use affiliations, demographics, demonstrations, and preference optimization, but face representativeness, steerability, consistency, subgroup accuracy, and prompt-sensitivity limitations. Park et al. use interview transcripts and can outperform demographic baselines; Haller et al. use in-context respondent QA pairs mainly for bias identification. Prior work by Yu et al. targets aggregate voting prediction with persona-based chain-of-thought prompting calibrated with ANES, rather than RL; the present method targets general preference profiles. Table 1 gives a Llama 3.1 8B ANES Right-group example: before training the answer is No; after SFT+GRPO the answer is Yes, with reasoning invoking inevitable inequality, incentives, and basic opportunities. The paper also cites Wei et al., Kojima et al., and Guo et al. for improvements from prompted/trained reasoning. Modeling a representative sample for voting prediction is described as computationally prohibitive.

The method learns individual-level survey stances using GRPO, with outputs required in the format <reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Data are persona-question-observed stance triples; personas may be respondents or political parties, and the system prompt includes only a country label, with alignment coming from answers rather than an explicit persona representation. Rewards are format (four tags, max 4), length (-|L-L*|, max 0), and correctness (1 for matching the survey answer), weighted alpha1=.25, alpha2=.01, alpha3=1. Optional SFT supplies formatted chain-of-thought warm starts before GRPO. Table 2: smartvote CH has 18 candidates, binary labels, 48 train and 12 topic-stratified test questions; WoM DE has 6 parties, Yes/Neutral/No labels, training count in Table 5 and 30 EU&I test questions; ANES 2020 US has 21 respondents, three labels, 67 train and 12 random test questions. No internal contradiction found in this part.

Table 3 reports macro-F1 (per-unit macro-F1 averaged across units), over 8 runs at T=1.0; figures use F1. Results generally show smartvote highest, WoM above ANES, and SFT+GRPO usually strongest. Magistral SFT+GRPO: smartvote 70.73, WoM 53.21, ANES 45.43; Llama SFT+GRPO: 66.88, 52.53, 40.66; Qwen SFT+GRPO: 65.11, 49.38, 38.44. No internal contradiction found in this part.

Political groups are assigned Left/Center/Right. PCA’s first two components define position space: x is left-right, y conservative-liberal. final_notes:
Discussion limitations: opinion noise makes perfect F1 unlikely; per-profile training is costly; few or mismatched surveys limit individualized learning and cross-country comparison. Future work proposes shared models with compact personas, confidence/reliability estimates (e.g., reasoning scheme or value head), better questionnaires, uncertainty handling, and Neutral mitigation. Figure 7: F1 scores on original data, individuals ordered by smartvote PCA first component; left-most Right candidate is correctly placed (Fig. 6). Flipping all train/test answers worsens Left candidates and improves Right candidates, but Right still performs worse on average than Left candidates; disparity remains and may suggest Right positions are harder to learn. Figure discussion labels learning Right and Center harder than Left, though detailed claims focus on Right.

Conclusion: Structured reasoning improves individual opinion alignment, but Neutral and ideological disparities remain. Across Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters, SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; explicit Llama ANES exception: SFT 42.77(1.23) versus SFT+GRPO 40.66 (reported formatting malformed). Neutral stances are difficult, and accuracy varies across the political spectrum. Evidence: Tables 3 and Figures 3–4; Figure 4 performance–Neutral correlations significant at 5%.

Ethics: warns against deployment before ideological fairness problems are resolved. Uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions. Claims systematic underperformance on center and right-wing profiles and difficulty modeling neutral positions; cites Figure 3 ideology groups and Figure 4 top-right recall/performance–Neutral regressions. Premature deployment may disenfranchise viewpoints; biased models could undermine democratic representation.

Final reproducibility statement says code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation details are available; code/datasets repository linked, Appendix F gives training details, and Section E.5 describes PCA results. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed project and led planning/direction; Billeter contributed equally and led technical development, collection, training, evaluation, analysis; Vonlanthen advised; Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledgment thanks Hans Gersbach.

It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to generate a reasoning trace and final answer matching survey responses. GRPO rewards formatting, reasoning length, and correctness; SFT can provide a warm start, yielding SFT+GRPO. Experiments use Swiss smartvote candidates, German parties from Wahl-O-Mat, and U.S. respondents from ANES 2020 (79 items). German models are tested out of domain on EU&I (30 items); Swiss data use topic-stratified splits. Evaluated backbones include Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization and 8 stochastic runs at T=1.0. Baselines include random and majority; performance is reported mainly with macro-F1 and accuracy. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict; performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully eliminate bias. Key definitions: Y is the stance set; q_i is a question; p_j is a persona; y* is the observed stance; x is the reasoning trace; L is its length; rewards combine formatting, length, and correctness. Smartvote PCA uses left-right and conservative-liberal axes; counterfactual inversion flips answers and produces an approximately 180-degree rotation.

final_notes: Experiments: Table 3 reports macro-F1 means/SDs over 8 stochastic runs at T=1.0 for J4Q (Swiss), R2V (German), and M8C (U.S.). C6W/U9F are untrained baselines; H3D contextual ICL; N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters; V7K SFT warm start; QX2 GRPO; ZP4 SFT+GRPO. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B, K6Y=Qwen3 8B, W2E=Magistral 24B; latter two are reasoning-pretrained. All experiments use 4-bit quantization. R2V has six German parties and Yes/Neutral/No labels; B5X is out-of-domain EU&I. M8C/ANES 2020 has 79 items, with I7V conservative or O2K aggressive mappings; three respondents per answer option on a 7-point ideology item. J4Q/Smartvote 2023 has 75 items, 60 policy questions, binary Yes/No after collapsing four-point responses, and 18 candidates (3 each from six parties), with one question per topic held out. Spectrum groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right. Forty-seven models are trained, one per candidate/party/respondent. Results: ZP4 generally beats baselines except T9A on M8C; it is comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q is easiest, M8C hardest, and R2V exceeds M8C. T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E is best overall; QX2 trails ZP4. Training methods underperform on centrist/right groups versus left; V7K exceeds other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall is worst for every M8C individual; X8J has highest Neutral rate. Removing Neutral improves all groups and ZP4 relative to H3D. Representation shifts center-right horizontally and centerward vertically, with no overall left shift. Biased initialization harms underrepresented perspectives, especially X8J; inversion benefits X8J but does not erase the left/right learnability gap. Counterfactual inversion flips every J4Q answer, approximately rotates positions 180°; P7N worsens, X8J improves but remains below P7N, and converting P7N to X8J does not remove disparity. Discussion limitations include respondent variation, computational cost, and survey limitations. Future work proposes bias mitigation, persona-conditioned models, confidence estimates, purpose-built questionnaires, and improved uncertainty handling. Conclusion: ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across all three datasets. Abstract claims that structured reasoning trained through reinforcement learning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; remains competitive with strong baselines; and still leaves bias requiring additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. The work releases methods and datasets and frames opinion models as potentially useful for shaping fairer, more popular policies.

Abstract claims that structured reasoning trained through reinforcement learning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics; remains competitive with strong baselines; and still leaves bias requiring additional mechanisms for faithful political digital twins. The work releases methods and datasets and frames opinion models as potentially useful for shaping fairer, more popular policies.

Introduction says reasoning improves opinion alignment: survey-trained agents generate rationales and choices, receiving rewards for matching respondents’ answers and learning survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Digital twins require accurate political-behavior simulation, while demographic/affiliation prompting is unstable and misses real distributions. Preference consistency uses known individual opinions; interviews provide strong persona performance but are costly. Surveys and Voting Advice Applications capture structured population opinions but have limited adoption for individual-agent training.

Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; a benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; and answer-inversion analysis showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Figure 1 describes initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements/ground-truth answers to establish a reasoning template, followed by QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards to improve reasoning.

errors.claim: “Our results show that reasoning consistently improves alignment.”
errors.location: This part, Contributions, “Benchmarking on real-world political data”
errors.evidence: The same part states: “the Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception is discussed in Section 4.3.” The earlier notes likewise record that SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, “with exceptions.”
errors.explanation: The claim of consistent improvement conflicts with the explicitly acknowledged Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception.

errors.claim: “We train 47 models, one per candidate, party, or respondent.”
errors.evidence: The paper’s dataset counts are 18 smartvote candidates, 6 Wahl-o-Mat parties, and 21 ANES respondents, for a total of 45 units (18 + 6 + 21 = 45).

The paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. Group-relative policy optimization rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start. Experiments involve Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. Models generate a reasoning trace and final stance; GRPO rewards formatting, desired reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers, while SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data harms the underrepresented perspective. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 Time Series (79 U.S. policy items; respondent models), German Wahl-O-Mat (six parties: CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), EU&I 2024 as German out-of-domain test, and Swiss smartvote 2023 (candidate models; topic-stratified split). Labels are Yes/Neutral/No; Swiss four-point responses are collapsed to Yes/No. Metrics include per-unit macro-F1, accuracy, recall, and standard deviations across eight runs.

Methods/backbones: GRPO is PPO-related and normalizes rewards within groups without a learned value function; SFT+GRPO is the warm-start method. Evaluated open-weight backbones are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization for training. Synthetic arguments use Llama 3.1 70B by default and Llama 3.3 70B for progressive/conservative bias tests.

Key analyses include PCA of candidate/agent positions, counterfactual answer inversion (approximately 180° rotation), demographic/persona prompting, and political distortion. Reward notation: R_format, R_length = negative absolute length error, R_correct, total R(r_i,y_i*); x_i is reasoning trace, y_i predicted answer, y_i* ground truth.

final_notes: Method learns individual-level stance alignment from survey tuples (persona, question, observed Yes/Neutral/No stance). GRPO uses fixed reasoning/answer format and rewards format, length, and correctness (weights .25/.01/1); optional SFT warm-start uses same format. No explicit persona representation; country label only in system prompt. Datasets: smartvote (CH; 18 candidates; binary labels; 48 train/12 test), WoM (DE; 6 parties; three labels; 30 EU&I test questions), ANES 2020 (US; 21 respondents; three labels; 67 train/12 test; default conservative recoding, aggressive robustness). Table 3 macro-F1: smartvote generally highest, WoM intermediate, ANES lowest; best SFT+GRPO Magistral: 70.73/53.21/45.43. Earlier text incorrectly says ANES peaks and smartvote is hardest. Caption attributes smartvote advantage to binary labels/no Neutral and WoM advantage over ANES to more training samples. SFT+GRPO generally best except Llama on ANES; reasoning backbones do not consistently help; Neutral classes lower performance; center/right groups underperform. Fig. 2: agents shift toward center-right on x-axis and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis; no overall left shift. Group averages: Right becomes more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Fig. 3: smartvote Left vs Center/Right disparity; WoM weaker; ANES generally lower. final_notes: Table 3 methods: C6W is random; U9F predicts the unit-training-set majority; H3D is contextual ICL using same-topic question–answer pairs (or a random subset under context limits); N8R uses Stammbach et al. hyperparameters. ZP4 generally outperforms naive and V7K baselines, except T9A on M8C; it is comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q binary answers yield considerably higher scores than M8C/R2V; R2V may benefit from more training samples. Text says M8C peaks highest and J4Q is hardest, a possible ranking inconsistency. T9A exceeds K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 alone trails ZP4, suggesting SFT initialization helps. Neutral datasets perform worse. Figure 3: ZP4 typically best; all methods underperform on centrist/right groups. Reasoning is generally coherent but can hallucinate or be inconsistent across topics. Ideology: J4Q P7N outperforms A4U/X8J; R2V weaker and P7N/A4U roughly equal; V7K exceeds other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall is worst for every M8C individual; X8J has highest Neutral rate and greatest difficulty. Removing Neutral improves F1 and narrows group differences but does not eliminate P7N–X8J differences. Agents shift center/right and centerward vertically; X8J becomes more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right/conservative. Biased initialization harms underrepresented groups, especially X8J. Inverting synthetic positions benefits X8J but harms P7N/A4U; remaining asymmetry may indicate intrinsically easier left profiles. Flipping every J4Q answer approximately rotates positions 180°; T9A is trained on flipped data and evaluated on original/flipped test answers. P7N worsens individually/on average; X8J improves but remains below P7N average. Limitations include respondent variation, computational intensity, scarce/misaligned surveys. Conclusion: ZP4 generally outperforms baselines across Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters; Neutral prediction is difficult and political-spectrum accuracy varies. Ethics warns of ideological disparities, centrist/right underperformance, Neutral difficulty, and premature deployment; advocates transparency and bias mitigation before real-world use. Reproducibility statement says code/datasets are released at the listed GitHub repository, with documentation covering training details, hyperparameters, PCA implementation/results, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, sample-size analysis, and inversion details. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed and led planning/direction; Billeter led technical

The paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. Group-relative policy optimization rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start. Experiments involve Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. Models generate a reasoning trace and final stance; GRPO rewards formatting, desired reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers, while SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data harms the underrepresented perspective. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 Time Series (79 U.S. policy items; respondent models), German Wahl-O-Mat (six parties: CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), EU&I 2024 as German out-of-domain test, and Swiss smartvote 2023 (candidate models; topic-stratified split). Labels are Yes/Neutral/No; Swiss four-point responses are collapsed to Yes/No. Metrics include per-unit macro-F1, accuracy, recall, and standard deviations across eight runs.

Methods/backbones: GRPO is PPO-related and normalizes rewards within groups without a learned value function; SFT+GRPO is the warm-start method. Evaluated open-weight backbones are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization for training. Synthetic arguments use Llama 3.1 70B by default and Llama 3.3 70B for progressive/conservative bias tests.

Key analyses include PCA of candidate/agent positions, counterfactual answer inversion (approximately 180° rotation), demographic/persona prompting, and political distortion. final_notes: The paper claims structured reasoning trained through RL produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, and Swiss politics, remains competitive with strong baselines, and still has bias requiring further mechanisms. It argues reasoning improves opinion alignment: survey-trained agents generate rationales and choices, receive rewards for matching respondents, and learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Digital twins need accurate political-behavior simulation; demographic/affiliation prompting is unstable, interviews are costly, and surveys/VAAs have limited adoption for individual-agent training. Contributions include QX2-based explicit reasoning, benchmarks of German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions, and answer-inversion analysis showing ideological variation in alignment quality. Figure 1 uses synthetic-statement fine-tuning for a reasoning template, followed by QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards. errors.claim: “Our results show that reasoning consistently improves alignment.”

errors.evidence: The same part states: “the Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception is discussed in Section 4.3.” The earlier notes likewise record that SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, “with exceptions.”
errors.explanation: The claim of consistent improvement conflicts with the explicitly acknowledged Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception.

errors.claim: “Every training method underperforms on center and right-leaning groups.”
errors.evidence: Section 4.5 states: “On smartvote, Center and Right clearly outperform Left.” It also states that “For Right in smartvote and ANES, SFT also outperforms every other method on average.”
errors.explanation: The broad Figure 3 summary says all methods underperform for Center and Right, but the later detailed interpretation says Center and Right outperform Left on smartvote and that SFT is best for Right in smartvote and ANES.

errors.claim: “Learning Right and Center positions is harder than Left ones.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Section 4.5 notes that on smartvote, Center and Right outperform Left; specifically, “smartvote Center/Right outperform Left.”
errors.explanation: The broad claim that both Right and Center positions are harder to learn than Left conflicts with the reported smartvote results, where Center and Right achieve better performance than Left. The Figure 7 evidence described here directly supports only a remaining Right-versus-Left disparity, not the claim about Center.

errors.claim: “We find systematic ideological performance disparities: consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Section 4.5 smartvote results report that Center and Right outperform Left. The notes also record that the paper states “Learning Right and Center positions is harder than Left ones,” conflicting with those smartvote results.
errors.explanation: The ethics statement presents center and right underperformance as a general finding, but the reported smartvote results show Center and Right performing better than Left, so the broad claim is inconsistent with the paper’s own results.

final_notes: Discussion limitations: opinion noise, per-profile training/computational cost, scarce or mismatched surveys, and few individuals/parties constrain results. Future work proposes compact persona-conditioned models, confidence/reliability estimates, value heads, better questionnaires, uncertainty handling, and bias mitigation/Neutral handling. Figure 7: flipping all train/test answers worsens Left candidates and improves Right candidates, but Right still performs worse on average than original Left; remaining disparity may suggest Right positions are harder to learn. The text claims “Learning Right and Center positions is harder than Left ones,” conflicting with Section 4.5 smartvote results, where Center and Right outperform Left. Figure 7 notes the left-most Right candidate is correctly placed and uses original F1 points plus post-flip changes. Conclusion claims structured reasoning improves alignment, with SFT+GRPO generally outperforming baselines across Swiss smartvote, German Wahl-o-Mat, and U.S. ANES, while noting the Llama ANES exception (SFT 42.77 > SFT+GRPO 40.66), uneven performance, and Neutral difficulty. It claims Neutral and ideological disparities remain, citing Figures 3–4 and significant 5% performance–Neutral correlations. Ethics statement warns against deployment, cites systematic underperformance on center/right profiles and difficulty with Neutral positions, and identifies Figures 3 and 4 as evidence; its broad center/right underperformance claim conflicts with the smartvote results. Reproducibility statement says code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation details are available; Appendix F gives training details and Section E.5 describes PCA results. Author contributions and acknowledgments contain no substantive empirical claims.

errors.claim: “Our results show that reasoning consistently improves alignment.”
errors.location: This part, Contributions, “Benchmarking on real-world political data”
errors.evidence: The same part states: “the Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception is discussed in Section 4.3.” The earlier notes likewise record that SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, “with exceptions.”
errors.explanation: The claim of consistent improvement conflicts with the explicitly acknowledged Llama 3.1 8B ANES exception.

errors.claim: “Every training method underperforms on center and right-leaning groups.”
errors.evidence: Section 4.5 states: “On Wahl-o-Mat, Left and Center perform roughly equally.”
errors.explanation: If Center underperforms means it has lower F1 than Left, the claim that every method underperforms on Center conflicts with the later statement that Left and Center perform roughly equally on Wahl-o-Mat.

errors.claim: Section 4.8 states that biased SFT data affects “Right [candidates] more strongly than Left,” while also stating that “Left candidates suffer more from adverse bias than Right candidates.”
errors.evidence: The section says: “Ideological SFT bias mainly harms and shifts underrepresented groups, especially Right candidates” and “biased data mainly shifts underrepresented groups, again affecting Right more strongly than Left.” It later says: “Left candidates suffer more from adverse bias than Right candidates.”
errors.explanation: These claims directly disagree about which group is more affected by adverse or biased SFT data.

errors.claim: “Right is more strongly harmed and shifted” and “Right candidates are again affected more strongly than Left candidates.”
errors.evidence: The earlier notes record that Section 4.8 also claims that “Left suffers more,” creating an opposing comparison of the groups’ harm.
errors.explanation: The paper gives incompatible conclusions about which group is more strongly affected: this part consistently says Right, while the earlier Section 4.8 claim says Left.

final_notes:
Method: individual-level stance prediction with GRPO; outputs use <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Rewards include format (max 4), length penalty, and correctness (alpha1=.25, alpha2=.01, alpha3=1); optional SFT warm starts precede GRPO. Datasets: smartvote CH (18 candidates, 48 train/12 topic-stratified test policy questions), WoM DE (6 parties, Yes/Neutral/No, 30 EU&I OOD test), ANES 2020 (79 items, 67 train/12 test, 21 respondents; conservative/aggressive 3-class recodings). Table 3: Magistral/Llama/Qwen SFT+GRPO macro-F1 on smartvote 70.73/66.88/65.11, WoM 53.21/52.53/49.38, ANES 45.43/40.66/38.44; Llama ANES SFT is higher (42.77). Warm starts generally beat GRPO alone.

PCA groups Left/Center/Right. Right individuals move leftward; Left/Center move rightward/conservative; no clear left-right bias. Neutral recall is worst for every ANES individual; Right has highest Neutral base rate. Removing Neutral improves F1 but preserves Left–Right gap; alternative recoding makes Center and Right nearly identical. F1/accuracy negatively correlate with Neutral base rate; removing Neutral preserves gap. Biased SFT harms the opposing ideological group; Section 4.8 has unresolved wording about whether Right is affected more or Left suffers more. Figure 6 says Right is more strongly harmed/shifted than Left.

Flipping all smartvote answers approximately rotates positions 180 degrees. Right improves, Left/Center worsen; post-flip Right remains below Left’s original F1, while Left drops roughly to Right’s original level. Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with explicit Llama ANES exception (SFT 42.77 vs SFT+GRPO 40.66); Neutral and ideological disparities remain. Figure 4 correlations are stated in conclusion to be significant at 5%.

Ethics statement: warns against deployment before ideological fairness problems are resolved; reports consistent performance disparities for Center and Right profiles and difficulty modeling Neutral positions. Claims evidence from Figure 3 (ideology groups) and Figure 4 (Neutral recall and performance–Neutral regressions). Uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions.

Reproducibility statement says code, datasets, training details, and PCA implementation details are available via the cited GitHub repository; Appendix F gives training details and Section E.5 describes PCA results. Author contributions: Berdoz project design/direction; Billeter equal contribution and technical development/data/training/evaluation/analysis; Vonlanthen advisor; Wattenhofer PI supervision. Acknowledgments thank Hans Gersbach.

The paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. Group-relative policy optimization rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start. Experiments involve Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. Models generate a reasoning trace and final stance; GRPO rewards formatting, desired reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers, while SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data harms the underrepresented perspective. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 Time Series (79 U.S. policy items; respondent models), German Wahl-O-Mat (six parties: CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), EU&I 2024 as German out-of-domain test, and Swiss smartvote 2023 (candidate models; topic-stratified split). Labels are Yes/Neutral/No; Swiss four-point responses are collapsed to Yes/No. Metrics include per-unit macro-F1, accuracy, recall, and standard deviations across eight runs.

Methods/backbones: GRPO is PPO-related and normalizes rewards within groups without a learned value function; SFT+GRPO is the warm-start method. Evaluated open-weight backbones are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization for training. Synthetic arguments use Llama 3.1 70B by default and Llama 3.3 70B for progressive/conservative bias tests.

Key analyses include PCA of candidate/agent positions, counterfactual answer inversion (approximately 180° rotation), demographic/persona prompting, and political distortion. Reward notation: R_format, R_length = negative absolute length error, R_correct, total R(r_i,y_i*); x_i is reasoning trace, y_i predicted answer, y_i* ground truth.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. final_notes: The paper studies individual-level opinion alignment/modeling using survey-based preference profiles for German parties, U.S. voters, and Swiss candidates, aiming to create political digital twins. It uses GRPO with format, reasoning-length, and correctness rewards; only country is in the system prompt and no explicit persona representation is provided. SFT may precede GRPO. Table 3: smartvote generally scores highest, WoM above ANES; Llama 3.1 8B GRPO on smartvote (55.14) is below ICL (55.97), so reasoning does not consistently improve alignment. SFT+GRPO generally beats naive/SFT baselines except Llama on ANES; peak score 70.73 on smartvote, ANES hardest at 45.43. Magistral is best overall; neutral classes are harder; center/right groups less learnable. Agents may hallucinate, reason illogically, or fail to maintain stance. Figures 2–6: agents shift center-right on the left-right axis and toward center on conservative-liberal; Left/Center become more right-wing/conservative, Right more left-wing, with no overall left shift. Neutral recall is worst on ANES; removing Neutral improves all groups but leaves a Left–Right gap. Progressive SFT bias harms Right, conservative bias harms Left, without consistently benefiting the opposite group; Right is more adversely affected. Conservative-biased and default SFT produce similar PCA shifts, suggesting base-model alignment drives centerward movement. Inversion results are internally inconsistent: an earlier account says inversion helps Left and harms Right, whereas Section 4.9 and Figure 7 say flipping all answers harms Left and improves Right. Section 4.9 says Right still does not reach original Left F1, while Left falls to roughly original Right level. Figure 7 similarly says Right remains worse on average than Left after flipping, suggesting Right positions are harder to learn. Conclusion claims SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines, Neutral remains challenging, and accuracy varies across the political spectrum. It also calls the agents persona-conditioned, conflicting with the earlier statement that no explicit persona representation is provided. Ethics statement reports systematic underperformance on center and right-wing profiles and difficulty modeling neutral positions, consistent with earlier findings; it cautions against premature deployment and advocates bias mitigation. Reproducibility statement says code

final_notes: Figure 3: SFT+GRPO typically works best overall, but all methods perform worse for Center and Right groups than Left; subgroup winners can differ. For Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO, Left outperforms Center/Right on smartvote; similar but weaker patterns occur on WoM and ANES. On WoM, Left and Center are roughly equal. SFT performs best for Right profiles on smartvote and ANES, while larger WoM training sets may explain relatively strong Right performance there. Neutral is hardest: ANES Neutral recall is worst for every individual, and Neutral base rate is highest for Right respondents, harming performance. F1 and accuracy negatively correlate with Neutral base rate at 5% significance. Removing Neutral improves all groups and narrows Left–Center gap but does not eliminate Left–Right gap. Alternative recoding preserves the negative correlation but makes Center and Right nearly identical, suggesting recoding contributes to the original gap. Appendix B gives hallucination/illogical reasoning and cross-topic failure examples; Table 1 shows an answer changing to Yes after training. Agents do not perfectly reproduce candidates. Figure 2 reports no overall left shift: agents shift center-right on the left-right axis and toward the center on the conservative-liberal axis. Right individuals become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative. Figures 5–6: Progressive-biased SFT harms Right and inconsistently affects Left; conservative-biased SFT harms Left without consistently benefiting Right. Bias mainly harms underrepresented groups, with Right suffering more strongly. Conservative-biased and default SFT produce similar shifts, suggesting Figure 2’s centerward shift may derive mainly from base-model alignment. Figure 7: Flipping all smartvote answers helps Right but worsens Left and Center. Right still performs worse on average than Left after flipping; inversion does not eliminate disparity. Limitations include opinion noise, per-profile computational cost, scarce/mismatched surveys, and limited cross-country comparability. Future work proposes compact persona-conditioned models, confidence/reliability estimates, value heads, purpose-built questionnaires, and improved Neutral handling. Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines across smartvote, Wahl-o-Mat, and ANES, but an Llama ANES exception is reported where SFT exceeds SFT+GRPO. Neutral and ideological disparities remain.

The paper asks whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one model per respondent, candidate, or party; models generate a rationale and final answer. Group-relative policy optimization rewards formatting, reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers; supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provide a warm start. Experiments involve Swiss candidates, German parties, and U.S. voters. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased fine-tuning data mainly harms underrepresented perspectives. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

The paper studies whether reasoning improves LLM alignment with individual political opinions. It trains one political agent per respondent, candidate, or party to model a preference profile/persona. Models generate a reasoning trace and final stance; GRPO rewards formatting, desired reasoning length, and agreement with survey answers, while SFT on synthetic arguments provides a warm start. SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines, with exceptions, and performs best on smartvote. Neutral answers are difficult to predict, and performance varies by ideology. Biased SFT data harms the underrepresented perspective. Agents retain political distortions, so the method does not fully remove bias.

Datasets/settings: ANES 2020 Time Series (79 U.S. policy items; respondent models), German Wahl-O-Mat (six parties: CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Die Linke, AfD), EU&I 2024 as German out-of-domain test, and Swiss smartvote 2023 (candidate models; topic-stratified split). Labels are Yes/Neutral/No; Swiss four-point responses are collapsed to Yes/No. Metrics include per-unit macro-F1, accuracy, recall, and standard deviations across eight runs.

Methods/backbones: GRPO is PPO-related and normalizes rewards within groups without a learned value function; SFT+GRPO is the warm-start method. Evaluated open-weight backbones are Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Magistral 24B, with 4-bit quantization for training. Synthetic arguments use Llama 3.1 70B by default and Llama 3.3 70B for progressive/conservative bias tests.

Key analyses include PCA of candidate/agent positions, counterfactual answer inversion (approximately 180° rotation), demographic/persona prompting, and political distortion. Reward notation: R_format, R_length = negative absolute length error, R_correct, total R(r_i,y_i*); x_i is reasoning trace, y_i predicted answer, y_i* ground truth.

final_notes:
Table 1 caption’s claim that IA2→SFT beats SFT across the board is contradicted by BBCN accuracy (27.9 vs 31.8) and unchanged SST2 ECE (0.20 vs 0.20). IA2→SFT beats ICL in accuracy on AGN, FinS, PoemS, SST2, not BBCN.

Table 2: IA2→SFT beats SFT on GSM8K (73.6 vs 70.9), GSM8Ks (68.8 vs 64.5), HMathA (55.3 vs 50.4), and SciQ (40.8 vs 35.0), though it can be worse than ICL.

Section 5.2: IA2 increases ICL activation similarity; IA2→SFT retains more similarity than SFT. Similarity generally improves calibration, but extreme similarity/alignment may hurt accuracy.

Figure 4: SFT-only weight updates are nearly orthogonal to IA2-only and IA2→SFT updates; performant IA2→SFT models share about 39% of spanned weight space with IA2-only models.

Table 3: For Qwen, N=4, IA2+SFT exceeds SFT-only on all datasets. Discussion claims both SFT-only and IA2→SFT drop versus Table 2, but IA2→SFT on HMathA is unchanged (54.0%).

Table 4: Soft-label SFT nearly reaches IA2+SFT on GSM8K (36.1 vs 37.0) and exceeds standard SFT (28.2); on SST2 it exceeds standard SFT (55.9 vs 52.3) but is below IA2+SFT (66.9).

Table 5: Across GSM8K and HMathA shot counts, IA2→SFT consistently beats SFT-only. ICL exceeds IA2→SFT at every listed count, with the gap narrowing as shots increase. IA2-only exceeds ICL on GSM8K at N=4 and N=8.

Table 6: For (IA)3 on Llama models, IA2→SFT exceeds SFT-only and ICL accuracy in every listed row.

Section 7 states SFT performs worse than ICL, but no direct comparison sufficient to establish a contradiction is recorded.

Conclusion claims IA2 consistently improves SFT accuracy and calibration, contradicted by BBCN accuracy (27.9 vs 31.8) and unchanged SST2 ECE (0.20 vs 0.20).

Abstract claims: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute cost. The paper reports that ICL and SFT yield distinct activation patterns and thus use different functional mechanisms. It introduces ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation method intended to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 used as a priming step before SFT is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration, based on extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks and two model families.

Abstract: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute/context cost. Paper reports distinct ICL vs. SFT activation patterns and different functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) is a self-distillation method that collects ICL activations and enforces alignment with them, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like internal reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy and calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT.

Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. SFT fine-tunes weights on N input-output pairs, generating G response tokens and minimizing cross-entropy against ground truth. ICL concatenates demonstration pairs I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] with query Xt, without weight updates, to produce a response; paper focuses on classic input-output demonstrations. Activations are hidden SA outputs, represented for L layers and R tokens as A of size L×R×d. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

Section 3: ICL activations (100 test samples across datasets/models) and SFT activations are compared at output-token positions. Abstract/introduction: SFT specializes behavior by training weights; ICL adapts at inference through instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings but with higher inference/context cost. Paper claims distinct ICL/SFT activation patterns and functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) collects ICL activations, enforces alignment, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like reasoning. It allegedly improves accuracy/calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT. Across text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, and over 13,000 models, ICL and SFT on the same data allegedly do not align in activation space; IA2 improves SFT and provides an adaptation signal unavailable to SFT-only training. Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. SFT fine-tunes weights on N input-output pairs, generating G response tokens and minimizing cross-entropy against ground truth. ICL concatenates demonstration pairs I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] with query Xt, without weight updates, to produce a response; paper focuses on classic input-output demonstrations. Activations are hidden SA outputs, represented for L layers and R tokens as A of size L×R×d. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. final_notes: Section 4 presents a two-step pipeline: IA2 aligns self-attention behavior on query X with the base model’s behavior on I∘X, using MSE on activations; after IA2 convergence, generated responses undergo ordinary SFT on ground-truth answers. Formal IA2 concerns newly generated token index −1, while practical loss aligns all G response-token positions, creating an unresolved objective mismatch. Experiments use Qwen3/Llama-3.2 families, 12 benchmarks, and >13,000 models. Table 1 (Qwen, N=4): IA2→SFT generally outperforms SFT, but is worse on ECE for PoemS and STF, conflicting with the conclusion’s claim of consistently improved calibration. It beats ICL in accuracy in 4/5 rows but has higher ECE than ICL in every row. Table 2: IA2→SFT accuracy exceeds SFT-only on GSM8K, GSM8Ks OOD, HMathA, and SciQ; it can be worse than ICL. IA2→SFT retains more ICL activation similarity than SFT and lies between IA2 and SFT. Figure 4: SFT-only updates are almost orthogonal to IA2 and IA2→SFT; best IA2→SFT models share ~39% weight-space span with IA2-only. Table 3: IA2+SFT exceeds SFT-only on GSM8K, GSM8Ks, HMathA. Table 5: IA2→SFT beats SFT-only in every row, but ICL does not exceed every training method for GSM8K at N=4 or 8. Table 6: IA2→SFT exceeds SFT-only and ICL accuracy in all five rows. Discussion proposes LoRA/selective-IA2 ablations, prompt optimization, finer-grained learning-rate control; extreme alignment may hurt performance. Reproducibility statement claims code and paper/appendix plus README suffice to fully reproduce results using repeatable random seeds. Acknowledgments list ONR, Amazon Research Award, Open Philanthropy, and Andrea Wynn.

errors.claim: “The comparison quantity … is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors and has shape \(L\times R\), while the studied sequences are \(T=[I\circ X]\) with demonstrations and \(T=X\) without them.”
errors.evidence: \(I\circ X\) and \(X\) generally contain different numbers of tokens, so their activation tensors have different sequence-length dimensions, whereas token-wise cosine similarity requires corresponding token positions and is asserted to have a single shape \(L\times R\).
errors.explanation: As stated, the two tensors being compared do not generally share the same \(R\), so a token-wise similarity tensor with shape \(L\times R\) is dimensionally undefined unless an alignment, truncation, or padding procedure is specified.

errors.explanation: As described, the two activation sequences have incompatible token dimensions for token-wise similarity. errors.claim: “Minimize the mean squared error with respect to model parameters” in Eq. (4).

errors.explanation: The displayed objective is an unnormalized sum of norms, not a mean squared error: it has neither a factor \(1/N\) nor a squared norm. Thus the stated loss and the equation are inconsistent.

final_notes: Section 4: R8D/IA2 first primes parameters from Θ to Θ′, then collects outputs and trains on ground-truth responses with Q7M loss. IA2 seeks layerwise processing alignment, SA([I∘X];WQKVO)≈SA(X;W~QKVO), rather than output similarity. Eq. (4) is an unnormalized sum of unsquared norms despite being called MSE. Section 5: Up to 50 epochs, learning rates 1e−4/3e−4/1e−3; >13,000 models. Rank-8 LoRAs on WQ/WK/WO; N capped at 16 (Llama), 8 (Qwen); G=200; target training uses ground-truth response length. P4Z generally beats H9C and usually exceeds V2K U6R, with somewhat worse calibration; it loses to V2K on OOD W3F/Y8J and N5Q U6R and often has worse D8P. Table 2: P4Z exceeds H9C in every listed multi-token case but sometimes underperforms V2K (L9S, V7B). H9C updates are nearly orthogonal to other methods; high-performing P4Z shares ~39% mean spanned weight space with J3N. R8D/priming provides otherwise unreachable subspaces; priming raises K4X and sequential training retains it. Similarity lowers D8P smoothly, but extreme alignment need not maximize U6R; ground-truth and functional alignment combine best. Section 6: T6B outperforms H9C when trained on V2K responses; H9C/P4Z trained on V2K responses are worse than ground-truth versions. T6B combines LR8D and βLQ7M, using generated response tokens for G>1. P4Z costs one V2K activation-collection pass, then inference cost matches H9C. Table 4: F5W improves multi-token Q7M but is weaker single-token; T6B is near it. Table 6 (Llama-3.2, N=4): P4Z significantly above H9C and V2K U6R in every listed case. Section 7 finds Q7M worse than V2K in present experiments. Conclusion: V2K often encodes richer, more generalizable patterns; R8D shifts models into a more adaptable weight subspace inaccessible to Q7M alone. Future work concerns diversity, catastrophic forgetting, and post-trained/RL-tuned models.

Abstract claims that across 12 popular benchmarks and two model families, P4Z significantly improves output U6R and calibration, with practical adaptation and insight into internal mechanics. It defines R8D as self-distillation intended to replicate V2K activation patterns in weight-trained models, encouraging V2K-like internal reasoning; the priming signal is unavailable through H9C.

Introduction: Generic LLMs can be adapted to specialized applications using PEFT. Q7M generalization often requires many labeled samples, while V2K demonstrations/instructions consume context and increase inference compute. The research question is whether information-rich V2K activations improve Q7M quality. Hypothesis: these activations encode generalizable contextual patterns potentially absent from few-shot weight adaptation, which may use shortcuts or overfit target responses. Similar outputs do not imply similar internal processing. Response-text context-to-weight distillation may reproduce outputs without reproducing functioning. Figure 1 says standard Q7M enforces output-space agreement between response and target (the third pipeline step), whereas the proposed pipeline collects V2K activations, enforces functional alignment, then trains against target responses; comparison charts aggregate performance across models/datasets, with details in §5. No internal contradiction found so far.

R8D is self-distillation intended to replicate V2K activation patterns in weight-trained models, encouraging V2K-like internal reasoning; the priming signal is unavailable through H9C.

Introduction: Generic LLMs can be adapted using PEFT. Q7M generalization may require many labeled samples, while V2K demonstrations/instructions consume context and inference compute. Hypothesis: V2K activations encode generalizable contextual patterns potentially absent from few-shot weight adaptation. Similar outputs do not imply similar internal processing. Figure 1 says standard Q7M enforces output-space agreement, whereas the proposed pipeline collects V2K activations, enforces functional alignment, then trains against target responses.

Background: Q7M/SFT changes weights and trains cross-entropy over generated response tokens versus ground truth. V2K/ICL uses concatenated input-output demonstrations without weight updates. SA is causal, using prior tokens; activations are \(A\in\mathbb R^{L\times R\times d}\). Activation similarity is described as token-wise cosine similarity with shape \(L\times R\), but it compares \(T=[I\circ X]\) against \(T=X\), which generally have different token lengths; this is a dimensional inconsistency unless an alignment/padding/truncation method is later specified.

errors.claim: “Activation similarity, \(\operatorname{asim}(A_1,A_2)\), is the token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors. Its size is \(L\times R\).”
errors.evidence: The paper then states that it studies \(T=[I\circ X]\) for ICL and \(T=X\) without ICL, where \(I\) contains demonstration tokens. Thus the corresponding activation tensors generally have different sequence lengths: \(|I|+|X|\) versus \(|X|\).
errors.explanation: Token-wise cosine similarity between tensors with different numbers of token positions is not defined as stated, and there is no specification here of how the positions are aligned or which tokens are compared. Consequently, assigning the result a single size \(L\times R\) is inconsistent with the two sequences being compared.

errors.claim: “Our proposed IA2 → SFT training method outperforms standard SFT across the board.”
errors.evidence: For the AGN→BBCN evaluation, SFT-only accuracy is 31.8, whereas IA2→SFT accuracy is 27.9. For STF→STF, both methods have ECE 0.29, so IA2→SFT does not outperform SFT on that metric.
errors.explanation: The table contains at least one lower IA2→SFT accuracy and one tied ECE, contradicting the claim that it outperforms SFT across the board.

errors.claim: “IA2 → SFT improves single-token accuracy and calibration over SFT only in almost all cases,” including the cited Table 1 examples.

errors.explanation: In every cited example, IA2 → SFT has lower accuracy than SFT only, so these examples contradict the claim that it improves accuracy over SFT only.

errors.explanation: The FinS → FinS example does not show IA2 → SFT exceeding ICL accuracy; it is substantially lower. The paper’s earlier summary also notes no consistent IA2 advantage over ICL.

errors.claim: “In some multi-token settings, such as Qwen on GSM8K and HMathA, ICL exceeds every training method, including IA2-based training.”
errors.evidence: In Table 3 for GSM8K, ICL accuracy is 76.4, while IA2-only accuracy is 77.4 and IA2 + SFT accuracy is 77.0. Table 2 likewise reports ICL 76.4 versus IA2 77.4.
errors.explanation: The claim is true for HMathA, but not for GSM8K: IA2-only and IA2 + SFT both exceed ICL.

errors.explanation: The stated comparison may hold numerically, but the cited final column reports IA2 + SFT rather than IA2 → SFT, so it does not show the claimed result.

errors.claim: “We find SFT worse than ICL.” The claims-and-evidence section similarly says, “This study finds SFT worse than ICL.”
errors.evidence: Table 6 in the notes reports SFT exceeding ICL on SciQr (64.5 vs. 60.0) and FinS* (58.2 vs. 56.6).
errors.explanation: The unqualified claim that SFT is worse than ICL conflicts with Table 6, where SFT outperforms ICL on two evaluation rows. The claim would need to be qualified as applying only to some tasks or aggregate comparisons.

final_notes:
Conclusion: IA2 uses ICL-like internal processing to improve SFT; ICL and SFT adapt via different mechanisms, with ICL often encoding richer/generalizable patterns. Claims IA2 moves models into an adaptable weight subspace inaccessible to SFT, supported by Figure 4 and §5.2: IA2-only/IA2→SFT overlap ~39% on average; SFT-only updates nearly orthogonal. Conclusion claims extensive experiments show consistent SFT accuracy/calibration improvements, citing Table 1 SST2→SST2 (accuracy 65.2 vs 90.4; ECE .22 vs .06), Table 2 HMathA→HMathA (50.4 vs 55.3), and Figures 1/3.

Table 2 (Qwen3-4B-Base, N=4, multi-token): GSM8K w/o ICL 56.4, ICL 76.4, SFT 70.9, IA2 77.4, IA2→SFT 73.6; GSM8Ks* 45.4, 68.4, 64.5, 66.2, 68.8; HMathA 21.0, 60.4, 50.4, 47.8, 55.3; SciQ 15.4, 37.5, 35.0, 6.9, 40.8. IA2→SFT beats SFT on all four but can be below ICL. Broad claims that it usually exceeds ICL conflict with AGN, FinS, SST2. Table 3: ICL-response training; IA2+SFT exceeds SFT, but ICL does not exceed every method (GSM8K ICL 76.4 < IA2 77.4 and IA2+SFT 77.0). Discussion mislabels final column IA2→SFT vs table IA2+SFT. Table 4 KD improves SFT but is below IA2+SFT on SST2. Table 5 IA2→SFT beats SFT every row and closes ICL gap. Table 6 Llama: IA2→SFT beats SFT and ICL all rows; SFT exceeds ICL on SciQr and FinS*. Related Work’s unqualified “SFT worse than ICL” is overbroad. Reproducibility and acknowledgments contain no claims contradicting earlier content.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations (100 test samples, SST2/AGNews and other datasets, Qwen3/Llama models with 16, 28, or 36 layers) against SFT activations, measured at output-token positions. Figure 2 reports small similarity for SFT-only, greater similarity for IA2→SFT, and better alignment near initial/final layers than middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes SFT should not directly replace ICL and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT.

The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 seeks modified attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3). For each sample, collect ICL response Ŷ and output-position activations A_ICL (shape L×G×d), then feed [X∘Ŷ] without demonstrations and minimize activation-difference loss (Eq. 4). final_notes:
Conclusion states ICL and SFT use different mechanisms; ICL often encodes richer/generalizable patterns. IA2 is presented as enabling ICL-like behavior and moving models into a weight subspace inaccessible to SFT alone. It claims extensive experiments show consistent improvements in SFT accuracy and calibration, citing Table 1 (SST2→SST2: 65.2 vs 90.4 accuracy; ECE 0.22 vs 0.06), Table 2 (HMathA→HMathA: 50.4 vs 55.3), and Figures 1/3. §5.2 reports ~39% average overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, with SFT-only updates almost completely orthogonal.

Issues retained: “We find SFT worse than ICL” is supported by Table 2’s four tasks (70.9 vs 76.4; 64.5 vs 68.4; 50.4 vs 60.4; 35.0 vs 37.5) but contradicted as an unqualified generalization by Table 6, where SFT exceeds ICL in three of five rows. IA2→SFT beats SFT-only on all four Table 2 tasks, exceeds SFT-only in Tables 3 and 5, and Table 6 says it exceeds both SFT and ICL in all five rows. Table 4: soft-label SFT nearly reaches IA2+SFT on multi-token GSM8K but not single-token SST2. AGN has numerical/text inconsistency: 27.9 vs 31.8 accuracy, .52 vs .35 ECE, and AGN→BBCN vs AGN→AGN. FinS claim that IA2→SFT usually exceeds ICL conflicts with reported 63.6 vs 78.7 / 67.4→78.7. Final reproducibility and acknowledgments sections contain no internal contradictions.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations from T=[I∘X] with SFT activations from T=X over 100 test samples across datasets including SST2 and AGNews, using Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models (1B/16 layers, 3B/28, 4B/36). Figure 2 reportedly shows low SFT–ICL alignment, better near initial/final layers and worse in middle layers. IA2→SFT aligns much more with ICL and performs much better than SFT-only (Figure 1). ICL is claimed to be better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy than SFT. No internal contradiction found in this part.

Section 4 presents IA2→SFT. IA2 seeks to align no-demonstration processing with ICL by modifying attention weights, targeting output-position activations for each response token. For each sample, generate an ICL response Y-hat using demonstrations I, collect A_ICL from [I∘X], then feed [X∘Y-hat] without demonstrations and minimize activation difference (Equation 4). After IA2 convergence, collect responses from the modified model and perform standard SFT against ground-truth Y. Reported evidence: FinS accuracy 67.4→78.7 and ECE .31→.16 (Table 1); GSM8K accuracy 64.5→68.8 after GSM8K training (Table 2). No internal contradiction identified.

Section 5 compares adaptation methods on single-token and multi-token tasks, using few-shot training sets of N=2,4,8,16,…, five sets per N. IA2 collects activations using the other N−1 training samples as demonstrations; evaluation uses 500 separate examples. Single-token tasks include sentiment (SST2, FinS, PoemS), StrategyQA True/False, AGNews/BBCNews, and remapped-choice SciQr/QASCr. Multi-token tasks include GSM8K/GSM8Ks, HMathA, and generative SciQ. Qwen3-4B-Base is used for all tasks; Llama-3.2-1B for single-token tasks except SciQr (Llama-3.2-3B); Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct is secondary model for multi-token tasks. LoRA rank 8 modifies WQ, WK, WO. Abstract claims: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute cost. The paper reports that ICL and SFT yield distinct activation patterns and thus use different functional mechanisms. Abstract: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute/context cost. Paper reports distinct ICL vs. SFT activation patterns and different functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) is a self-distillation method that collects ICL activations and enforces alignment with them, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like internal reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy and calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT.

Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

Abstract/introduction: SFT specializes behavior by training weights; ICL adapts at inference through instructions/demonstrations, with potentially better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings but higher inference/context cost. Paper claims distinct ICL/SFT activation patterns and functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) collects ICL activations, enforces alignment, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy/calibration, especially low-data, using the same data as SFT. Across text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, and over 13,000 models, ICL and SFT on the same data allegedly do not align in activation space; IA2 improves SFT and provides an adaptation signal unavailable to SFT-only training.

Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. SFT fine-tunes weights on N input-output pairs, generating G response tokens and minimizing cross-entropy against ground truth. ICL concatenates demonstration pairs I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] with query Xt, without weight updates, to produce a response; paper focuses on classic input-output demonstrations. Activations are hidden SA outputs, represented for L layers and R tokens as A of size L×R×d. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. No internal contradiction identified in this part.
