errors.claim: “The comparison quantity … is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors and has shape \(L\times R\), while the studied sequences are \(T=[I\circ X]\) with demonstrations and \(T=X\) without them.”
errors.evidence: \(I\circ X\) and \(X\) generally contain different numbers of tokens, so their activation tensors have different sequence-length dimensions, whereas token-wise cosine similarity requires corresponding token positions and is asserted to have a single shape \(L\times R\).
errors.explanation: As stated, the two tensors being compared do not generally share the same \(R\), so a token-wise similarity tensor with shape \(L\times R\) is dimensionally undefined unless an alignment, truncation, or padding procedure is specified.

errors.claim: “The output-position comparison is \(\mathrm{K4X}(A_{\mathrm{V2K}},A_{\mathrm{Q7M}})\).”
errors.location: This part; compared with Background in the notes
errors.evidence: The paper defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activations from \(T=[I\circ X]\) and \(T=X\), which generally have different token lengths. This part specifies only an “output-position comparison” and does not specify an alignment, padding, or truncation procedure.
errors.explanation: As described, the two activation sequences have incompatible token dimensions for token-wise similarity. Restricting the comparison to output positions could resolve this, but the required correspondence or extraction procedure is not stated, so the claimed K4X comparison remains dimensionally underspecified.

errors.claim: “Minimize the mean squared error with respect to model parameters” in Eq. (4).
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{R8D}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\|A^i-A^i_{\mathrm{V2K}}\right\|\).
errors.explanation: The displayed objective is an unnormalized sum of norms, not a mean squared error: it has neither a factor \(1/N\) nor a squared norm. Thus the stated loss and the equation are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P4Z outperforms standard Q7M across the board.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 shows P4Z underperforming V2K on OOD W3F/Y8J (U6R 27.9 vs. 28.8; D8P 0.40 vs. 0.12), on N5Q (U6R 62.4 vs. 66.0; D8P 0.29 vs. 0.07), and on several other calibration comparisons where lower D8P is better (e.g., W3F in-domain 0.35 vs. 0.13).
errors.explanation: Thus P4Z does not outperform the comparator across all reported U6R and D8P results, even if Q7M refers to V2K or another standard method.

errors.claim: “The baseline improves on standard Q7M in the multi-token case” (Table 4 caption).
errors.location: This part, Table 4 caption and accompanying paragraph
errors.evidence: The paragraph states that “F5W = SFT (soft labels) … perform[s] significantly worse than standard Q7M in the multi-token case,” while Table 4 reports F5W at 55.9 U6R versus H9C (the standard Q7M comparator) at 52.3 for B7V.
errors.explanation: The caption says the soft-label baseline improves over standard Q7M, whereas the accompanying text says it performs significantly worse. The Table 4 values support improvement, not the paragraph’s claim.

final_notes: Section 4: R8D/IA2 first primes parameters from Θ to Θ′, then collects outputs and trains on ground-truth responses with Q7M loss. IA2 seeks layerwise processing alignment, SA([I∘X];WQKVO)≈SA(X;W~QKVO), rather than output similarity. Eq. (4) is an unnormalized sum of unsquared norms despite being called MSE. Section 5: Up to 50 epochs, learning rates 1e−4/3e−4/1e−3; >13,000 models. Rank-8 LoRAs on WQ/WK/WO; N capped at 16 (Llama), 8 (Qwen); G=200; target training uses ground-truth response length. Single-token metrics U6R and D8P; multi-token only correctly formatted answers, no calibration. Qwen3-4B-Base throughout; Llama variants as noted. P4Z generally beats H9C and usually exceeds V2K U6R with somewhat worse calibration; J3N can perform strongly. Table 1 contradicts “P4Z outperforms standard Q7M across the board”: P4Z loses to V2K on OOD W3F/Y8J and N5Q U6R and often has worse D8P. Table 2: P4Z exceeds H9C in every listed multi-token case but sometimes underperforms V2K (L9S, V7B). H9C updates nearly orthogonal to other methods; high-performing P4Z shares ~39% mean spanned weight space with J3N. Priming provides otherwise unreachable subspaces; similarity lowers D8P smoothly, but extreme alignment need not maximize U6R. Section 6: Table 3 shows T6B outperforms H9C when trained on V2K responses; H9C/P4Z trained on responses are worse than when trained on ground truths. T6B jointly/self-distills with R8D+βQ7M, using generated tokens for G>1. Table 4 compares soft-label KD (M8G/F5W): B7V F5W=55.9 U6R versus H9C=52.3 and T6B=66.9. Priming means IA2 before SFT; IA2 → SFT is sequential, while IA2 + SFT uses simultaneous losses. The abstract reports that IA2 priming significantly improves SFT accuracy and calibration across 12 benchmarks and two model families. Reported findings include improved SFT accuracy and calibration, different weight subspaces identified by IA2 versus SFT, and no consistent IA2-based advantage over ICL, particularly on some multi-token math tasks. Additional analyses cover simultaneous IA2 and SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method. Key definitions: activation similarity is token-wise cosine similarity; IA2 uses mean squared activation matching, SFT uses cross-entropy; LoRA rank is 8 in main experiments; training is capped at 50 epochs. Models include Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 1B/3B, with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct also tested. Single-token tasks use accuracy/ECE; multi-token tasks use parsed exact match. IA2 evidence cited: Table 1 FinS → FinS accuracy 67.4 versus 78.7 and ECE 0.31 versus 0.16; Table 2 HMathA → HMathA accuracy 50.4 versus 55.3. No internal contradiction found so far.

errors.claim: “Activation similarity, \(\operatorname{asim}(A_1,A_2)\), is the token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors. Its size is \(L\times R\).”
errors.evidence: The paper then states that it studies \(T=[I\circ X]\) for ICL and \(T=X\) without ICL, where \(I\) contains demonstration tokens. Thus the corresponding activation tensors generally have different sequence lengths: \(|I|+|X|\) versus \(|X|\).
errors.explanation: Token-wise cosine similarity between tensors with different numbers of token positions is not defined as stated, and there is no specification here of how the positions are aligned or which tokens are compared. Consequently, assigning the result a single size \(L\times R\) is inconsistent with the two sequences being compared.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations (100 test samples, SST2/AGNews and other datasets, Qwen3/Llama models with 16, 28, or 36 layers) against SFT activations, measured at output-token positions. Figure 2 reports small similarity for SFT-only, greater similarity for IA2→SFT, and better alignment near initial/final layers than middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes SFT should not directly replace ICL and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT.

The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 seeks modified attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3). For each sample, collect ICL response Ŷ and output-position activations A_ICL (shape L×G×d), then feed [X∘Ŷ] without demonstrations and minimize activation-difference loss (Eq. 4). After IA2, collect responses from the modified model and apply standard SFT cross-entropy using ground-truth Y. Claims: SFT has little activation similarity to ICL (Figure 2); IA2→SFT improves adaptation, with Table 1 FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7 and ECE 0.31 vs 0.16, and Table 2 GSM8K accuracy 64.5 vs 68.8. Earlier notes: abstract reports improved SFT accuracy/calibration across 12 benchmarks but no consistent IA2 advantage over ICL; prior results include HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3, SST2 65.2 vs 90.4 (ECE 0.22 vs 0.06), SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8. Main models Qwen3-4B-Base, Llama-3.2 1B/3B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; LoRA rank 8, 50-epoch cap. Activation similarity is token-wise cosine; earlier concern that ICL [I∘X] and no-ICL X may have different sequence lengths. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

After IA2, it collects modified-model responses and applies standard SFT cross-entropy with ground-truth Y. SFT reportedly has little activation similarity to ICL (Fig. 2). steps.notes_before: Conclusion claims ICL and SFT use different mechanisms; IA2 enables ICL-like behavior and moves models into a weight subspace inaccessible to SFT. It says extensive experiments show consistent improvements in SFT accuracy/calibration and cites Table 1 SST2 accuracy 65.2→90.4, ece .22→.06, Table 2 HMathA 50.4→55.3, and Figures 1/3. This unqualified consistency claim conflicts with earlier single-token results: IA2→SFT is below SFT for AGN (27.9 vs 31.8), FinS (67.4 vs 78.7), and SST2 (65.2 vs 90.4; likely the compared methods), despite gains elsewhere. final_notes: The conclusion claims IA2 consistently improves SFT accuracy and calibration, contradicted by BBCN accuracy (IA2→SFT 27.9 vs. SFT 31.8) and unchanged SST2 ECE (0.20 vs. 0.20). Table 1’s claim that IA2→SFT beats SFT across the board is similarly contradicted. IA2 improves ICL activation similarity; IA2→SFT retains more similarity than SFT, while extreme similarity can hurt accuracy. SFT-only updates are nearly orthogonal to IA2-related updates; performant IA2→SFT models share about 39% of spanned weight space with IA2-only models. Table 3 says IA2+SFT beats SFT-only throughout, but its discussion incorrectly says HMathA IA2→SFT drops versus Table 2 when it is unchanged at 54.0%. Soft-label SFT nearly matches IA2+SFT on GSM8K, exceeds standard SFT, and is intermediate on SST2. ICL exceeds training methods on HMathA and GSM8K N=2. Section 7 says the improved SFT pipeline addresses memorization/overfitting and catastrophic forgetting, while the conclusion says catastrophic forgetting remains a future effect to test. Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors address the claim that the ICL vs IA2→SFT accuracy gap widens with more shots (contradicted by Table 5 showing the gap shrinking), so the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: “The comparison quantity … is token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors and has shape \(L\times R\), while the studied sequences are \(T=[I\circ X]\) with demonstrations and \(T=X\) without them.”
errors.evidence: \(I\circ X\) and \(X\) generally contain different numbers of tokens, so their activation tensors have different sequence-length dimensions, whereas token-wise cosine similarity requires corresponding token positions and is asserted to have a single shape \(L\times R\).
errors.explanation: As stated, the two tensors being compared do not generally share the same \(R\), so a token-wise similarity tensor with shape \(L\times R\) is dimensionally undefined unless an alignment, truncation, or padding procedure is specified.

errors.claim: “The output-position comparison is \(\mathrm{K4X}(A_{\mathrm{V2K}},A_{\mathrm{Q7M}})\).”
errors.location: This part; compared with Background in the notes
errors.evidence: The paper defines activation similarity as token-wise cosine similarity between activations from \(T=[I\circ X]\) and \(T=X\), which generally have different token lengths. This part specifies only an “output-position comparison” and does not specify an alignment, padding, or truncation procedure.
errors.explanation: As described, the two activation sequences have incompatible token dimensions for token-wise similarity. Restricting the comparison to output positions could resolve this, but the required correspondence or extraction procedure is not stated, so the claimed K4X comparison remains dimensionally underspecified.

errors.claim: “Minimize the mean squared error with respect to model parameters” in Eq. (4).
errors.evidence: Equation (4) defines \(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{R8D}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\|A^i-A^i_{\mathrm{V2K}}\right\|\).
errors.explanation: The displayed objective is an unnormalized sum of norms, not a mean squared error: it has neither a factor \(1/N\) nor a squared norm. Thus the stated loss and the equation are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “P4Z outperforms standard Q7M across the board.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 shows P4Z underperforming V2K on OOD W3F/Y8J (U6R 27.9 vs. 28.8; D8P 0.40 vs. 0.12), on N5Q (U6R 62.4 vs. 66.0; D8P 0.29 vs. 0.07), and on several other calibration comparisons where lower D8P is better (e.g., W3F in-domain 0.35 vs. 0.13).
errors.explanation: Thus P4Z does not outperform the comparator across all reported U6R and D8P results, even if Q7M refers to V2K or another standard method.

errors.claim: “On some multi-token Qwen mathematics cases, including L9S and V7B, V2K exceeds every training method.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows for L9S at N=4, J3N U6R is 77.4 versus V2K’s 76.4, and at N=8, J3N is 78.8 versus V2K’s 77.2.
errors.explanation: Although V2K exceeds the other methods in the listed V7B cases, it does not exceed every training method for L9S at N=4 or N=8.

errors.claim: “P4Z’s gap to V2K widens quickly with more shots.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 gives P4Z–V2K gaps of −06.6, −02.8, and −01.2 for L9S at N=2, 4, and 8, respectively; the absolute V2K advantage shrinks from 6.6 to 1.2 points. For V7B, the gaps likewise move from −09.9 to −05.1 to −02.7.
errors.explanation: In both datasets, P4Z’s gap relative to V2K narrows rather than widens as the shot count increases.

final_notes: Section 4: R8D/IA2 first primes parameters from Θ to Θ′, then collects outputs and trains on ground-truth responses with Q7M loss. IA2 seeks layerwise processing alignment, not output similarity. Eq. (4) is an unnormalized sum of unsquared norms despite being called MSE. It cites ~39% average overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, with SFT-only updates almost orthogonal. However, the accuracy-consistency claim is contradicted by earlier results: IA2→SFT is below SFT on SST2 (65.2 vs 90.4), AGN (27.9 vs 31.8), and FinS (67.4 vs 78.7), despite improving all four multi-token Table 2 tasks. Table 5 shows IA2→SFT remains below ICL, with gaps shrinking as N increases; Table 6 has IA2→SFT above SFT and ICL in displayed rows. Priming means IA2 before SFT; IA2 → SFT is sequential, while IA2 + SFT uses simultaneous losses. Experiments span 12 benchmarks, two model families, and over 13,000 trained models. Reported findings include improved SFT accuracy and calibration, different weight subspaces identified by IA2 versus SFT, and no consistent IA2-based advantage over ICL, particularly on some multi-token math tasks. Additional analyses cover simultaneous IA2 and SFT, soft-label distillation, and an alternative parameter-efficient tuning method. Key definitions: activation similarity is token-wise cosine similarity; IA2 uses mean squared activation matching, SFT uses cross-entropy; LoRA rank is 8 in main experiments; training is capped at 50 epochs. Models include Qwen3-4B-Base and Llama-3.2 1B/3B, with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct also tested. Single-token tasks use accuracy/ECE; multi-token tasks use parsed exact match. No internal contradiction found in this glossary part.

errors.claim: “Activation similarity, \(\operatorname{asim}(A_1,A_2)\), is the token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors. Its size is \(L\times R\).”
errors.evidence: The paper then states that it studies \(T=[I\circ X]\) for ICL and \(T=X\) without ICL, where \(I\) contains demonstration tokens. Thus the corresponding activation tensors generally have different sequence lengths: \(|I|+|X|\) versus \(|X|\).
errors.explanation: Token-wise cosine similarity between tensors with different numbers of token positions is not defined as stated, and there is no specification here of how the positions are aligned or which tokens are compared. Consequently, assigning the result a single size \(L\times R\) is inconsistent with the two sequences being compared.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations (100 test samples, SST2/AGNews and other datasets, Qwen3/Llama models with 16, 28, or 36 layers) against SFT activations, measured at output-token positions. Figure 2 reports small similarity for SFT-only, greater similarity for IA2→SFT, and better alignment near initial/final layers than middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes SFT should not directly replace ICL and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT.

The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 seeks modified attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3). For each sample, collect ICL response Ŷ and output-position activations A_ICL (shape L×G×d), then feed [X∘Ŷ] without demonstrations and minimize activation-difference loss (Eq. 4). After IA2, collect responses from the modified model and apply standard SFT cross-entropy using ground-truth Y. Claims: SFT has little activation similarity to ICL (Figure 2); IA2→SFT improves adaptation, with Table 1 FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7 and ECE 0.31 vs 0.16, and Table 2 GSM8K accuracy 64.5 vs 68.8. Earlier notes: abstract reports improved SFT accuracy/calibration across 12 benchmarks but no consistent IA2 advantage over ICL; prior results include HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3, SST2 65.2 vs 90.4 (ECE 0.22 vs 0.06), SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8. Main models Qwen3-4B-Base, Llama-3.2 1B/3B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; LoRA rank 8, 50-epoch cap. Activation similarity is token-wise cosine; earlier concern that ICL [I∘X] and no-ICL X may have different sequence lengths. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

After IA2, it collects modified-model responses and applies standard SFT cross-entropy with ground-truth Y. SFT reportedly has little activation similarity to ICL (Fig. 2). Results noted: FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7 and ECE 0.31 vs 0.16 (Table 1); GSM8K accuracy 64.5 vs 68.8 (Table 2); prior HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3, SST2 65.2 vs 90.4 (ECE 0.22 vs 0.06), SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8. errors.claim: “Extensive experiments show consistent improvements in SFT accuracy and calibration” and “IA2 improves SFT accuracy and calibration,” citing SST2 accuracy 65.2 versus 90.4.

steps.notes_before: Conclusion claims ICL and SFT use different mechanisms and that ICL often encodes richer/generalizable patterns. It says IA2 enables ICL-like behavior, moves models into a weight subspace inaccessible to SFT, and gives consistent accuracy/calibration improvements. It cites ~39% average overlap between IA2-only and IA2→SFT, with SFT-only updates almost orthogonal. However, the accuracy-consistency claim is contradicted by earlier results: IA2→SFT is below SFT on SST2 (65.2 vs 90.4), AGN (27.9 vs 31.8), and FinS (67.4 vs 78.7), despite improving all four multi-token Table 2 tasks. IA2→SFT can also be below ICL. Table 2: GSM8K 73.6 vs SFT 70.9; GSM8Ks* 68.8 vs 64.5; HMathA 55.3 vs 50.4; SciQ 40.8 vs 35.0. Table 3 uses ICL responses and IA2+SFT exceeds SFT-only. Soft-label SFT nearly matches IA2+SFT on multi-token GSM8K but not SST2. Table 5 shows IA2→SFT remains below ICL, with gaps shrinking as N increases; Table 6 has IA2→SFT above SFT and ICL in displayed rows. Activation collection has one-time cost; inference matches SFT-only. Future work concerns diversity, catastrophic forgetting, and RL-tuned models.

Abstract claims: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute cost. The paper reports that ICL and SFT yield distinct activation patterns and thus use different functional mechanisms. It introduces ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation method intended to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. Abstract: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute/context cost. Paper reports distinct ICL vs. SFT activation patterns and different functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) is a self-distillation method that collects ICL activations and enforces alignment with them, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like internal reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy and calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT.

Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. SFT fine-tunes weights on N input-output pairs, generating G response tokens and minimizing cross-entropy against ground truth. ICL concatenates demonstration pairs I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] with query Xt, without weight updates, to produce a response; paper focuses on classic input-output demonstrations. Activations are hidden SA outputs, represented for L layers and R tokens as A of size L×R×d. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

steps.notes_before: Experimental settings: single-token outputs are one label/token (classification, True/False, or MCQ); multi-token outputs are variable-length open-ended generations. Single-token tasks: sentiment uses SST2, Financial Phrasebank (FinS), and Poem Sentiment (PoemS); the text says SST2 and FinS are used for training and all three for evaluation, but also claims this yields one ID and two OOD datasets (potential inconsistency unless models are trained separately). StrategyQA is True/False. News uses AGNews for training and AGNews/BBCNews for evaluation. Remapped-choice SciQr is used for training and SciQr/QASC-r for evaluation. Multi-token tasks: train/evaluate GSM8K and GSM8Ks; HMathA advanced math; SciQ generation rather than MCQ. Few-shot datasets vary N in [2,4,8,16,...], with five sets per N. IA2 activations are collected for each query using the other N−1 training samples as random-order ICL demonstrations, reusing identical data across methods. Evaluation uses a separate 500 samples per task. Multi-token outputs use chain-of-thought-style reasoning and task-specific answer parsing: GSM8K/GSM8Ks numerical answer after #### (or common variants), HMathA boxed answer, SciQ support text followed by #### and exact string matching.

final_notes: Section 7 related work says the paper finds SFT worse than ICL, citing aggregated Figure 1 and Table 2 (SFT vs ICL: GSM8K 70.9 vs 76.4; HMathA 50.4 vs 60.4). The conclusion states that ICL and SFT use different mechanisms, ICL often encodes richer/generalizable patterns, and IA2 enables ICL-like internal behavior by moving models into a more adaptable weight subspace inaccessible to SFT alone. Future work concerns diversity, catastrophic forgetting, and RL-tuned models. The reproducibility statement says code, experimental details, README, and repeatable random seeds support full reproduction; acknowledgments list ONR, Amazon Research Award, Open Philanthropy, and Andrea Wynn.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations (100 test samples, SST2/AGNews and other datasets, Qwen3/Llama models with 16, 28, or 36 layers) against SFT activations, measured at output-token positions. Figure 2 reports small similarity for SFT-only, greater similarity for IA2→SFT, and better alignment near initial/final layers than middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes SFT should not directly replace ICL and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT.

The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 seeks modified attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3). For each sample, collect ICL response Ŷ and output-position activations A_ICL (shape L×G×d), then feed [X∘Ŷ] without demonstrations and minimize activation-difference loss (Eq. 4). After IA2, collect responses from the modified model and apply standard SFT cross-entropy using ground-truth Y. Claims: SFT has little activation similarity to ICL (Figure 2); IA2→SFT improves adaptation, with Table 1 FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7 and ECE 0.31 vs 0.16, and Table 2 GSM8K accuracy 64.5 vs 68.8. Earlier notes: abstract reports improved SFT accuracy/calibration across 12 benchmarks but no consistent IA2 advantage over ICL; prior results include HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3, SST2 65.2 vs 90.4 (ECE 0.22 vs 0.06), SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8. Main models Qwen3-4B-Base, Llama-3.2 1B/3B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; LoRA rank 8, 50-epoch cap. Activation similarity is token-wise cosine; earlier concern that ICL [I∘X] and no-ICL X may have different sequence lengths. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

Abstract claims: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute cost. The paper reports that ICL and SFT yield distinct activation patterns and thus use different functional mechanisms. It introduces ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation method intended to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 used as a priming step before SFT is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration, based on extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks and two model families.

Abstract: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute/context cost. Paper reports distinct ICL vs. SFT activation patterns and different functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) is a self-distillation method that collects ICL activations and enforces alignment with them, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like internal reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy and calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT.

Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. errors.claim: “Activation similarity, \(\operatorname{asim}(A_1,A_2)\), is the token-wise cosine similarity between two activation tensors. Its size is \(L\times R\).”
errors.evidence: The paper then states that it studies \(T=[I\circ X]\) for ICL and \(T=X\) without ICL, where \(I\) contains demonstration tokens. Thus the corresponding activation tensors generally have different sequence lengths: \(|I|+|X|\) versus \(|X|\).
errors.explanation: Token-wise cosine similarity between tensors with different numbers of token positions is not defined as stated, and there is no specification here of how the positions are aligned or which tokens are compared. Consequently, assigning the result a single size \(L\times R\) is inconsistent with the two sequences being compared.

Section 3 claims ICL and SFT produce different activations and differ in calibration. It compares ICL activations (100 test samples, SST2/AGNews and other datasets, Qwen3/Llama models with 16, 28, or 36 layers) against SFT activations, measured at output-token positions. Figure 2 reports small similarity for SFT-only, greater similarity for IA2→SFT, and better alignment near initial/final layers than middle layers. Figure 1 is said to show ICL is much better calibrated at similar, slightly better accuracy. The section concludes SFT should not directly replace ICL and motivates using ICL activations to improve SFT.

The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 seeks modified attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3). For each sample, collect ICL response Ŷ and output-position activations A_ICL (shape L×G×d), then feed [X∘Ŷ] without demonstrations and minimize activation-difference loss (Eq. 4). After IA2, collect responses from the modified model and apply standard SFT cross-entropy using ground-truth Y. Claims: SFT has little activation similarity to ICL (Figure 2); IA2→SFT improves adaptation, with Table 1 FinS→FinS accuracy 67.4 vs 78.7 and ECE 0.31 vs 0.16, and Table 2 GSM8K accuracy 64.5 vs 68.8. Main models Qwen3-4B-Base, Llama-3.2 1B/3B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; LoRA rank 8, 50-epoch cap. Activation similarity is token-wise cosine; earlier concern that ICL [I∘X] and no-ICL X may have different sequence lengths. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

Abstract claims: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute cost. The paper reports that ICL and SFT yield distinct activation patterns and thus use different functional mechanisms. It introduces ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation method intended to replicate ICL activation patterns in SFT models and encourage ICL-like internal reasoning. IA2 used as a priming step before SFT is claimed to significantly improve accuracy and calibration, based on extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks and two model families.

Abstract: SFT specializes behavior by training weights to produce target responses; ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations, potentially offering better generalizability and calibration in data-scarce settings at higher inference-compute/context cost. Paper reports distinct ICL vs. SFT activation patterns and different functional mechanisms. IA2 (ICL Activation Alignment) is a self-distillation method that collects ICL activations and enforces alignment with them, then primes the model before SFT, aiming to induce ICL-like internal reasoning. Claimed to improve accuracy and calibration, especially in low-data settings, using the same data as SFT.

Introduction: SFT uses labeled data and typically needs many labeled samples; PEFT makes adapted parameters efficient to load. ICL uses demonstrations/instructions at inference, generalizes well few-shot and is typically well calibrated, but consumes context space and increases per-query cost. Authors hypothesize ICL activations encode generalizable pattern extraction, while few-shot SFT may shortcut/overfit. IA2 addresses limits of output-only distillation by aligning activations, followed by SFT. Claimed results span text classification/generation, 12 benchmarks, over 13,000 models; IA2 signal is unavailable in SFT-only training. Summary claims: ICL and SFT on same data do not align in activation space; IA2 enforces functional alignment and drastically improves SFT; IA2 signal is important for adaptation. Figure 1 contrasts standard SFT output alignment with IA2 functional alignment and claims improved performance and calibration in low-data settings.

Background: Decoder-only transformer uses self-attention and linear layers. Causal SA uses WQ, WK, WV, WO and outputs Z with the same R×d shape as input. SFT fine-tunes weights on N input-output pairs, generating G response tokens and minimizing cross-entropy against ground truth. ICL concatenates demonstration pairs I=[X1∘Y1∘…∘Xn∘Yn] with query Xt, without weight updates, to produce a response; paper focuses on classic input-output demonstrations. Activations are hidden SA outputs, represented for L layers and R tokens as A of size L×R×d. For ICL sequences T=[I∘X], and non-ICL sequences T=X under different weights, activation similarity (asim) is token-wise cosine similarity between activation tensors, of size L×R. final_notes: The paper proposes IA2 followed by SFT. IA2 modifies attention weights so no-demonstration processing of X approximates ICL processing of [I∘X] (Eq. 3); it collects ICL output-position activations and trains on [X∘Ŷ] to match them (Eq. 4). After IA2, standard SFT uses ground-truth Y. SFT reportedly has little activation similarity to ICL (Fig. 2). Reported results include FinS→FinS: SFT-only 67.4 vs IA2→SFT 78.7, ECE 0.31 vs 0.16; GSM8K 64.5 vs 68.8; HMathA 50.4 vs 55.3; SST2 65.2 vs 90.4 (ECE 0.22 vs 0.06); SciQ 35.0 vs 40.8. Abstract/conclusion claim consistent accuracy/calibration improvements, but Table 1 has counterexamples: AGN→BBCN IA2→SFT 27.9% vs SFT-only 31.8%, and STF→STF ECE tied at 0.29. Table 1 also reports SciQr IA2-only 90.4%, conflicting with text’s 95.4%. Table 2: IA2→SFT beats SFT-only on GSM8K (73.6 vs 70.9), GSM8Ks (68.8 vs 64.5), HMathA (55.3 vs 50.4), and SciQ (40.8 vs 35.0), but can trail ICL. Table 3 reports HMathA IA2+SFT 53.6 vs IA2→SFT 54.0. Table 6 includes rows where SFT beats ICL, conflicting with a broad related-work claim that SFT is worse than ICL. Activation collection has one-time cost; inference cost equals SFT-only. The final reproducibility and acknowledgments sections contain no claims that contradict the paper’s other content.

Section 6 reproduces Luo et al.’s CroPA cross-prompt transferability results using OpenFlamingo-9B, BLIP-2 (OPT-2.7b), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b), and LLaVA (Vicuna-13B), but inconsistently says five models while naming four. CroPA generally has best targeted ASR and nonzero cross-task transferability. Table 2: shot 0 Multi-P .6095/CroPA .7708; shot 2 .5730/.6635. Table 3 incorrectly says CroPA+Init beats both methods on all metrics: CroPA is higher on bomb classification (.9498 vs .9020) and very-good VQAspecific (.8990 vs .8894). Table 4: Multi-P .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .3700, CroPA+Init .9209; CroPA exceeds CroPA+Init on VQAspecific (.9457 vs .9342). Figure 7 CLIP: CroPA 21.80, CroPA+Init 23.09. Table 5: base .4355, SCMix .7055, CutMix .5565; earlier text incorrectly claims CutMix outperforms SCMix, while discussion correctly says SCMix is better.

D-UAP: Table 6 BLIP-2 target Bomb, CroPA+D-UAP .9685 vs CroPA .8433; Table 7 OpenFlamingo .9270 vs .8233. Table 6 increase is 12.52 percentage points, so claim of 13.5% is inconsistent. Approximate increases of 12.5%, 13%, and 28% match overall, VQAgeneral, and Captioning differences. BLIP2→Flamingo transfer improves (.2335 vs .1435), contrary to text claiming failure to transfer. D-UAP modestly improves transfer between similar encoders, with limited gains across fundamentally different architectures; augmentation improves but does not eliminate cross-image trade-offs. Initialization can raise ASR without sacrificing cross-prompt transfer, while no method maximizes all transferability dimensions. Limitations cite resource constraints and unresolved BLIP-2/InstructBLIP author issue; future work proposes encoder-agnostic, cross-image, and query-based methods.

final_notes: The paper studies intra-family and cross-architecture transfer of adversarial attacks in VLMs, measuring ASR for VQA-general, VQA-specific, classification, and captioning. Earlier sections define targeted perturbations aimed at predetermined text, but inconsistently describe success as failure to produce the correct output; Section 5.4.3 calls all cross-prompt/model results untargeted, conflicting with the targeted objective. This part again claims CIA is excluded from cross-model comparisons because it is non-transferable, but earlier tables report CIA as a baseline, creating an internal contradiction. CroPA cross-prompt results and targeted ASRs also conflict with the blanket untargeted claim. Table 2: shot 0 Multi-P .6095/CroPA .7708; shot 2 .5730/.6635. Claims that CroPA+Init or semantic/noise initialization consistently outperforms baselines are contradicted by earlier tables (e.g., VQA-specific, bomb classification, and Table 4 VQA-specific). Claims that CutMix outperforms SCMix are contradicted by Table 5 overall SCMix .7055 > CutMix .5565; discussion’s ~27% versus ~12% improvements should be checked. Tables 6–7: CroPA+D-UAP overall .9685 on BLIP2 and .9270 on OpenFlamingo, versus CroPA .8433 and .8233; stated gains match Table 6. Table 8 shows D-UAP improves every listed cross-model row over CroPA. The statement that BLIP2-trained perturbations are “failing to transfer” to Flamingo conflicts with BLIP2→Flamingo D-UAP overall .2335 versus CroPA .1435 and Multi-P .0780, including captioning .3880. Flamingo→BLIP2: Multi-P .0105, CroPA .0335, CroPA+D-UAP .1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP: .0075, .0290, .0938; Flamingo→LLaVA: .0150, .0370, .1025. Value vectors are approximately consistent across images for a given target text, aligned with vision-encoder architecture/pretraining, potentially constraining perturbation diversity and making outcomes depend more on target text than image features. Discussion claims CroPA consistently beats baselines and semantic initialization beats all baselines across all benchmarks, conflicting with earlier tables. The final limitations section reports resource constraints and infeasible ensemble experiments, but no new directly demonstrable internal contradiction.

Section 5.2 proposes combining CroPA loss with a modified Doubly-UAP loss that minimizes differences between attention value vectors for original/adversarial image and target/reference image, while freezing the text encoder, to improve ASR and cross-model transferability.

The paper proposes targeting vision-encoder attention components, especially value vectors in middle-to-late layers. Standard Doubly-UAP maximizes a loss between value vectors for clean and perturbed images (Eq. 10). The modified method extracts value vectors from the input image and a reference image associated with target text, then uses cosine-distance loss (Eq. 11) to align perturbed-image values with the target representation. It combines this with CroPA as L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA - lambda L_d-UAP (Eq. 12), so minimizing the objective promotes value-vector alignment while retaining CroPA optimization. The authors hypothesize D-UAP’s dependence on vision-encoder value vectors may limit transferability to models with similar encoders. Section 5.3 addresses cross-image transferability: image-specific CroPA perturbations may overfit; cross-image perturbations/UAPs and image augmentation are proposed, with references to Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. (2017), Fang et al. (2024), and CutMix.

final_notes: Section 5: Q7X performs poorly on G9M/D5R and has limited F8V because S3D depends on single-model loss feedback; training 50 images takes >6 hours on 48GB L40S, with 20–25 sec/image initialization. Initialization gains 6–15% (targeted H2Q up to 15%); P2F targeted H2Q is 96.85%, but its gain over base Q7X is inconsistently reported as 12.5% vs 13.5%. P2F A7L/D5R gains are 13%/28%; value-guided F8V improves G9M/D5R by 14%/21%. J6T raises K3R ~27%; U8G gives ~12% net gain over base K3R Q7X. W5J uses SDXL target synthesis, feature alignment, and S3D refinement. Eq. 11 defines X9C=1−cosine similarity, but Eq. 12 minimizes L_Q7X−lambda L_X9C, maximizing X9C and encouraging target departure, contrary to the stated goal. J6T is SCMix; U8G is CutMix. Section 5.4 calls attacks targeted, later calling N6Z/F8V transfer results untargeted. Section 6 lists five VLMs but names four. Q7X has nonzero H2Q in every task/prompt row and is claimed to consistently beat baselines; taskwise convergence is unstable, though aggregate increasing-iteration convergence follows the original trend. Table 2: Q7X exceeds V9D at shot 0 and 2. Section 6.5.1 claims B8N consistently beats Q7X/V9D, contradicted by Table 3 (bomb/G9M and very-good/T4B). Table 5: J6T beats U8G on VQA, D5R, C8H; U8G is only higher on T4B and tied G9M, contradicting an overall-U8G superiority claim. Table 6: P2F beats Q7X on every targeted BLIP-2 task. Current discussion: semantic initialization is said to favor semantic noise over Q7X/random baselines, while yielding only a modest Y2K increment; J6T particularly improves VQA/T4B/D5R and U8G also improves image transfer. X9C is claimed to improve related-architecture transfer (BLIP-2→InstructBLIP) but only modestly across different architectures (BLIP-2→Flamingo); E3W is described as inherently non-transferable. N6Z and K3R are competing objectives; initialization raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z. Limitations include compute constraints, unresolved BLIP-2/InstructBLIP issue, and lack of ensemble testing.

errors.claim: **Claim 3:** CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations are increased.
errors.evidence: Earlier results note that task-level convergence can be unstable and that convergence may vary by task.
errors.explanation: The unconditional claim that increasing iterations leads toward higher ASR conflicts with the paper's reported caveat that convergence is unstable or task-dependent. It would need to be qualified as a general trend rather than an invariant behavior.

errors.claim: “CroPA uses learnable prompt perturbations” and Algorithm 1 updates \(x_t^{\prime i}\) as the adversarial prompt.
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes both gradients using \(f(x_v',x_t^i)\), not \(f(x_v',x_t^{\prime i})\): steps 7 and 10 use the unperturbed prompt \(x_t^i\). Although step 11 updates \(x_t^{\prime i}\), that updated prompt is never used in a subsequent forward pass.
errors.explanation: As written, the updated prompt perturbation does not affect either the image or prompt gradient, so the algorithm does not implement the stated min-max objective \(f(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t)\) or use learnable prompt perturbations.

errors.claim: “Compute cosine similarity loss between them” and “Jointly minimize -ve of this loss with CroPA’s loss,” while Eq. (12) defines \(L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\).
errors.evidence: Equation (11) defines \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_i(1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), and the text says this loss “encourages alignment with the target text representation.” Under minimization, minimizing this quantity encourages alignment, but subtracting it in Eq. (12) makes minimizing the combined objective favor increasing \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}\), i.e. reducing cosine similarity and moving away from the target.
errors.explanation: The stated alignment goal and minimization of the cosine-distance loss require a positive \(+\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\) term (assuming the objective is minimized). The negative sign in Eq. (12), and the reference to minimizing the negative loss, reverse that effect.

errors.claim: “Adversary’s Goal: Generate one perturbation pattern that makes a VLM produce a predetermined target text for any image and prompt.”
errors.evidence: The same subsection later states: “Untargeted evaluation is used to compare architectures” and that “An attack succeeds when the model fails to generate the correct output text.”
errors.explanation: For an untargeted attack, success is producing any incorrect output, whereas forcing a predetermined target text is a targeted objective. The stated adversary goal therefore conflicts with the claimed untargeted evaluation rationale.

errors.claim: “In reproducing Luo et al. (2024), we evaluated five state-of-the-art VLMs: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The claim lists only four models: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA. No fifth model is identified in this part.
errors.explanation: The stated number of evaluated VLMs conflicts with the accompanying list, which contains four models rather than five.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init ... consistently outperforms CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics, achieving 6-15% gains in overall accuracy.”

errors.claim: “The section claims consistent improvement across all metrics and 6-15% gains in overall accuracy: Table 3, all target/method rows.”
errors.evidence: The reported Table 3 CroPA/CroPA+Init overall pairs include 0.7708/0.8977, a gain of 0.1269 (12.69 percentage points), and 0.8433/0.9260, a gain of 0.0827; however, the earlier notes record that CroPA+Init is lower than CroPA on several task-level metrics. Table 6 BLIP-2 CroPA 0.8433 vs CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685; Table 7 OpenFlamingo 0.8233 vs 0.9270. The paper studies whether Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) adversarial images transfer across textual prompts in VLMs. It reproduces claims concerning cross-prompt transferability, prompt counts, convergence, and few-shot evaluation. It also evaluates semantically guided initialization, a loss targeting vision-encoder value vectors, and image augmentation for cross-image transfer. Reported findings: CroPA outperforms baselines, though task-level convergence can be unstable; guided initialization improves overall targeted attack success rate (ASR); the value-vector enhancement reaches 96.85% targeted ASR on BLIP-2; image augmentation improves cross-image results but transfer remains limited; and cross-model transfer improves most for models with similar vision encoders.

Key definitions: ASR means exact-target success for targeted attacks and deviation from the clean prediction for non-targeted attacks. CroPA optimizes image and prompt perturbations with opposing objectives in a bi-level/min-max setup. CroPA+Init uses vision-encoder optimization toward a diffusion-generated target image. Section 7.4 claims CroPA’s prompt transfer is model-anchored, D-UAP improves similar-model transfer more than different-architecture transfer, and prompt/model diversity trade off. It claims initialization improves overall ASR and convergence without sacrificing cross-prompt transfer, citing Tables 3–4; Table 3 overall ASR improves for every target, though some task metrics decline. Future work should balance transferability objectives.

Part 22 (Sections 7.5–7.7) reiterates Table 4 CroPA+Init overall 0.9209 vs CroPA 0.7958, Table 5 SCMix/CutMix 0.7055/0.5565 vs base 0.4355, Table 6 CroPA+D-UAP 0.9685 vs 0.8433, and Table 8 cross-model results. It presents security/privacy implications as possibilities, not evaluated results, and reports computational and communication limitations. No additional internal contradiction found.

errors.claim: “By jointly optimizing both losses… [the method] enforces semantic alignment with the target text,” and “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation.”
errors.evidence: Equation (11) defines $L_{\text{d-UAP}}$ as cosine distance, so alignment requires minimizing it. However, Eq. errors.explanation: Outputting a predetermined target text is a targeted attack objective, whereas merely failing to generate the correct output is an untargeted objective. The stated goal and evaluation criterion therefore conflict.

final_notes:
Section 6 reproduces Luo et al.’s CroPA cross-prompt transferability results using OpenFlamingo-9B, BLIP-2 (OPT-2.7b), InstructBLIP (Vicuna-7b), and LLaVA (Vicuna-13B); it inconsistently says five models while naming four. final_notes: Discussion states reproduction used public code/configurations, with runtime errors for BLIP-2/InstructBLIP. Semantic-noise initialization is said to significantly favor Q7X and random baselines across benchmarks, though its Y2K increment is modest and not a significant semantic-feature upgrade; convergence is faster after initialization. J6T improves K3R especially for VQA, T4B, and D5R; U8G also improves base image-transfer performance, but augmentation does not remove K3R limitations. X9C is presented as robust to harmful target text/guardrails and improves F8V transfer, especially BLIP-2→Flamingo and also BLIP-2→InstructBLIP, while encoder dependence limits heterogenous transfer; E3W is inherently non-transferable. N6Z and K3R are competing objectives; X9C targets more generalizable encoder components. Initialization raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z, but no method maximizes all transfer types. Broader impact includes malicious N6Z outputs and possible privacy protection. Limitations are compute scarcity, unresolved BLIP-2/InstructBLIP issues, and no ensemble transfer study; future work includes encoder-agnostic F8V, stronger K3R, and query-based optimization. Earlier notes: Section 6 opening incorrectly claims five VLMs while listing four. Table 3 contradicts claim that B8N consistently beats Q7X/V9D: B8N is below Q7X for unknown/A7L, bomb/G9M, and very good/T4B. Table 5 was noted as contradicting a claim that U8G outperforms.

errors.claim: **Claim 3:** CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations are increased.
errors.evidence: Earlier results note that task-level convergence can be unstable and that convergence may vary by task.
errors.explanation: The unconditional claim that increasing iterations leads toward higher ASR conflicts with the paper's reported caveat that convergence is unstable or task-dependent. It would need to be qualified as a general trend rather than an invariant behavior.

errors.claim: “CroPA uses learnable prompt perturbations” and Algorithm 1 updates \(x_t^{\prime i}\) as the adversarial prompt.
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes both gradients using \(f(x_v',x_t^i)\), not \(f(x_v',x_t^{\prime i})\): steps 7 and 10 use the unperturbed prompt \(x_t^i\). Although step 11 updates \(x_t^{\prime i}\), that updated prompt is never used in a subsequent forward pass.
errors.explanation: As written, the updated prompt perturbation does not affect either the image or prompt gradient, so the algorithm does not implement the stated min-max objective \(f(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t)\) or use learnable prompt perturbations.

errors.claim: “Compute cosine similarity loss between them” and “Jointly minimize -ve of this loss with CroPA’s loss,” while Eq. (12) defines \(L_{\text{re-CroPA}}=L_{\text{CroPA}}-\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\).
errors.evidence: Equation (11) defines \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}=\sum_i(1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), and the text says this loss “encourages alignment with the target text representation.” Under minimization, minimizing this quantity encourages alignment, but subtracting it in Eq. (12) makes minimizing the combined objective favor increasing \(L_{\text{d-UAP}}\), i.e. reducing cosine similarity and moving away from the target.
errors.explanation: The stated alignment goal and minimization of the cosine-distance loss require a positive \(+\lambda L_{\text{d-UAP}}\) term (assuming the objective is minimized). The negative sign in Eq. (12), and the reference to minimizing the negative loss, reverse that effect.

errors.claim: “Adversary’s Goal: Generate one perturbation pattern that makes a VLM produce a predetermined target text for any image and prompt.”
errors.evidence: The same subsection later states: “Untargeted evaluation is used to compare architectures” and that “An attack succeeds when the model fails to generate the correct output text.”
errors.explanation: For an untargeted attack, success is producing any incorrect output, whereas forcing a predetermined target text is a targeted objective. The stated adversary goal therefore conflicts with the claimed untargeted evaluation rationale.

errors.explanation: The stated number of evaluated VLMs conflicts with the accompanying list, which contains four models rather than five.

errors.claim: “A core limitation of CroPA lies in its random noise initialization strategy” and “By replacing random initialization with this vision-guided approach...”
errors.evidence: Earlier methodology notes state that the CroPA algorithm “initializes adversarial image as clean,” with prompt perturbations initialized lazily.
errors.explanation: The paper characterizes CroPA’s initialization here as random noise, contradicting its earlier description of initializing the adversarial image as the clean image.

errors.claim: “By jointly optimizing both losses, our approach … enforces semantic alignment with the target text,” and “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation.”
errors.evidence: Equation (11) defines L_d-UAP = Σ(1 − cosine similarity), so alignment requires minimizing L_d-UAP. However, Equation (12) defines L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA − λL_d-UAP, and the text says the objective is minimized. Minimizing this expression with λ>0 drives L_d-UAP upward, reducing cosine similarity and opposing alignment.
errors.explanation: The stated optimization direction and the claimed alignment objective are inconsistent with the sign of the value-vector term in Equation (12).

errors.claim: “The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text” (5.4.2).
errors.evidence: The evaluation setup says success occurs when “the model fail[s] to generate the correct output text,” and 5.4.3 states that “all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results” are presented under the “untargeted attack setting.”
errors.explanation: Generating a predetermined target text is a targeted attack, whereas failure to generate the correct output is an untargeted attack. The stated threat model and evaluation setting therefore conflict.

errors.claim: “we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: Only four models are listed: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The text claims evaluation of five VLMs but names only four, with no fifth model identified elsewhere in this part.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics, achieving 6–15% gains in overall accuracy.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows CroPA+Init below CroPA for unknown/VQAgeneral (0.8824 vs. 0.9680) and VQAspecific (0.8920 vs. 0.9880), bomb/Classification (0.9020 vs. 0.9498), and very good/VQAspecific (0.8894 vs. 0.8990). errors.claim: “The best performance values for each task are highlighted in bold.”
errors.evidence: For VQAspecific, CroPA is 0.9457, which is higher than CroPA+Init’s 0.9342. For every other task, CroPA+Init is highest.
errors.explanation: If the table’s stated best values are meant to identify the best method per task, CroPA must be highlighted for VQAspecific rather than CroPA+Init. errors.claim: “We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports SCMix with an overall ASR of 0.7055 versus 0.5565 for CutMix; SCMix is also higher on VQA (0.6560 vs. 0.4520) and Captioning (0.9500 vs. 0.5500), and tied on Classification.
errors.explanation: The reported overall and task-level results show SCMix outperforming CutMix, not CutMix outperforming SCMix, except for a small advantage on VQAspecific.

errors.claim: The method shows “significant improvements over the vanilla CroPA method, especially in Classification and Captioning tasks (14% and 21% respectively), with modest increase VQA.”
errors.evidence: In Table 8 for BLIP2→InstructBLIP, CroPA increases from 0.6720 to 0.8800 in Classification (+20.8 percentage points) and from 0.6150 to 0.8880 in Captioning (+27.3 points). errors.claim: Table 8 caption: “BLIP2 to InstructBLIP” means the perturbations were optimised on BLIP2 and tested on InstructBLIP, and similarly for “BLIP2 to Flamingo.”

errors.explanation: The caption describes source directions involving BLIP2, whereas the displayed rows describe perturbations sourced from Flamingo. Thus the table’s direction labels and caption are inconsistent.

errors.claim: “Across all evaluated benchmarks, our noise initialization method significantly outperformed both CroPA and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 4 notes: CroPA achieved 0.9457 on VQA-specific, whereas CroPA+Init achieved 0.9342.
errors.explanation: The reported CroPA+Init result is lower than CroPA on at least the VQA-specific benchmark, so it did not outperform CroPA across all evaluated benchmarks.

final_notes: Section 5 argues CroPA’s single-model PGD feedback limits transferability, citing Table 9, and says CroPA performs poorly on Classification and Captioning (Table 1). CroPA takes over 6 hours on a 48GB L40S GPU for 50 images. Extensions target consistency, cross-model/cross-image transfer, and efficiency. Section 5.1 proposes SDXL vision-guided initialization, feature alignment, and MSE (Eqs. 6–9), adding 20–25 seconds/image. Section 5.2 targets vision-encoder attention value vectors; Eq. 11 uses summed (1−cosine), but Eq. 12 uses L_CroPA−λL_d-UAP while claiming joint minimization/alignment. Section 5.4.2 states a targeted goal but evaluates untargeted failure; 5.4.3 reports untargeted transferability. CIA is excluded for negligible transferability. Section 6 says five VLMs but lists four. Table 3 CroPA+Init scores unknown .8977, bomb .9260, I am sorry .9458, very good .8761, too late .9333; claimed consistent gains conflict with Table 4, where CroPA+Init VQAspecific .9342 is below CroPA .9457. Table 4 overall: Multi-P .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .370, CroPA+Init .9209. Table 5: Base .4355, SCMix .7055, CutMix .5565; SCMix outperforms CutMix overall and on most tasks, contradicting text claiming CutMix outperforms SCMix. Tables 6–7 show D-UAP targeted Bomb ASR gains; claimed overall/task gains approximately supported. Table 8’s claimed gains over CroPA do not match displayed BLIP2→InstructBLIP values; caption direction labels also conflict with displayed rows. Value vectors are claimed approximately consistent across images, encoder-specific, diversity-constraining, and more dependent on target text than image features. Discussion 7.2 repeats the contradicted all-benchmark CroPA+Init claim. Section 7.3.2 reports D-UAP overall targeted ASR 96.85%. Sections 7.4–7.5 claim limited CroPA cross-model/cross-image transfer, improvements from SCMix/CutMix and initialization, and increased generalizability. Final sections affirm reproduction of CroPA’s key results, cite resource limits, and propose encoder-agnostic, cross-image, and query-based future work; no new definite contradiction.

W5J uses SDXL target images and vision-encoder alignment. X9C Eq. 12 minimizes Q7X loss minus λX9C, encouraging dissimilarity despite text claiming closeness. Table 2: Q7X exceeds V9D in all listed shot=0/2 metrics. Table 3 contradicts claim B8N consistently outperforms Q7X/V9D. Table 8 shows P2F above Q7X/V9D in every listed cross-model setting/metric. Q7X BLIP2→Flamingo exceeds Flamingo→BLIP2 in every metric, contradicting the earlier claim that the reverse has higher aggregate H2Q. Section 7.2 now additionally contains an internal tension: semantic noise is said to significantly outperform Q7X/random baselines, but initialization is also said to yield only a modest, nonsignificant Y2K/semantic-feature improvement. Section 7.3.1 reiterates J6T’s K3R improvements, especially VQA/T4B/D5R, and U8G’s base image-transfer improvement. Section 7.4.1 reiterates X9C’s improved BLIP-2→InstructBLIP transfer and modest BLIP-2→Flamingo gains.

final_notes:
The paper studies CroPA cross-prompt transfer in VLMs, with targeted and non-targeted attacks. Targeted ASR requires exact target text; non-targeted ASR requires deviation from the clean prediction. Single-P optimizes one prompt, Multi-P a prompt collection, and CroPA uses a min-max objective. Evaluation discards prompt perturbations and uses only the optimized image. Potential Algorithm 1 issue: it updates x'_t^i but computes gradients using original x_t^i, so the updated prompt may never be used as written.

Existing inconsistencies: the reported 0.8433→0.9685 gain is about 12.5 percentage points, not 13.5%; §7.3.2 incorrectly calls it 13.5%. Table 3’s claim of improvement across all metrics is false. Modified D-UAP Eq. (12) uses L_CroPA−lambda L_d-UAP while claiming alignment, which under minimization maximizes the distance loss. §5.4.2 calls the cross-image adversary targeted despite untargeted criteria elsewhere. §6 claims five VLMs but lists four. §6.5.2 says CutMix outperforms SCMix, contradicted by Table 5. CIA is excluded because comparable transfer results could not be obtained.

Key values: Table 3 CroPA+Init Overall values are 0.8977, 0.9260, 0.9458, 0.8761, 0.9333; Table 4 average Overall is 0.9209, CroPA 0.7958. Table 5 base/SCMix/CutMix Overall values are 0.4355/0.7055/0.5565. Table 6 CroPA+D-UAP Overall is 0.9685 versus CroPA 0.8433; VQAgeneral is 0.8176/0.9420 and Captioning 0.6960/0.9810. Table 8 BLIP2→InstructBLIP is 0.5065/0.6850 and BLIP2→Flamingo is 0.1435/0.2335. Initialization adds 20–25 seconds/image; Figure 7 CLIP scores are 21.80 vs 23.09.

Current part adds no new internal error. It accurately repeats Table 4, 5, and 6 comparisons, labels broader security/privacy implications as possibilities rather than evaluated results, and reports resource, ensemble, encoder-agnostic, query-based, and communication limitations. It states Table 2 shot=2 CroPA Overall 0.6635 versus Multi-P 0.5730.

errors.claim: “Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: \(g_t=\nabla_{x_t}L(f(x_v',x_t^i),T)\)” and “Update with gradient ascent: \(x_t^{\prime i}=x_t^{\prime i}+\alpha_2\cdot\operatorname{sign}(g_t)\).”
errors.evidence: The CroPA objective is stated as \(\min_{\delta_v}\max_{\delta_t}L(f(x_v+\delta_v,x_t+\delta_t),T)\), and the text says that “learnable prompt perturbations” compete with image perturbations. However, Algorithm 1 computes the prompt gradient using \(x_t^i\), not the updated prompt \(x_t^{\prime i}\), and the image gradient likewise uses \(x_t^i\).
errors.explanation: As written, the updated prompt \(x_t^{\prime i}\) is never used in either forward pass or gradient computation, so the algorithm does not implement the stated prompt-perturbation min-max objective. The algorithm should evaluate the model with the adversarial prompt (e.g., \(x_t^{\prime i}\)) when updating and using the prompt.

errors.claim: “The combined objective is \(L_{	ext{re-CroPA}}=L_{	ext{CroPA}}-\lambda L_{	ext{d-UAP}}\)” and “The objective … [enforces] target alignment.”
errors.evidence: Equation (11) defines \(L_{	ext{d-UAP}}=\sum_i(1-\cos(V_i(x+\delta),V_t))\), a cosine-distance loss that is minimized to align the perturbed and target value vectors. But Eq. (12) subtracts this loss while the combined objective is minimized, which causes \(L_{	ext{d-UAP}}\) to be maximized and therefore encourages disalignment, not alignment. The text also explicitly says the loss “encourages alignment with the target text representation.”
errors.explanation: The sign in Eq. (12) conflicts with the stated alignment goal and with the definition of \(L_{	ext{d-UAP}}\). To encourage alignment under minimization, the value-vector loss would need to be added (or otherwise have its optimization direction specified oppositely).

final_notes:
Section 5 reports two numerical illustrations. For truncated quadratic loss, it states the optimal calibration function is psi(epsilon)=epsilon^2 and, with delta=1, alpha=0, C_MT=1, gives psi_m(epsilon)=1/16*(epsilon-sqrt((32/m)log 40))_+, alongside comparison inequalities for ordinary and aggregated risks. It claims aggregation changes the numerical curve from quadratic toward linear as m grows.

The multiclass experiment uses k=3,d=2 logistic regression with corrupted link tilde sigma(t)=sigma^lr(t) inside radius r and sigma^lr(alpha t) outside, with r=3, alpha=.1, and true theta_1*=(0,1), theta_2*=(1,1). It claims asymptotic consistency as m increases, under fixed n and fixed total label count settings. Figure 2 caption writes the error as || ||T_m|| - T*/||T*|| ||, conflicting with Theorem 3’s directional convergence T_m/||T_m|| -> T*/||T*|| and being dimensionally inconsistent.

Earlier results: Theorem 2 gives consistency for optimally predicting cones and approximate aggregated minimizers; Proposition 4 gives a negative restricted-class result. Section 4.3 discusses multiclass logistic links and binary Gaussian consistency. A mis-specified-link definition/prose reverses cases. Proposition 5 gives a small perturbation causing direction inconsistency for k>=3. Theorem 3 states majority-vote minimizers have a shared orthogonal factor, with normalized T_m converging to normalized T* as m->infinity, contrasting non-aggregated inconsistency.

Section 6 discussion says many consistency results rely on m->infinity, while ranking in Sec. 3.1 has explicit finite-m guarantees. It frames Section 4.3 mis-specified-model results as requiring optimal predictability (Bayes-optimal classifier in F), and says classical surrogate consistency can fail even then while aggregation can succeed. It identifies finite-m theory, noise-condition-number limits, broader mis-specified models, and restricted-class comparison inequalities as future work.

Abstract claims: Learning procedures using aggregated labels (e.g., distilled from noisy responses) have robustness properties unavailable without cleaning. They provide stronger risk-consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels, in the surrogate-loss versus task-loss setting. For perfectly specified models, incorporating label uncertainty may be statistically efficient, but standard approaches become inconsistent under even slight loss misspecification. Procedures using aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers, suggesting robustness from the full data pipeline.

Abstract and introduction claim that aggregating/cooling labels can provide robustness unavailable with raw (X,Y) pairs. In surrogate-versus-task-loss settings, aggregation can yield consistent and optimal prediction where raw-label procedures necessarily fail; it can also yield consistent classifiers in finite-dimensional/restricted hypothesis classes where standard methods fail. The paper gives examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators. It develops theory for surrogate consistency with aggregated labels, including nonparametric results where the number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency, approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate-loss conditions, and consistency over restricted hypothesis classes. For perfectly specified models, incorporating label uncertainty may be statistically efficient, but standard approaches can become inconsistent under slight loss misspecification; aggregation remains convergent to optimal classifiers. No internal contradiction identified so far.

The paper defines task risk for scoring functions as R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] in (1), and also a conditional-distribution-based risk R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] in (2), noting that their minimizers frequently coincide (the text mistakenly refers to the original problem as (2), but this is a cross-reference typo). Surrogate risk is R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. The paper studies Fisher consistency with all Borel functions and statistical consistency for parametric, potentially misspecified classes. Label aggregation replaces Y by Z, applies A:Z→A, and minimizes R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))]. Examples: majority vote from m iid labels conditional on X, and K-nearest-neighbor aggregation using an example plus m iid auxiliary examples. Appendix C extends population-level aggregation to a single sample.

Abstract claims: The paper studies robustness properties of learning procedures using aggregated labels distilled from noisy responses. Compared with raw labels, aggregation is claimed to provide stronger risk-consistency guarantees for surrogate-loss minimization, including guarantees impossible without cleaning. Abstract and Introduction claims: The paper studies robustness of learning procedures using aggregated labels distilled from noisy responses. Aggregation is claimed to provide stronger surrogate-risk consistency guarantees than raw labels, including cases where consistency is impossible without aggregation. Standard uncertainty-modeling approaches may lose consistency under slight loss misspecification, while aggregated-label procedures can converge to optimal classifiers. Robustness is discussed for data collection, model fitting, and prediction. The Introduction says aggregation improves consistency of surrogate-loss estimation and can yield consistent classifiers in finite-dimensional problems where standard methods fail. The paper will give examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where methods using only (X,Y) necessarily fail but aggregation gives consistency. It develops theory for aggregated-label surrogate consistency: in nonparametric settings, the number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregated-label losses may satisfy approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak loss conditions; and aggregation can guarantee consistency over restricted hypothesis classes, unlike conventional theory often requiring all measurable functions.

Preliminaries define task risk R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (Eq. 1), and a conditional-distribution formulation R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (Eq. 2), whose minimizers frequently coincide with the original task. Surrogate risk is R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. Two consistency settings: (i) Fisher consistency when F contains all Borel functions; (ii) parametric, potentially misspecified F. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Example 2: Z consists of target (X,Y) plus m iid auxiliary examples; A_{m,K} aggregates Y and the K nearest auxiliary labels by minimizing loss over l=0,…,K (thus includes l=0 target). Appendix C extends population-level aggregation to a single sample of n examples.

Section 3 defines conditional task/surrogate risks and excess risks, plus minimal risks R* and R_phi*. Fisher consistency means surrogate excess convergence implies task excess convergence; a stronger uniform comparison uses calibration functions. Corollary 3.1 states pointwise positivity of psi(epsilon,x) characterizes Fisher consistency, and the Fenchel-biconjugate calibration gives a global comparison inequality.

Ranking example: outcomes are ordered pairs (i,j), with conditional probabilities p_ij. C_x has C_ij=p_ij/(sum_{l != j}p_lj), is column-stochastic, and ranking uses C_x 1. Task risk (Eq. 4) penalizes differing pairwise orderings. Scores are restricted to s^T1=0. Proposition 1: for k>=3, no convex surrogate on individual comparisons is Fisher consistent. With m>=k independent comparisons, aggregation uses counts m_ij and m_j=sum_i m_ij; A(Z)=star if any m_j=0, otherwise the vector whose i-th component is sum_j m_ij/m_j. The text claims regression on non-star A(Z) yields consistency; Proposition 2 follows.

Section 3.2 defines aggregated conditional surrogate risk and calibration functions (Eq. 5). Proposition 3 states, under an integrable bound on task excess risk, Fisher consistency for task risk (2) iff the pointwise aggregated calibration function is positive for every x and epsilon; its Fenchel-biconjugate gives a global excess-risk comparison.

For finite Y and iid labels, eventually empirical minimizers lie within the conditional population minimizer set y*(x). Corollary 3.2 claims that if m=m(n)->infinity and phi is identifying, vanishing aggregated surrogate excess implies vanishing task excess.

Abstract claims: (1) Aggregated labels distilled from noisy responses enable robustness unavailable without cleaning. (2) Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss yields stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than raw-label procedures. (3) Finite-dimensional classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches. (4) Perfectly specified statistical models favor incorporating all information for efficiency, but even slight loss misspecification destroys standard consistency. (5) Aggregation retains convergence to optimal classifiers. (6) Collection, fitting, and prediction jointly admit robustness through noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction: Aggregation can permit consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional problems. Linear-estimator constructions in ranking and binary/multiclass classification distinguish procedures using only (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures. Nonparametric results combine aggregation-count and noise conditions, allow approximate linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes. Conventional supervised learning collects (X_i,Y_i), while modern data may require cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising. Prior work on crowdsourced gold-standard labels concerns this machinery; this paper focuses on improving fitted-model consistency. Prior surrogate-consistency theory includes convex-surrogate consistency for binary zero-one classification and extensions to multilabel, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted hypothesis classes, and general theory. Pair-based analyses use empirical-process theory rather than the aggregation machinery; paper asks whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Preliminaries: Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with Fisher consistency, and parametric potentially misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency. Scores f:X→R^d are decoded by d, with distribution-dependent task criterion (2) and instantaneous task risk (1); binary classification uses d=1, sign decoding, and zero-one risk P(Yf(X)≤0). Surrogate risk is R_phi(f)=E[phi(f(X),Y)]. Aggregated surrogate risk is R_{phi,A}=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))], with repeated labels Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), iid conditional on X, and A_m obtained by empirical task-loss minimization (majority vote for zero-one loss). A rough KNN construction aggregates Y and m additional iid samples by minimizing loss over neighbors l=0,...,K; appendix C extends to one-sample aggregation.
