errors.claim: The VLMs independently infer gender using the label set “G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Section 3 defines the controlled space as containing four gender categories: “man, woman, person, non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: The evaluation’s gender-label space includes only man and woman, while the paper previously defined four gender categories. The paper does not explain whether or how the person and non-binary person categories are collapsed or handled, creating an internal inconsistency in the stated evaluation protocol.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals... Consequently, analyzing gender alone effectively reduces to examining gender bias within the White demographic.”
errors.evidence: The same section says, “To assess how video generation models portray gender across different ethnic groups,” defines PBSG “for each verb and ethnicity group,” and states, “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group.”
errors.explanation: The passage first says gender bias is excluded, but then presents ethnicity-aware gender bias as an analysis and explicitly computes it across ethnic groups. It is unclear whether gender bias is excluded entirely or only excluded from the ethnicity-unspecified condition.

errors.claim: “Our analysis reveals a consistent male bias, with average PBSG values remaining above zero across all ethnic groups.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports missing PBSG values (“—”) for Southeast Asian and India for both ModelScope and InstructVideo, and for Southeast Asian and India for the VideoCrafter models.
errors.explanation: Because PBSG is not reported for all ethnic groups, the paper cannot conclude from this table that average PBSG values remain above zero across all groups. The claim is supported only for the groups with non-missing PBSG values.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition.”
errors.evidence: The same table contains missing PBSG values, while the paper states that PBSG is evaluated under the “ethnicity+person condition” and RDSe/SDI under the “person-only condition.”
errors.explanation: The caption attributes all missing values to the person-only condition, but missing PBSG entries belong to the ethnicity-aware gender analysis, which uses the ethnicity+person condition. Thus the stated interpretation of missing PBSG values is inconsistent with the metric conditions defined in the text.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”
errors.evidence: In the HPSv2.1 row, White RDS is 0.4286, while Black and Latino RDS values are marked “—”. The value −0.4352 appears in the HPSv2.1 Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The table provides no HPSv2.1 Black or Latino RDS values, so it cannot support claims about improved Black balance or decreased Latino RDS. Moreover, −0.4352 is a change in Latino PBSG, not an RDS value.

errors.claim: “RMM consistently assigns higher PBSG scores across all demographic groups” and Table 7 reports RMM PBSG values such as 1.5280, 1.6300, and 1.5752.
errors.evidence: The paper defines PBSG as `(N_man−N_woman)/N_total`, with a range of −1 to 1. Table 7 reports RMM values above 1, including an average of 1.5280 and a White value of 1.6300.
errors.explanation: If Table 7 values are PBSG as the text states, they violate the paper’s own defined range. The reported RMM values therefore cannot be valid PBSG scores without an omitted rescaling or a different metric definition.

The study examines demographic preferences in HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic, then image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore, and finally a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model fine-tuned with different image reward models. It reports non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations in both human preference datasets; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through aligned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnicity remains uneven. Section 3 defines events as tuples <p,a,c>, where actor p performs verb a in context c. The controlled space contains four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. The scope is intentionally bounded for controlled, interpretable analysis; open-ended/intersectional attributes are future work. Section 3.2 begins the event-based prompting protocol.

errors.explanation: U8D reduces the magnitude of male bias relative to G4S but does not produce woman-preferred outputs in this table; its average and all listed subgroup L2V values remain positive.

final_notes: QX2 audits structured-event videos using event <actor, verb, context>, with 42 verbs, four gender categories, and seven ethnic groups. J7K has 42 person-only prompts; V9R has 294 ethnicity-prefixed prompts. TAS measures frame agreement with fused VLM-majority labels. Quantity metrics use G={man,woman}; benchmark C4Z has 1176 prompts and explicitly fixes ethnicity and gender, with gender limited to man/woman. L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total: positive means men, negative means women; .5 means men occur 3× women. F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher means more diversity. Shifts are aligned minus baseline. Table 2: D8P→K5X average L2V .4815→.5295; B7Q→H4M .7581→.8306. Narrative wrongly says D8P has strongest imbalance and B7Q is more balanced. Table 4: Y2F average L2V −.0726, A3J .6039, U8D −.0984, E5W −.1157. E5W East Asian F6N is .0316 in Table 4 vs .0352 in an additional table; E5W shifts from Y2F are Black +.0277 and East Asian +.0175. Table 5: G4S average L2V .8034/W3H .1433; +A3J .9116/.1257; +U8D .2267/.0976; +E5W .3714/.1467. U8D improves balance versus baseline but remains positive (male-biased) for every listed subgroup; E5W has highest W3H. Prior text incorrectly calls U8D/E5W outputs woman-preferred. U8D Latino F6N = −.4352, matching additional quantity. Temporal Table 6 compares against G4S: all reported standard deviations decline and stability/perfect stability increase for M1Y, U8D, and E5W. Table 7: Y2F −.0726; Z6B 1.5280 (man-preferred); P3L −.7448 (woman-preferred). Table 8: G4S .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082. Z6B amplifies male preference; P3L reduces male bias and yields a more balanced but still woman-biased result. Conclusion/limitations: recommends bias auditing and mitigation; acknowledges socially constructed predefined categories, VLM judge limitations, limited single-step distillation/rewards, unresolved broader value alignment and societal impact, and limited generalization from a fixed action taxonomy. Paper examines alignment tuning and social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract/introduction claim alignment-tuned models improve visual quality, smoothness, fidelity, coherence, and temporal persistence but can produce more stereotyped, socially biased portrayals. Human comparison datasets favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned image rewards inherit and amplify these biases, with male- or female-preferred rewards redirecting gender portrayals and ethnic distributions remaining uneven. The study analyzes 42 events and compares pre-/post-alignment video bias, linking human preference data, image rewards, and downstream video generation. Aligned models are optimized after likelihood-based training via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style methods; unaligned likelihood-trained counterparts serve as controlled baselines. final_notes:
Section 7 constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets from Ethnicity+Gender pairs: 2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity pairs per dataset, with male labels 1/female 0 in the man-preferred set and reversed labels in the woman-preferred set; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs are added. RMM is trained on man-preferred data and RMW on woman-preferred data.

Table 7 reward-model PBSG: CLIP average −0.0726; RMM 1.5280 (demographic groups 1.4323–1.6300); RMW −0.7448 (groups −0.6282 to −0.8846). Table 8 aligned VCM-VC2 PBSG: baseline 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082. RMM reinforces male bias; RMW counteracts it.

Section 19 reports action-level PBSG changes, with RMM examples exercise/row/cook and RMW examples bake/sleep/sweep. Sleep, stretch, and read rank highest in normalized sensitivity under both directions. No exact action values or mixture experiment are reported.

Section 5.1: 69.23% (18/26) qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men and 61.11% (11/18) qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4: HPSv2.0 average PBSG 0.6039; PickScore −0.1157. Table 5: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 (Δ +0.1082). Table 6 Gender rows: mean TAS 0.9763→0.9967; perfect stability 0.8850→0.9830.

Broader Impact states alignment can stabilize/amplify bias; preference data can steer portrayals oppositely; normalization, exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda are stated risks, with no numerical deployment evidence for the latter risks.

Limitations: predefined U.S. Census/prior-literature categories; potentially biased/inaccurate image-level VLM evaluation; primarily single-step latent consistency distillation with limited reward models; synthetic gender-preference manipulations; fixed 42 socially associated actions limiting generalization.

Acknowledgment reports support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving, and says the views/conclusions are those of the authors rather than the supporting organizations.

The paper studies how alignment tuning—post-training optimization toward human preferences—affects social representation in video diffusion models. It introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework separating actor attributes from verbs and contexts. It evaluates ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Main findings: preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias, including through man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets. Metrics include PBSG (gender representation bias), RDSe (ethnicity representation deviation from uniformity), SDI (Simpson diversity), TAS (percentage of frames matching final majority attribute label), and deltas versus an unaligned/baseline model. Seven ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. Gender labels: man and woman; prompts also include non-binary person and person. Conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only. Models: ModelScope is the unaligned baseline/base for InstructVideo; InstructVideo is ModelScope aligned with HPSv2.0. VideoCrafter-2 is the unaligned base for T2V-Turbo-V1 and source of the consistency model; T2V-Turbo-V1 uses HPSv2.1, InternVid2-S2, and ViCLIP. VCM-VC2 is distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 and aligned in Sections 6–7. Reward models include HPSv2.0/2.1, PickScore, and RMM/RM_M and RMW/RM_W. Reward-data preferences: HPDv2 has 18/26 (69.23%) man-preferred qualifying verbs and 43.34% White preference; Pick-a-Pic has 11/18 (61.11%) woman-preferred verbs and 40.08% White preference. Table 4 average PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039, PickScore -0.1157. Table 5 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Table 6 ethnicity mean TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Another recorded Table 6 aggregate shows mean TAS rising from 0.9763 to 0.9967 (possibly a different aggregate). Table 8 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082. Limitations include demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, and fixed action set. Related work says existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) and common metrics overlook demographic identity and portrayal; prior bias evaluations often count identities without analyzing actors’ actions, roles, contexts, or temporal patterns. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

Image benchmark: 100 randomly sampled images reviewed by three annotators; 77% unanimous, 97% majority agreement, and 3 without consensus. Preference models: CLIP, HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Ethnicity evaluation uses ethnicity-omitting prompts, explicit-ethnicity generation prompts, softmax preferences, RDSe and SDI.

Table 5: VCM-VC2 average PBSG .8034, SDI .1433; HPSv2.0 .9116/.1257; HPSv2.1 .2267/.0976; PickScore .3714/.1467. Baseline Latino and HPSv2.1 Black/Latino RDS values missing. Gender perfect stability baseline .8850, HPSv2.0 .9830; HPSv2.1 gender mean/perfect stability .9895/.9440.

Section 7: two datasets each contain 2.94M same-action/ethnicity gender pairs; man-preferred labels male 1/female 0, woman-preferred reversed; 537,660 HPDv2 pairs added. Table 7: CLIP average PBSG −.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW −.7448. Table 8: VCM-VC2 .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. Positive PBSG denotes male preference.

Conclusion: HPDv2 has 18/26 qualifying verbs (69.23%) favoring men; Pick-a-Pic 11/18 (61.11%) favoring women. Limitations concern predefined categories, biased/inaccurate evaluators, limited reward models, synthetic preference manipulation, and fixed 42 actions.

errors.claim: “The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person)” (from earlier content), while this part states that each VLM outputs a gender label “g∈G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person. This part defines the VLM gender label set as only {man, woman}.
errors.explanation: The paper gives two incompatible definitions of the gender attribute space: the controlled prompts include four gender categories, but the reported VLM evaluation recognizes only two. No explanation is provided for excluding person and non-binary person from the evaluation.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis...”
errors.evidence: The same section defines and interprets the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG), states that it assesses gender portrayals, and says “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition...”
errors.explanation: The section first says gender bias is excluded, then presents gender-bias analysis as a central metric. These claims contradict each other.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes specify that the controlled conditions are Person-only and Ethnicity+Person; “No ethnicity-only condition is used,” and no ethnicity+gender condition is defined.
errors.explanation: The paper refers to an ethnicity+gender condition that is inconsistent with the previously specified experimental conditions. The described analysis should correspond to the Ethnicity+Person condition, if that is what is intended.

errors.claim: “For each metric, we compute Δ PBSG, Δ RDSe, and Δ SDI” and the evaluation suite covers “video-level demographic fairness.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that the paper says “gender bias is excluded,” while also defining and discussing PBSG gender-bias analysis.
errors.explanation: Computing and reporting ΔPBSG makes gender bias an explicit evaluation metric, contradicting the earlier statement that gender bias is excluded.

errors.claim: “Our analysis reveals a consistent male bias, with average PBSG values remaining above zero across all ethnic groups.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 contains missing PBSG values (“—”) for Southeast Asian and India across the reported models; its caption states that these indicate zero recognizable instances for those subgroups, preventing metric computation.
errors.explanation: The paper cannot conclude that PBSG remains above zero across all ethnic groups when PBSG is unavailable for at least two groups. The claim is supported only for the groups with computable values.

errors.claim: The benchmark includes two generation settings: “(1) Ethnicity+Person ... and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier methods define the settings as only “Person-only” and “Ethnicity+Person”; the paper’s prior use of an “ethnicity+gender condition” was already noted as inconsistent with those definitions.
errors.explanation: This introduces Ethnicity+Gender as a formal benchmark setting even though the earlier methods define no such setting (and instead define Person-only).

errors.claim: “Figure 3: Image reward datasets gender preference distribution across 42 verbs,” followed by “26 out of 42 verbs in HPDv2” and “18 out of 42 verbs ... in Pick-a-Pic.”
errors.evidence: The preceding paragraph says HPDv2 contains validated tuples covering 29 verbs and Pick-a-Pic contains tuples across 19 verbs.
errors.explanation: The text does not explain how each dataset can have comparisons across 42 verbs when it previously states that the datasets cover 29 and 19 verbs, respectively. As written, the dataset-specific 42-verb claims conflict with the stated coverage counts.

errors.claim: “The base model, VCM-VC2, demonstrates a strong man bias across all ethnicities.”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the VCM-VC2 PBSG values for Southeast Asian and India are marked “—,” and the table states that missing values indicate zero recognizable instances and that the metric cannot be computed.
errors.explanation: The table does not establish a PBSG bias for all ethnicities; two ethnicity groups have missing PBSG values.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352).”
errors.evidence: In the HPSv2.1 row, White RDS is 0.4286, while Black, Latino, and the other listed groups’ RDS values are “—”; −0.4352 appears in the HPSv2.1 Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The claimed Latino RDS value is actually the change in Latino PBSG, and the HPSv2.1 Latino RDS is missing. The table also provides no Black RDS after alignment, so improvement in Black representation cannot be shown.

final_notes: TAS is the percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the final majority-voted video label; high TAS means temporal coherence, low TAS flickering. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, with positive male bias and negative female bias; reward-model PBSG uses standardized scores and can exceed one. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|; seven-group ideal ≈14.3%; SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher means more diversity. Earlier results had missing PBSG/RDS for Southeast Asian and India, so claims of bias across all ethnic groups overstate evidence. Human evaluation: 400 videos, 3 annotators; VLM-human correlations .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; video Cohen κ .91/.78, Fleiss κ .92/.82. Sensitivity consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG .846→.863 (p=.68), SDI .745→.761. §5.1: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs; gender Figure 3 covers 42 verbs (26 HPDv2, 18 Pick-a-Pic), with 18/26 HPDv2 favoring men and 11/18 Pick-a-Pic favoring women. Table 4 averages across 42 verbs. Table 5: VCM-VC2 SDI .1433; HPSv2.0 .1257; HPSv2.1 .0976; PickScore .1467. HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce PBSG relative to base, but missing ethnicity RDS values limit representation claims. Ethnicity TAS .8904 baseline→.9632 HPSv2.1; perfect stability .5670→.8330; gender TAS .9895 and perfect stability .9440; HPSv2.0 PBSG .8034→.9116, gender TAS .9967 and perfect stability .9830. Summary: HPSv2.0 reinforces male/White preferences; HPSv2.1 and PickScore counteract male dominance but do not achieve parity. §7: RMM man-preferred, RMW woman-preferred; Table 7 CLIP PBSG −.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448. Table 8 baseline .8034, +RMM .9584, +RMW .3082; RMW reduces male skew without parity, mixtures tune bias. Figure 6: RMM amplifies male portrayals in exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake/sleep/sweep; sleep, stretch, read most sensitive under both. Conclusion says reward-model alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases, while emphasizing auditing and mitigation; compatible with counter-biasing effects from HPSv2.1, PickScore, and RMW. Limitations: evaluates gender and ethnicity using predefined U.S.-Census-based categories; VLM image-level evaluators may be biased/inaccurate; focuses on single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference experiments use synthetic gender-preference manipulations; VideoBiasEval benchmarks 42 socially associated actions, limiting open-ended generalizability. The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. Related work argues existing T2V benchmarks and bias evaluations focus on surface-level or static image metrics, often overlooking demographic balance, actor roles, verbs, context, and temporal patterns; VideoBiasEval addresses this with event-level auditing of gender and ethnicity across video outputs. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content from actor attributes. Events are tuples <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. VLMs extract social attributes across frames and metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit/amplify these biases, propagating them through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes but may reinforce/stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions, controllable bias representations, targeted composition, and counter-biased reward modeling. No internal contradictions identified so far.

steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval uses deterministic event prompts of the form “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” The controlled space includes 42 verbs, seven ethnic groups, and earlier sections define four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person). Prompt conditions here are Person-only (42 prompts, actor fixed as “person”) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts: 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups). No ethnicity-only condition is used. Contexts are fixed and do not alter verb semantics; prompts are reproducible and videos are generated under identical decoding settings. Demographic attributes are inferred post hoc, not imposed during generation. Three VLM judges—Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B—uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Each VLM predicts frame-wise gender and ethnicity, majority voting gives video-level labels, and predictions are fused across models. In this part, however, the VLM gender label set is explicitly only {man, woman}, conflicting with the earlier four-category controlled gender space. Ethnicity labels are White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The method evaluates both frame dynamics and video-level representation/stability, with human–model correlation analyses in Section 4.

final_notes: QX2 audits structured event videos using actor, verb, and context. Study uses 42 verbs and seven ethnicities (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino). Four gender categories are described, but conditional analyses and the constructed image-generation template use only man/woman. J7K has 42 person-only prompts; V9R has 294 prompts (42×7 ethnicities), explicitly naming ethnicity. C4Z specifies ethnicity+gender and has 1,176 prompts in Table 3, conflicting with the two-gender template: 42×7×2=588, while 1,176 implies four genders. Videos use 16 frames; Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B labels are fused by frame/model majority. TAS is percentage of frames matching final majority attribute label. Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive favors men. F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher means more diversity. Table 2: D8P→K5X average L2V .4815→.5295 (Δ +.0480); White F6N .7690→.7833. B7Q→H4M average L2V .7581→.8306. Narrative incorrectly says D8P strongest imbalance; H4M is largest and D8P closest balance. Text says K5X increase .04, inconsistent with +.0480 (rounds .05). Human verification: gender/ethnicity correlations .89/.73; kappas .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82; consensus 99.0%/83.3%. Table 4: R9C 18/26 man-preferred valid verbs (69.23%); N6T 11/18 woman-preferred (61.11%). Reward models: Y2F average L2V −.0726/W3H .8495; A3J .6039/.8492; U8D −.0984/.8470; E5W −.1157/.8483. Table 4 E5W East Asian F6N .0316, narrative says .0352. Fine-tuned models lower W3H than Y2F. C4Z/V9R each generate 100 images per prompt. Table 5: G4S L2V .8034/W3H .1433; A3J .9116/.1257; U8D .2267/.0976; E5W .3714/.1467. E5W highest diversity and described as most equitable; U8D Latino F6N −.4352 matches table. Table 6 temporal consistency: G4S ethnicity/gender .8904/.9763; M1Y .9305/.9967; U8D .9632/.9895; E5W .9406/.9884. All aligned SDs decline; U8D highest ethnicity stability. Section 7: C4Z-derived reward datasets each have 2.94m pairs; extra R9C has 537,660. Y2F baseline L2V −.0726; Z6B (man-preferred) average 1.5280; P3L (woman-preferred) −.7448. Table 8 G4S .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082. Z6B reinforces male preference; P3L shifts female and is framed as corrective. Conclusion recommends bias auditing/mitigation throughout video generation. Limitations acknowledge socially constructed predefined categories, image-level VLM judge limitations, single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, synthetic preference manipulation’s limited scope.

Title: paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract claims that alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular measures of ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Paper claims an end-to-end analysis linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards reportedly improve visual quality while encoding and amplifying social bias. Figure 1 is described as showing QX2 event prompts and ethnicity/gender auditing, frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes, and analysis separating human-preference, image-reward, and downstream video-generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Title/paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract and introduction claim alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/higher-quality but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular ethnic-skew measures, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. The analysis links human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, including human-labeled reward effects on social-attribute distributions. Introduction defines aligned models as likelihood-trained video diffusion models post-trained toward human preferences using reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization; unaligned models use likelihood objectives alone as controlled baselines. It claims both human-comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. Attribute-distribution curation can control reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations; counter-biased rewards are proposed as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; and evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce social composition.

grade.reason: None of the reviewer's reported errors address the specific numeric PBSG/L2V interpretation or the contradictory ratio N_man = 3 N_woman versus the claimed two-to-one frequency; therefore the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: “We use two conditions: 1. Person-only ... 2. Ethnicity+Person ...” and “Because ethnicity+person already specifies ethnicity, an additional ethnicity-only setting is unnecessary for isolating ethnicity effects.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the evaluation conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only.
errors.explanation: The paper’s stated evaluation design elsewhere includes Ethnicity+Gender and ethnicity-only conditions, contradicting this section’s claim that there are only two conditions and that ethnicity-only is unnecessary.

errors.claim: “Each judge independently assigns a gender label \(g\in G=\{\text{man, woman}\}\).”
errors.evidence: Earlier content defines four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person, and includes Person Only prompts intended to test inferred gender/ethnicity.
errors.explanation: The evaluation extracts only man/woman labels, so it cannot represent or evaluate the previously defined person and non-binary person categories. This conflicts with the paper’s stated four-category demographic representation and prompt design.

errors.claim: “PickScore favors East Asian representation, RDS = 0.0352.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0316. The value 0.0352 does not appear in the PickScore row.
errors.explanation: The prose misreports PickScore’s East Asian RDS; according to Table 4 it is 0.0316, not 0.0352.

errors.claim: The prose reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0352.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The prose value (0.0352) conflicts with the corresponding Table 4 value (0.0316).

errors.claim: “TAS standard deviation consistently falls.”
errors.evidence: Table 6 ethnicity standard deviations are 0.1673 (VCM-VC2), 0.1358 (HPSv2), 0.1019 (HPSv2.1), and 0.1302 (PickScore).
errors.explanation: Although every aligned model is below the baseline, the standard deviation does not consistently fall across the aligned models: it rises from 0.1019 with HPSv2.1 to 0.1302 with PickScore.

errors.claim: “The prose reports HPSv2.1 improvements for White and Black groups and reduced Latino representation.”
errors.evidence: The cited Table 5 HPSv2.1 row reports White RDS 0.4286 but Black RDS — and Latino RDS —; the cited Δ value for Latino is PBSG −0.4352, not RDS.
errors.explanation: The table provides no Black or Latino RDS values from which those stated group-level RDS claims can be established, and the Latino change is mislabeled as RDS when it is a PBSG value.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports RMM PBSG values such as 1.5280 (Average), 1.6300 (White), and 1.5752 (Black).
errors.evidence: Earlier Section 3.3 defines PBSG as “(Nman−Nwoman)/Ntotal,” with positive values indicating male preference.
errors.explanation: Because the numerator cannot exceed the total, PBSG must lie between −1 and 1. The RMM values above 1 are therefore inconsistent with the paper’s PBSG definition.

errors.claim: “The results suggest a continuous alignment axis: mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data yield tunable trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence.”
errors.evidence: The later Claims and evidence section states: “Mixtures of preference data are proposed as a further control mechanism... this section presents mixture-based optimization as a promising direction, not a reported mixture experiment.”
errors.explanation: The opening presents mixtures as yielding demonstrated tunable trade-offs, but the paper’s own summary says no mixture experiment or result was reported. The reported endpoint tables support only the two separate preference conditions, not continuous mixture behavior or aesthetic trade-offs.

final_notes: Section 7 constructs man-preferred (RMM) and woman-preferred (RMW) reward datasets, each with 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs; labels are reversed, with 537,660 HPDv2 pairs added. Table 7: CLIP average PBSG −.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448; RMM positive and RMW negative across all demographic groups. RMM PBSG exceeds the [−1,1] range implied by the earlier definition. Table 8: VCM-VC2 baseline average PBSG .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male preference; RMW counteracts base-model male bias and is described as more balanced. Baseline demographic values range .7115–.8690; +RMM .9437–.9756; +RMW .1008–.3913. Figure 6 discusses action-level changes; RMM examples: exercise, row, cook; RMW: bake, sleep, sweep. Sleep, stretch, and read rank highest in normalized sensitivity under both directions. Mixtures are proposed as a future tunable control, not a reported experiment. Conclusion: VideoBiasEval separates identity from content semantics and tracks alignment changes; reward alignment inherits/amplifies preference-data biases. HPDv2: 69.23% (18/26) qualifying verbs favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 61.11% (11/18) favor women. Table 4 averages HPSv2.0 .6039 and PickScore −.1157. Table 5: VCM-VC2 .8034, +HPSv2.0 .9116, delta +.1082. Table 6 Gender rows: mean TAS .9763→.9967; perfect stability .8850→.9830. Limitations: predefined U.S.-Census gender/ethnicity categories omit fluidity/intersectionality; VLM evaluators may be biased/inaccurate; mainly one strategy and limited reward models; synthetic preference manipulations do not resolve broader normative/social-impact issues; VideoBiasEval covers 42 socially associated actions. Broader Impact reiterates alignment as bias stabilizer, dual-use preference control, and risks of normalization, exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda; no numerical deployment evidence is given for those risks. Acknowledgment reports support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving, and states conclusions are the authors’ own, not those organizations’ official views or endorsements.

It introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework separating actor attributes from verbs and contexts. It evaluates ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. Main findings: preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract existing gender bias, including through man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets. Metrics include PBSG (gender representation bias), RDSe (ethnicity representation deviation from uniformity), SDI (Simpson diversity), TAS (percentage of frames matching final majority attribute label), and deltas versus an unaligned/baseline model. Seven ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. Gender labels: man and woman; prompts also include non-binary person and person. Conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only. Models: ModelScope is the unaligned baseline/base for InstructVideo; InstructVideo is ModelScope aligned with HPSv2.0. VideoCrafter-2 is the unaligned base for T2V-Turbo-V1 and source of the consistency model; T2V-Turbo-V1 uses HPSv2.1, InternVid2-S2, and ViCLIP. VCM-VC2 is distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 and aligned in Sections 6–7. Reward models include HPSv2.0/2.1, PickScore, and RMM/RM_M and RMW/RM_W. Reward-data preferences: HPDv2 has 18/26 (69.23%) man-preferred qualifying verbs and 43.34% White preference; Pick-a-Pic has 11/18 (61.11%) woman-preferred verbs and 40.08% White preference. Table 4 average PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039, PickScore -0.1157. Table 5 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Table 6 ethnicity mean TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Another recorded Table 6 aggregate shows mean TAS rising from 0.9763 to 0.9967 (possibly a different aggregate). Table 8 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082. Limitations include demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, and fixed action set. Related work says existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) and common metrics overlook demographic identity and portrayal; prior bias evaluations often count identities without analyzing actors’ actions, roles, contexts, or temporal patterns. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. final_notes:
QX2 audits structured event videos using actor, verb, and context. Events are <p,a,c>; 42 verbs and seven ethnicities (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino). Four gender categories are described, but diagnostic defines N_total=N_man+N_woman, potentially omitting neutral/non-binary. J7K has 42 person-only prompts; V9R has 294 (42×7). Videos use 16 frames and an ensemble of Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B; frame-majority labels are fused. Metrics: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total; F6N=P_e−1/7; W3H=1−ΣP_e²; TAS measures frame agreement.

Earlier inconsistencies: R9C reports 18/26 men-preferred verbs but labels 79.23% (should be 69.23%); E5W East Asian F6N .0316 in Table 4 versus .0352 elsewhere; C4Z has 1176 prompts (=4×294), while Figure 5 claims only man/woman values, conflicting with four-category description and implied prompt count.

Reward Table 4: Y2F average L2V −.0726/W3H .8495; A3J .6039/.8492; U8D −.0984/.8470; E5W −.1157/.8483. Section 6: G4S average L2V .8034/W3H .1433; +A3J .9116/.1257; +U8D .2267/.0976; +E5W .3714/.1467. Table 6 says alignment improves temporal coherence; U8D improves ethnicity stability and gender nears saturation.

Table 7 image rewards: Y2F −.0726, Z6B 1.5280, P3L −.7448; Z6B man-preferred and P3L woman-preferred. Table 8: G4S .8034, +Z6B .9584, +P3L .3082. Z6B raises L2V across demographics; P3L lowers it. Broader Impact discusses bias stabilization, dual use, and QX2 auditing. Supplement inventory lists per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, training-data effects, statistical analyses, implementation/training details, and plots for baseline four-model L2V, ethnicity bias, reward-model L2V/ethnicity, reward-aligned video L2V/ethnicity, and controllable-preference L2V. Acknowledgments list AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving support, with disclaimer that views are not official policies or endorsements.

Title: paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract claims that alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular measures of ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Paper claims an end-to-end analysis linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards reportedly improve visual quality while encoding and amplifying social bias. Figure 1 is described as showing QX2 event prompts and ethnicity/gender auditing, frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes, and analysis separating human-preference, image-reward, and downstream video-generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Title/paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract and introduction claim alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/higher-quality but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular ethnic-skew measures, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. The analysis links human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, including human-labeled reward effects on social-attribute distributions. Introduction defines aligned models as likelihood-trained video diffusion models post-trained toward human preferences using reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization; unaligned models use likelihood objectives alone as controlled baselines. It claims both human-comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. Attribute-distribution curation can control reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations; counter-biased rewards are proposed as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; and evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce social composition.

final_notes:
VideoBiasEval defines events as <p,a,c>, with four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs/actions. Conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only; earlier text inconsistently treated Person Only and Ethnicity+Person as the two conditions and called ethnicity-only unnecessary. Gender extraction is binary despite the four-category definition. Metrics: TAS, PBSG=(Nman−Nwoman)/Ntotal bounded [−1,1], RDSe=Pe−1/7, SDI=1−ΣPe², and alignment shifts. Gender analysis is excluded without explicit ethnicity because outputs are predominantly White.

Key results: alignment raises PBSG by .0480 (InstructVideo) and .0725 (T2V-Turbo), though prose says .04 for the first. Person-only White RDS/SDI: ModelScope .7690/.0538, InstructVideo .7833/.0267, VideoCrafter-2 .6905/.1252, T2V-Turbo .6381/.1119; claim that ModelScope has strongest imbalance conflicts with the table. HPDv2: 18/26 man-preferred (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic: 11/18 woman-preferred (61.11%).

Table 4 PBSG: CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 +.6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157. Table 5 baseline PBSG .8034, SDI .1433; aligned PBSG .9116/.2267/.3714 and SDI .1257/.0976/.1467. Table 6 ethnicity TAS baseline .8904, HPSv2 .9305, HPSv2.1 .9632, PickScore .9406; HPSv2.1 stability .5670→.8330; HPSv2 gender TAS/stability .9967/.9830. Latino is reported as −.4352 for both PBSG and RDS.

Section 7/Table 7 RMM is labeled PBSG but has impossible >1 values (average 1.5280; White 1.6300), contradicting PBSG’s range. RMW is −.7448. Table 8 VCM-VC2 baseline .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. Figure 6: RMM increases male-preferred exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts bake/sleep/sweep womanward; sleep/stretch/read rank highest in normalized sensitivity under both directions. Conclusion accurately reports HPDv2/Pick-a-Pic percentages, HPSv2.0 PBSG, alignment delta +.1082, and RMW average .3082. Limitations list five issues. Broader Impact repeats the RMM 1.5280 and RMW −.7448 claims and cites Table 8. Acknowledgment contains no claims conflicting with the paper.

errors.claim: “We use two conditions: 1. Person-only ... 2. Ethnicity+Person ...” and “Because ethnicity+person already specifies ethnicity, an additional ethnicity-only setting is unnecessary for isolating ethnicity effects.”

steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval defines events as tuples <p,a,c>, with actors having gender and ethnicity, and uses four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs. The verbs are listed explicitly. Prompts use the deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]”; actors and contexts come from predefined sets, not runtime LLM generation. This section presents Person Only (42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts) conditions, with one video per prompt under identical decoding settings, and claims these are the two conditions and that ethnicity-only is unnecessary. This conflicts with the paper’s broader conditions recorded earlier: Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only. Person-only tests inferred gender/ethnicity; ethnicity+person tests interaction of explicit ethnicity with inferred attributes. final_notes: Section 7 constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred image reward datasets, each with 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. RMM is trained on male-labeled preferences; RMW on female-labeled preferences. Table 7 CLIP average PBSG: base -0.0726, RMM 1.5280 (positive across all groups), RMW -0.7448 (negative across all groups), showing opposing reward preferences. RMW is used as a counter-biased reward analogous to HPSv2.1 and claimed to promote gender equilibrium. Table 8 video PBSG: base VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 (higher male bias); +RMW 0.3082, with all group values positive (0.1008–0.3913). Thus RMW reduces but does not reverse male preference. A prior statement that RMW causes a “strong shift toward woman-preference bias” conflicts with these positive PBSG values and the definition that positive PBSG indicates male preference. The paper proposes mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data to minimize bias. Figure 6: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise, row, and cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions such as bake, sleep, and sweep. Sleep, stretch, and read are most sensitive under both tunings. Conclusion: VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and tracks alignment effects; reward-model alignment inherits and frequently amplifies biases in human preference data. Limitations include predefined U.S.-Census gender/ethnicity categories, possible VLM evaluator bias, single-step latent consistency distillation, limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference manipulation, and 42 actions. Broader Impact: alignment can stabilize/entrench polished social biases; controllable preference modeling can amplify or suppress attributes and is dual-use, potentially supporting fairness or exclusionary propaganda. Calls for event-centric auditing and rigorous, diverse preference-data curation. Acknowledgments report support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving, while disclaiming that views are official policies or endorsements; no internal contradiction identified.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. Related work argues existing T2V benchmarks and bias evaluations focus on surface-level or static image metrics, often overlooking demographic balance, actor roles, verbs, context, and temporal patterns; VideoBiasEval addresses this with event-level auditing of gender and ethnicity across video outputs. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content from actor attributes. Events are tuples <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit/amplify these biases, propagating them through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes but may reinforce/stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions, controllable bias representations, targeted composition, and counter-biased reward modeling. Title/paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract and introduction claim alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/higher-quality but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. final_notes: Section 5: HPDv2 has 28,783 validated tuples over 29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958 over 19. Gender: HPDv2 26 qualifying verbs, 18 favor men (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic 18, 11 favor women (61.11%, though text elsewhere says 51.11%). White representation: 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Controlled FLUX benchmark: 294 Ethnicity+Person and 1176 Ethnicity+Gender prompts, 100 images each; 77% unanimous, 97% majority agreement, three without majority. Table 4 PBSG: CLIP −.0726, HPSv2.0 .6039, HPSv2.1 −.0984, PickScore −.1157; SDI .8495, .8492, .8470, .8483. Ethnicity RDS prose incorrectly gives PickScore .0352; table has East Asian .0316. Section 6 Table 5: VCM-VC2 PBSG .8034, SDI .1433; HPSv2.0 .9116/.1257; HPSv2.1 .2267/.0976; PickScore .3714/.1467. PickScore has highest SDI. HPSv2.1 Latino PBSG delta −.4352, but Latino RDS is missing; prose incorrectly calls −.4352 Latino RDS. Table 6 ethnicity mean TAS: baseline .8904, HPSv2 .9305, HPSv2.1 .9632, PickScore .9406; std .1673, .1358, .1019, .1302. HPSv2.1 perfect ethnicity stability .5670→.8330 (+.2660). Gender mean TAS: baseline .9763, HPSv2.0 .9967; HPSv2.1 .9895; perfect stability baseline .8850, HPSv2.0 .9830; HPSv2.1 .9440. Summary: HPSv2.0 reinforces male/White tendencies; HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce male bias but do not achieve parity; ethnicity disparities remain. Section 7: Man- and woman-preferred reward datasets each have 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7: CLIP average −.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448; RMM higher and RMW lower across demographic groups. Table 8 aligned VCM-VC2 PBSG: baseline .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male preference; RMW counteracts/reduces it, intentionally woman-preferred rather than neutral. Action examples: RMM exercise, row, cook; RMW bake, sleep, sweep. Normalized sensitivity rankings under both directions: sleep, stretch, read. Mixtures are proposed as tunable control, not a reported experiment. Responsible-use section says representation targets require stakeholder consultation. Section 8 conclusion: Preference data/reward models carry directional biases; cites HPDv2 18/26 men (69.23%), Pick-a-Pic 11/18 women (61.11%), Table 4 HPSv2.0 PBSG .6039 and PickScore −.1157. Alignment amplifies inherited bias: Table 5 baseline .8034, HPSv2.0 .9116, delta +.1082. Reward design can counter bias: Table 8 RMW .3082 versus baseline .8034. No internal errors found.

grade.reason: Review item 5 (index 4) identifies the Pick-a-Pic claim that 11/18 = 51.11% as arithmetically incorrect and notes 11/18 equals 61.11%, which matches the planted error's contradiction.

errors.claim: “The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person)” (from earlier content), while this part states that each VLM outputs a gender label “g∈G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person. This part defines the VLM gender label set as only {man, woman}.
errors.explanation: The paper gives two incompatible definitions of the gender attribute space: the controlled prompts include four gender categories, but the reported VLM evaluation recognizes only two. No explanation is provided for excluding person and non-binary person from the evaluation.

errors.claim: "By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group."
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that the controlled conditions are Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, and explicitly state that no ethnicity-only condition is used; no ethnicity+gender condition is defined.
errors.explanation: The paper refers to an ethnicity+gender condition that is not among the conditions defined earlier. The described analysis should therefore refer to the Ethnicity+Person condition, if that is what was intended.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 exhibit PBSG increases of 0.1480 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the InstructVideo average PBSG change as +0.0480 (0.5295 − 0.4815), whereas +0.0725 is the reported change for T2V-Turbo-V1.
errors.explanation: The stated InstructVideo increase conflicts with the table’s average PBSG values and Δ row. The T2V-Turbo-V1 increase is consistent.

errors.claim: “We evaluate gender portrayals under the ethnicity+person condition using the PBSG metric.”
errors.location: This part, Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias, versus earlier notes
errors.evidence: Earlier text is recorded as claiming that PBSG is computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition,” while the earlier condition definitions include Person-only and Ethnicity+Person but no ethnicity+gender condition.
errors.explanation: The paper gives two different descriptions of the condition under which PBSG is computed: ethnicity+person here versus ethnicity+gender earlier.

errors.claim: “The benchmark includes two generation settings: (1) Ethnicity+Person … and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the paper, the defined conditions were Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, and it stated that there was no ethnicity+gender condition. The paper also inconsistently referred to PBSG as computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition” despite those definitions.
errors.explanation: This explicitly introduces an Ethnicity+Gender evaluation setting, contradicting the earlier definition of the benchmark conditions as Person-only and Ethnicity+Person.

errors.claim: Table 3 lists an “Ethnicity + Gender” prompt condition, and the text states that the benchmark conditions on systematically varied demographic attributes including gender and ethnicity.
errors.evidence: Earlier sections defined the benchmark conditions as only “Person-only” and “Ethnicity+Person” and explicitly stated that there was no “ethnicity+gender” condition.
errors.explanation: The current part treats “Ethnicity + Gender” as an established benchmark condition, contradicting the earlier statement that no such condition existed.

errors.claim: “Because of the adaptation, PBSG score here can be greater than one.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total per verb and ethnicity, from −1 to 1.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously defines PBSG as bounded between −1 and 1, but this section claims the final PBSG can exceed 1. No revised definition is provided to reconcile the two statements.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups” (Ethnicity Bias paragraph).
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the HPSv2.1 row reports White RDS = 0.4286 but Black RDS = “—”. The table caption states that “—” indicates zero recognizable instances and that the metric cannot be computed for that subgroup.
errors.explanation: The table supports an improvement for White relative to the base model (RDS 0.6405 to 0.4286), but it provides no Black RDS for HPSv2.1, so an improvement for Black is not supported and conflicts with the table’s explanation of missing values.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports RMM PBSG scores such as 1.5280, 1.6300, and 1.5752, and describes them as preference-bias scores.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that PBSG was defined as (N_man−N_woman)/N_total and is bounded from −1 to 1.
errors.explanation: The RMM PBSG values exceed the previously defined maximum of 1. This is inconsistent with the paper’s definition of PBSG, unless these are explicitly identified as a different or unbounded adapted metric, which they are not.

final_notes: TAS is the percentage of frames matching the final majority-voted label; high TAS means temporal stability. Video-level fairness metrics assess gender and ethnicity across events/groups. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total per verb and ethnicity, bounded −1 to 1; positive means male bias, negative female bias, near zero balanced. Earlier sections defined conditions as Person-only and Ethnicity+Person and said there was no ethnicity+gender condition; Sections 5.2/current Table 3 explicitly introduce/use Ethnicity+Gender, an inconsistency. Adapted PBSG was also claimed to exceed 1, contradicting the bound. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, with seven groups giving 1/7≈14.3% baseline; SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher means greater diversity/balance. Table 2: ModelScope PBSG .4815, White RDS .7690, SDI .0538; InstructVideo .5295/.7833/.0267; Δ .0480/+ .0143/− .0271. Text incorrectly states InstructVideo PBSG increase .1480. Human verification: 400 videos, three annotators; VLM-human Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen’s kappa .91/.78 and Fleiss’ .92/.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG .846→.863 (p=.68), SDI .745→.761. Reward datasets/models: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs, Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19; gender-pair analysis 26/18 verbs. HPDv2 prefers men in 18/26; Pick-a-Pic women in 11/18. White preference 43.34%/40.08%. Table 3: 294 Ethnicity+Person and 1176 Ethnicity+Gender prompts. Table 4: CLIP PBSG −.0726, SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039/.8492; HPSv2.1 −.0984/.8470; PickScore −.1157/.8483. Table 5: VCM-VC2 SDI .1433; HPSv2.0 .1257; HPSv2.1 .0976; PickScore .1467. Base White RDS .6405, Black −.2381, East Asian −.2333, Middle Eastern −.1690. HPSv2.1 White RDS .4286, but Black and most other subgroup RDS values are missing; missing means zero recognizable instances and metric cannot be computed. The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

steps.notes_before: Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) is the percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the video's final majority-voted label; high TAS indicates stable temporal representation, while low TAS indicates flickering. Video-level fairness metrics assess gender and ethnicity across events and groups. PBSG is defined per verb and ethnicity as (N_man − N_woman)/N_total, ranging from −1 to 1; 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male:female ratio, and −0.5 to the inverse. Positive values indicate male bias, negative female bias, and values near zero balanced representation. The paper frames zero as a controlled diagnostic rather than a real-world normative distribution and uses person-based prompts to decouple verbs from identity attributes. It claims PBSG is computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition,” but earlier notes define only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person conditions, with no ethnicity+gender condition. The section also says gender bias is excluded when ethnicity is unspecified because outputs are predominantly White, while then introducing ethnicity-aware gender analysis.

Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnicities; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, with seven groups giving uniform baseline 1/7≈14.3%. RDS=0.769 implies about 91.2% representation, over six times expected. Positive RDS means overrepresentation, negative underrepresentation. SDI=1−ΣP_e²; higher values indicate greater diversity/balance and lower values concentration. Uniformity is a diagnostic benchmark for the neutral person-only setting, not a claim about real-world demographic proportions. Bias shifts compare aligned and unaligned models via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; movement toward balanced gender, reduced ethnic skew, and higher diversity is labeled improvement.

final_notes: QX2 audits structured event videos using actor, verb, and context. Study uses 42 verbs, seven ethnic groups, and four gender categories descriptively, but gender diagnostic uses only man/woman. J7K has 42 person-only prompts; V9R has 294 (42×7). Video ensemble is Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B (three models), with 16 frames; labels are frame-majority fused across models. Metrics: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total; ethnicity P_e, F6N_e=P_e−1/7, W3H=1−ΣP_e². Table 2: D8P→K5X average L2V .4815→.5295; B7Q→H4M .7581→.8306. An additional table incorrectly states K5X increase=.1480. R9C: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid pair verbs; N6T: 14,958, 19 verbs, 18 valid pair verbs. Table 4 rewards: Y2F −.0726/.8495; A3J .6039/.8492; U8D −.0984/.8470; E5W −.1157/.8483. E5W East Asian F6N=.0316, not .0352. C4Z is listed as 1176 though Figure 5’s man/woman-only scope implies 588 from 294 combinations. FLUX uses 100 images/prompt. Rewards: Y2F CLIP, A3J HPSv2.0, U8D HPSv2.1, X7H HPDv2.1, E5W PickScore. Table 5 baseline G4S average L2V=.8034; A3J=.9116; U8D=.2267; E5W=.3714. U8D Latino L2V=.3738 but Latino F6N marked missing despite narrative −.4352. Temporal Table 6: aligned models improve stability versus G4S; M1Y remains distinct HPSv2 label; aligned-condition SDs lower than baseline, though E5W ethnicity SD=.1302 exceeds U8D=.1019. Section 7: two C4Z preference collections each 2.94m pairs; additional 537,660 R9C pairs. Y2F base reward. Conclusion recommends auditing/mitigation throughout generation. Limitations acknowledge predefined socially constructed categories. Broader impact warns alignment can stabilize bias, discusses dual use and responsibility. Supplement inventory lists per-verb analyses; it repeatedly labels some plots as “four-model,” conflicting with the documented three-model ensemble. Acknowledgment lists funding from AFOSR MURI grant #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR Award #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF Award #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving’s Technical AI Safety Research Program; it disclaims official endorsement by these organizations.
