Paper claims an end-to-end analysis linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards reportedly improve visual quality while encoding and amplifying social bias. Figure 1 is described as showing QX2 event prompts and ethnicity/gender auditing, frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes, and analysis separating human-preference, image-reward, and downstream video-generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Title/paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract and introduction claim alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/higher-quality but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular ethnic-skew measures, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. The analysis links human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, including human-labeled reward effects on social-attribute distributions. Introduction defines aligned models as likelihood-trained video diffusion models post-trained toward human preferences using reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization; unaligned models use likelihood objectives alone as controlled baselines. It claims both human-comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. Attribute-distribution curation can control reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations; counter-biased rewards are proposed as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; and evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce social composition.

final_notes: Section 7 constructs man-preferred and woman-preferred datasets, each with 2.94M same-action/same-ethnicity gender-opposed pairs, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. RMM assigns strongly positive PBSG across groups (average 1.5280); RMW assigns strongly negative PBSG (average −0.7448), showing opposite learned gender preferences. VCM-VC2 baseline PBSG average is .8034; alignment with RMM increases it to .9584, while RMW lowers it to .3082. RMW is described as counter-biased and producing more balanced portrayals, though it strongly shifts toward woman preference. Table 8 group averages: VCM .7925 White, .7758 Black, .8690 Latino, .7115 East Asian, .7945 Southeast Asian, .8634 India, .8071 Middle Eastern; +RMM .9595, .9524, .9756, .9437, .9447, .9640, .9709; +RMW .3341, .3913, .3314, .1008, .2639, .3446, .3894. Section 19: 42-action sensitivity analysis; RMM examples exercise, row, cook; RMW examples bake, sleep, sweep. Sleep, stretch, read rank highest in normalized sensitivity under both directions; no exact action-level values. Mixtures are proposed as future control, not reported experiment. Section 8 conclusion: VideoBiasEval separates identity attributes from content semantics and tracks alignment effects. HPDv2 has 18/26 (69.23%) qualifying verbs favoring men; Pick-a-Pic 11/18 (61.11%) favoring women; Table 4 averages HPSv2.0 .6039 and PickScore −.1157. Alignment: VCM-VC2 .8034 versus +HPSv2.0 .9116 (Δ +.1082). Limitations include predefined U.S.-Census categories, evaluator bias, limited reward models, synthetic preference manipulations, and fixed 42 actions. Broader Impact repeats: alignment may stabilize bias; Table 5 .8034→.9116; Table 6 gender TAS .9763→.9967 and perfect stability .8850→.9830. Table 7 RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448; Table 8 +RMM .9584, +RMW .3082. Risks of normalization, exclusion, homogenization, propaganda are stated without numerical deployment evidence. Acknowledgments list support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving, and disclaim endorsement by those organizations.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnicities; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, with seven groups giving uniform baseline 1/7≈14.3%. RDS=0.769 implies about 91.2% representation, over six times expected. Positive RDS means overrepresentation, negative underrepresentation. SDI=1−ΣP_e²; higher values indicate greater diversity/balance and lower values concentration. Uniformity is a diagnostic benchmark for the neutral person-only setting, not a claim about real-world demographic proportions. Bias shifts compare aligned and unaligned models via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; movement toward balanced gender, reduced ethnic skew, and higher diversity is labeled improvement.

Table 2: aligned variants increase average gender imbalance; all overrepresent White. Title: paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract claims that alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 provides event-based separation of verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular measures of ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Paper claims an end-to-end analysis linking human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards reportedly improve visual quality while encoding and amplifying social bias. Figure 1 is described as showing QX2 event prompts and ethnicity/gender auditing, frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes, and analysis separating human-preference, image-reward, and downstream video-generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Title/paper studies how alignment tuning shapes social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract and introduction claim alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/higher-quality but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender and ethnicity, with multi-granular ethnic-skew measures, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. The analysis links human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, including human-labeled reward effects on social-attribute distributions. Introduction defines aligned models as likelihood-trained video diffusion models post-trained toward human preferences using reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization; unaligned models use likelihood objectives alone as controlled baselines. It claims both human-comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. Attribute-distribution curation can control reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations; counter-biased rewards are proposed as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; and evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements reshape and sometimes reinforce social composition.

Table 4 evaluates CLIP, HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore on 42 verbs using PBSG, RDS, and SDI. Average PBSG: CLIP −0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 −0.0984, PickScore −0.1157. Table 8: VCM 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082. Section 8 conclusion: HPDv2 has 18/26 qualifying verbs favoring men (69.23%); Pick-a-Pic has 11/18 favoring women (61.11%). errors.claim: “The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person)” (from earlier content), while this part states that each VLM outputs a gender label “g∈G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person. This part defines the VLM gender label set as only {man, woman}.
errors.explanation: The paper gives two incompatible definitions of the gender attribute space: the controlled prompts include four gender categories, but the reported VLM evaluation recognizes only two. No explanation is provided for excluding person and non-binary person from the evaluation.

errors.claim: "By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group."
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that the controlled conditions are Person-only and Ethnicity+Person, and explicitly state that no ethnicity-only condition is used; no ethnicity+gender condition is defined.
errors.explanation: The paper refers to an ethnicity+gender condition that is not among the conditions defined earlier. The described analysis should therefore refer to the Ethnicity+Person condition, if that is what was intended.

errors.claim: “We apply our proposed evaluation framework to four state-of-the-art video diffusion models…” and “the aligned models include InstructVideo…, T2V-Turbo-V1…, InternVid2-S2…, and ViCLIP…”
errors.evidence: Table 2 contains results only for ModelScope, InstructVideo, Video-Crafter-V2, and T2V-Turbo-V1; InternVid2-S2 and ViCLIP do not appear in the table or in the subsequent analysis.
errors.explanation: The text presents InternVid2-S2 and ViCLIP as evaluated aligned models, but the reported evaluation includes only two aligned models and their two unaligned counterparts. Thus the claimed set of four evaluated models is inconsistent with the results presented here.

errors.claim: “The benchmark includes two generation settings: (1) Ethnicity+Person … and (2) Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Earlier text states that PBSG is computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition,” but also defines the relevant conditions as Person-only and Ethnicity+Person and says there is no ethnicity+gender condition.
errors.explanation: The paper is inconsistent about whether an Ethnicity+Gender condition exists: this section explicitly includes it, whereas the earlier description says the defined conditions exclude it.

errors.claim: Figure 5 states: “We only show the images with [gender] ∈ {man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Table 3 lists 1,176 prompts for the “Ethnicity + Gender” setting. The benchmark is described elsewhere as covering 42 verbs and seven ethnicities, so restricting gender to man and woman would yield 42 × 7 × 2 = 588 prompts, not 1,176.
errors.explanation: The reported prompt count implies four gender variants per verb–ethnicity combination, whereas the figure description specifies only two genders. The paper does not explain this factor-of-two discrepancy.

errors.claim: “PBSG score here can be greater than one.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define PBSG as “(N_man−N_woman)/N_total … ranging −1 to 1.”
errors.explanation: This section uses the same PBSG name but states that it can exceed 1, contradicting the paper’s earlier stated range. No distinct redefinition is given beyond score standardization.

errors.claim: “CLIP … achieves the lowest SDI score (0.8495), indicating relatively balanced ethnic representation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define SDI so that “higher means greater diversity/balance.”
errors.explanation: Under the paper’s own SDI interpretation, the lowest SDI indicates comparatively less balanced or diverse representation, not relatively balanced representation.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, HPSv2.1 has White RDS = 0.4286, compared with 0.6405 for VCM-VC2, but the Black RDS entry is “—” for HPSv2.1 (and therefore no Black RDS improvement is reported).
errors.explanation: The table supports improved White balance, but it provides no HPSv2.1 Black RDS value; its note says “—” means zero recognizable instances and prevents metric computation. Thus the claimed improvement for Black is not supported by the paper’s own data.

final_notes:
TAS section: ethnicity mean TAS rises .8904→.9632 after HPSv2.1; perfect stability .5670→.8330 (+.2660); gender TAS reaches .9895 and perfect stability .9440. Ethnicity TAS SD decreases by .0654. HPSv2.0 increases PBSG .8034→.9116, with gender TAS .9967 and perfect stability .9830. Summary says HPSv2.0 reinforces male/White preference, while HPSv2.1 and PickScore have woman-preferred reward patterns and counteract man-dominant bias, though neither achieves parity.

Section 7: man-preferred and woman-preferred datasets contain 2.94M Ethnicity+Gender preference pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7: CLIP average PBSG −.0726; RMM average 1.5280, positive across all seven ethnicities; RMW average −.7448, negative across all groups. Table 8: VCM-VC2 PBSG .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male preference; RMW shifts femaleward and reduces male bias. PBSG nominal range earlier −1 to 1, but standardized scores may exceed 1.

Summary/conclusion: controllable preference modeling directs social-attribute bias via dataset composition; RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals, while RMW counteracts bias. Across 42 actions, neutral activities can show large gender shifts; sleep, stretch, and read are top sensitivity-ranked under both tunings. VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics; reward alignment inherits and often amplifies human-preference biases, with RMW as a counter-biased exception.

Limitations: evaluates gender and ethnicity only; VLM evaluators may be biased/inaccurate; focuses on single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference experiments synthetically manipulate gender preference; VideoBiasEval uses a fixed 42-action set, limiting open-ended generalizability. Broader Impact states alignment tuning can stabilize and entrench stereotyped biases, while controllable preference modeling is dual-use: it can mitigate underrepresentation or amplify exclusionary/homogenizing views. Recommends event-centric auditing and rigorous, diverse preference-data curation. No internal contradictions identified. Acknowledgments list AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving support, with a disclaimer that views are those of the authors.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. Related work argues existing T2V benchmarks and bias evaluations focus on surface-level or static image metrics, often overlooking demographic balance, actor roles, verbs, context, and temporal patterns; VideoBiasEval addresses this with event-level auditing of gender and ethnicity across video outputs. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content from actor attributes. Events are tuples <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. VLMs extract social attributes across frames and metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit/amplify these biases, propagating them through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes but may reinforce/stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions, controllable bias representations, targeted composition, and counter-biased reward modeling. No internal contradictions identified so far.

steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval uses deterministic event prompts of the form “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” The controlled space includes 42 verbs, seven ethnic groups, and earlier sections define four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person). Prompt conditions here are Person-only (42 prompts, actor fixed as “person”) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts: 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups). No ethnicity-only condition is used. Contexts are fixed and do not alter verb semantics; prompts are reproducible and videos are generated under identical decoding settings. Demographic attributes are inferred post hoc, not imposed during generation. Three VLM judges—Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B—uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Each VLM predicts frame-wise gender and ethnicity, majority voting gives video-level labels, and predictions are fused across models. In this part, however, the VLM gender label set is explicitly only {man, woman}, conflicting with the earlier four-category controlled gender space. Ethnicity labels are White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The method evaluates both frame dynamics and video-level representation/stability, with human–model correlation analyses in Section 4.

steps.notes_before: Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) is the percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the video's final majority-voted label; high TAS indicates stable temporal representation, while low TAS indicates flickering. Video-level fairness metrics assess gender and ethnicity across events and groups. PBSG is defined per verb and ethnicity as (N_man − N_woman)/N_total, ranging from −1 to 1; 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male:female ratio, and −0.5 to the inverse. Positive values indicate male bias, negative female bias, and values near zero balanced representation. The paper frames zero as a controlled diagnostic rather than a real-world normative distribution and uses person-based prompts to decouple verbs from identity attributes. It claims PBSG is computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition,” but earlier notes define only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person conditions, with no ethnicity+gender condition. The section also says gender bias is excluded when ethnicity is unspecified because outputs are predominantly White, while then introducing ethnicity-aware gender analysis.

Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnicities; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, with seven groups giving uniform baseline 1/7≈14.3%. RDS=0.769 implies about 91.2% representation, over six times expected. Positive RDS means overrepresentation, negative underrepresentation. SDI=1−ΣP_e²; higher values indicate greater diversity/balance and lower values concentration. Uniformity is a diagnostic benchmark for the neutral person-only setting, not a claim about real-world demographic proportions. Bias shifts compare aligned and unaligned models via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; movement toward balanced gender, reduced ethnic skew, and higher diversity is labeled improvement.

QX2 audits structured event videos using actor, verb, and context. Event is <p,a,c>; study uses 42 verbs and seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino). Four gender categories are described, but diagnostic defines N_total=N_man+N_woman, potentially omitting neutral/non-binary. J7K has 42 person-only prompts; V9R has 294 (42×7). Table 2: D8P→K5X L2V .4815→.5295 and B7Q→H4M .7581→.8306; all overrepresent White. Reward data: R9C/HPDv2 men preferred 18/26 valid verbs; N6T/Pick-a-Pic women preferred 11/18.

grade.reason: Yes — the reviewer notes that Table 4 shows U8D (0.8470) has the lowest W3H/SDI and Y2F is 0.8495, contradicting the paper's claim that Y2F has the lowest diversity.

sol_grade.reason: The fourth reported error identifies Y2F’s lowest-diversity claim as wrong because Table 4 gives U8D a lower diversity score, using the same contradicting values.

errors.claim: “We use two conditions: 1. Person-only ... 2. Ethnicity+Person ...” and “Because ethnicity+person already specifies ethnicity, an additional ethnicity-only setting is unnecessary for isolating ethnicity effects.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the evaluation conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only.
errors.explanation: The paper’s stated evaluation design elsewhere includes Ethnicity+Gender and ethnicity-only conditions, contradicting this section’s claim that there are only two conditions and that ethnicity-only is unnecessary.

errors.claim: Each judge independently assigns a gender label \(g\in G=\{\text{man, woman}\}\).
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that VideoBiasEval uses four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person.
errors.explanation: The paper’s evaluation is defined over four gender categories, but this section restricts extracted gender labels to only two. No explanation reconciles the omission of the person and non-binary-person categories.

errors.claim: “ModelScope has the strongest imbalance: RDSWhite = 0.769 and SDI = 0.0538.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports InstructVideo with a higher White RDS of 0.7833 and a lower Overall SDI of 0.0267, compared with ModelScope’s 0.7690 and 0.0538.
errors.explanation: By both stated imbalance indicators—greater White overrepresentation (RDSWhite) and lower ethnic diversity (SDI)—InstructVideo shows a stronger imbalance than ModelScope, contradicting the claim that ModelScope has the strongest imbalance.

errors.claim: "Alignment increases average male skew... The prose reports the first increase as 0.04."
errors.evidence: The same bullet states that Table 2 gives the first alignment increase as "+0.0480" for Average PBSG.
errors.explanation: The prose value 0.04 does not match the table value 0.0480; if rounded to two decimal places, 0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “CLIP slightly favors White individuals, RDS = 0.0182, and has the lowest SDI, 0.8495.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports SDI values of 0.8495 for CLIP, 0.8492 for HPSv2.0, 0.8470 for HPSv2.1, and 0.8483 for PickScore.
errors.explanation: CLIP's SDI of 0.8495 is not the lowest; HPSv2.1 has the lowest SDI at 0.8470.

errors.claim: “PickScore favors East Asian representation, RDS = 0.0352.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports PickScore's East Asian RDS as 0.0316 (and its Middle Eastern RDS as −0.0271).
errors.explanation: The stated PickScore East Asian RDS, 0.0352, does not match the table's 0.0316.

errors.claim: The prose reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0352.
errors.evidence: Table 4 gives PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The prose value conflicts with the corresponding table value.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition (i.e., when ethnicity is not explicitly specified)”
errors.evidence: The following section states: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we use RDSe and SDI to assess balance,” and discusses the table’s RDS and SDI values as ethnicity-only results.
errors.explanation: The table caption attributes missing values to the person-only condition, whereas the accompanying ethnicity-bias analysis says these metrics are computed under the ethnicity-only condition. These are different evaluation conditions, so the stated interpretation of the missing values conflicts with the analysis.

final_notes: Section 6 evaluates VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Table 5 average PBSG/SDI: VCM-VC2 .8034/.1433; HPSv2.0 .9116/.1257; HPSv2.1 .2267/.0976; PickScore .3714/.1467. HPSv2.0 amplifies male bias; HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce it. VCM-VC2 favors White (RDS .6405), with Black, East Asian, and Middle Eastern underrepresented. HPSv2.1 improves White/Black balance but reduces Latino representation; PickScore is described as most equitable. Table 6 ethnicity mean TAS: VCM-VC2 .8904, HPSv2 .9305, HPSv2.1 .9632, PickScore .9406. HPSv2.1 ethnicity perfect stability rises .5670 to .8330. Gender: VCM-VC2 mean TAS/perfect stability .9763/.8850; HPSv2.0 .9967/.9830 (stable amplified bias). Section 7: RMM trains on man-preferred data, RMW on woman-preferred data. Table 7 reward PBSG: RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448; Table 8 video PBSG: baseline .8034, +RMM .9584, +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male bias; RMW counteracts it but shifts toward women. Conclusion emphasizes reward alignment can inherit/amplify preference bias. Section 5.1: 18/26 HPDv2 verbs favor men; 11/18 Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 HPSv2.0 .6039, PickScore −.1157. Broader Impact claims alignment stabilizes bias, citing Table 5 .8034→.9116 and Table 6 gender .9763/.8850→.9967/.9830. It describes preference control as dual-use; Table 7/8 values support opposite steering directions. Risks of normalization, exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda are stated without numerical deployment evidence. Limitations include predefined categories, potentially biased VLM evaluators, limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference manipulations, and primarily single-step latent consistency experiments. The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors challenge the paper's causal claim that reducing White overrepresentation directly causes diversity to fall; the reviewer issues focus on inconsistent attribute definitions, mislabeled conditions, missing table entries, and mischaracterized alignment effects, not the unsupported causal inference.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space ... [has] four gender categories” and includes “man, woman, neutral person, and non-binary person.”
errors.evidence: The attribute-extraction definition states that outputs are \(g\in G=\{\text{man,woman}\}\).
errors.explanation: The paper defines four gender categories for its attribute space, but the actual extraction label space contains only two and omits neutral/person and non-binary categories. No restriction or mapping from the four-category definition to the binary evaluation space is provided.

errors.claim: “D8P has the strongest imbalance, worsened in K5X; B7Q is moderately more balanced.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports average L2V values of D8P = 0.4815, K5X = 0.5295, B7Q = 0.7581, and H4M = 0.8306. It also reports B7Q’s per-ethnicity L2V values as generally higher than D8P’s.
errors.explanation: Because higher absolute L2V indicates greater gender imbalance, D8P does not have the strongest imbalance among the four models, and B7Q is less balanced than D8P according to the reported averages.

errors.claim: “V9R specifies ethnicity alone”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that “V9R combines ethnicity and verb.”
errors.explanation: This contradicts the earlier description of V9R as an ethnicity-plus-verb prompt, rather than an ethnicity-only prompt.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W East Asian F6N is 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity gives a different value for the same reported metric.

errors.claim: V9R is described as specifying ethnicity alone.
errors.location: Current benchmark description / notes from earlier parts
errors.evidence: The V9R example is: “An East Asian person is baking cookies in a cozy kitchen...” and Table 3 states that benchmark prompts contain “ethnicity when specified, verbs, and context.” Earlier methods describe V9R as combining ethnicity and verb.
errors.explanation: The characterization of V9R as ethnicity-only conflicts with the earlier definition and the V9R prompt example, which explicitly includes the verb and context.

errors.claim: “U8D improves White/Black balance”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports baseline White L2V = 0.7925 and Black L2V = 0.7758, a difference of 0.0167, whereas +U8D reports White L2V = 0.1321 and Black L2V = 0.2381, a larger difference of 0.1060.
errors.explanation: By the table’s White-versus-Black L2V values, U8D makes the two groups less equal rather than more balanced.

errors.claim: “A3J amplifies man preference while locking it temporally, with nearly all videos perfectly gender-stable.”
errors.evidence: The text explicitly says “Temporal results use another reward-version label (M1Y = HPSv2), retained distinctly in the temporal table.” Table 6 reports temporal results for G4S, +M1Y, +U8D, and +E5W, but no +A3J row; the nearly-all-perfect gender-stability value (0.9830) belongs to +M1Y.
errors.explanation: The temporal locking result is reported for M1Y, not A3J. A3J’s man-preference increase is shown in Table 5, but its temporal stability is not reported here.

final_notes: QX2 audits structured event videos with four stated gender categories and seven ethnic groups, but extraction defines gender only as man/woman. Three VLM judges label 16 frames per video; frame-majority labels are fused; TAS/T8Q measures temporal identity coherence. L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total; positive favors men. Ethnic metrics: P_e, F6N_e=P_e−1/7, W3H=1−sum P_e²; higher W3H means greater diversity. Table 2 averages: L2V D8P .4815, K5X .5295, B7Q .7581, H4M .8306; White F6N .7690, .7833, .6905, .6381; W3H .0538, .0267, .1252, .1119. Narrative reverses D8P/H4M imbalance and D8P/B7Q balance. Reward Table 4: Y2F average L2V −.0726, A3J .6039, U8D −.0984, E5W −.1157; all fine-tuned models lose diversity. E5W East Asian F6N .0316 vs .0352 in additional table. V9R earlier combines ethnicity and verb, though later calls it ethnicity alone; C4Z is Ethnicity+Gender. Current benchmark uses man/woman; gender-omitted prompts score generated prompts conditioned on ethnicity, gender, verb/context. Table 5 baseline G4S average L2V .8034/W3H .1433; A3J .9116/.1257; U8D .2267/.0976; E5W .3714/.1467. U8D White/Black L2V .1321/.2381 versus baseline .7925/.7758, so White–Black L2V gap increases. Table 6 temporal rows use M1Y (not A3J), U8D, E5W; M1Y gender perfect stability .9830, U8D .9440, E5W .9410. Section 7: Image reward Table 7 Y2F avg −.0726; Z6B 1.5280 (Man-Preferred RMM), P3L −.7448 (Woman-Preferred RMW). Table 8 G4S avg L2V .8034; +Z6B .9584, +P3L .3082. Z6B reinforces male preference; P3L shifts toward women and is described as more balanced. Conclusion recommends bias auditing/mitigation. Limitations acknowledge socially constructed predefined categories, VLM judge limitations, single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards, synthetic gender-preference manipulation's limited scope, and fixed socially associated action taxonomy limiting open-ended generalization. Broader Impact warns alignment can stabilize bias, discusses dual use and responsibility, and recommends QX2-style multi-granular audits. Supplementary inventory lists additional 42-verb analyses, training-data/reward-model/video post-training details, statistical analyses, gender plots 7/8/12/10/9/11/13, ethnicity plot 14, reward-model gender plots 19–25 and ethnicity plots 26–29, reward-aligned gender plots 30–37(b) and ethnicity plot 38, and controllable-preference gender plots 39–43. No internal contradiction found in Parts 13–14. Acknowledgments report support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF,

Title: paper examines alignment tuning and social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract claims alignment-tuned models produce smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate to generation. QX2 separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Paper presents an end-to-end analysis of human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. It claims human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality while unintentionally encoding/amplifying social bias, motivating bias-aware assessment and mitigation. Figure 1 is described as showing QX2 prompts/audit, frame-wise VLM attribute inference and aggregation, and analysis separating human preference, image-reward, and downstream video-generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Title: paper examines alignment tuning and social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract/introduction claim alignment-tuned models produce smoother, more stereotyped, and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate to generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. The paper analyzes human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions. Introduction states both human comparison collections favor White representations and exhibit non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit and amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. It claims attribute-distribution curation can control image-reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations, with targeted composition/counter-biased rewards as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Aligned models are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization; unaligned likelihood-only models are controlled baselines. Contributions: comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; connected preference-data–reward–video analysis of bias inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements can reshape or reinforce social composition, plus controllable-preference mitigation guidance.

Title: paper examines alignment tuning and social bias in video diffusion models. Abstract/introduction claim alignment-tuned models produce smoother, more stereotyped, and temporally persistent portrayals; preference-data biases enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate to generation. QX2 (VideoBiasEval) separates event verbs/contexts from actor gender/ethnicity and measures ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Human comparison collections favor White representations and show non-neutral gender preferences; learned rewards inherit/amplify these patterns, male- or female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals, and ethnic distributions remain uneven. Attribute-distribution curation can control image-reward datasets, learned preferences, and video representations, with targeted composition/counter-biased rewards as mitigation. Analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Aligned models are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences; unaligned likelihood-only models are controls. Contributions include event-prompt/multi-granularity auditing and linked preference-data–reward–video analysis of bias inheritance, amplification, and stabilization.

Related work: standard T2V metrics (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) use FVD, CLIP-Score, and object consistency without identity/portrayal audits. GRiT can verify a doctor but not flag exclusively white male doctors; Y2F rewards textual fidelity rather than demographic balance. QX2 provides ethnicity-/gender-aware, event-centric auditing. Prior image/language bias studies focus on portraits or isolated objects; StableBias, DALL-Eval, and SocialCounterfactuals chiefly count identities and seldom activities. Independent demographic audits can miss recurring role stereotypes; joint actor–verb–context analysis exposes scenario-dependent and narrative/temporal bias.

Conditional gender metric L2V = (N_man − N_woman)/N_total, with N_total=N_man+N_woman, range [-1,1]; positive favors men, negative women, near-zero balance. L2V=.5 means men are 3x women; -.5 inverse. Gender-only analysis is excluded because unspecified ethnicity predominantly yields White individuals. Ethnic metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnic outputs; F6N_e= P_e−1/7 (uniform neutral-J7K reference), and W3H=1−sum P_e² (Simpson diversity). Positive/negative F6N indicate over/underrepresentation; higher W3H means greater diversity. Example F6N=.769 implies P=.912 (91.2%), over six times 1/7. Shift metrics are ΔL2V, ΔF6N_e, ΔW3H; balance, reduced skew, and higher diversity are improvements.

final_notes:
Section 6: VCM-VC2 alignment with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5 average PBSG: baseline .8034, HPSv2.0 .9116, HPSv2.1 .2267, PickScore .3714; SDI: .1433, .1257, .0976, .1467. Baseline RDS: White .6405, Black −.2381, East Asian −.2333, Middle Eastern −.1690. HPSv2.1 White RDS .4286; Black/Latino RDS missing, despite prose claiming Black improvement. Caption says missing values mean zero recognizable instances under person-only, while prose says ethnicity-only. Table 6 ethnicity TAS: baseline .8904, HPSv2 .9305, HPSv2.1 .9632, PickScore .9406; SDs .1673, .1358, .1019, .1302. HPSv2.1 perfect ethnicity stability .5670→.8330; gender mean TAS baseline .9763→HPSv2.0 .9967, perfect stability .8850→.9830. HPSv2.1 gender TAS/perfect stability .9895/.9440. Summary: HPSv2.0 amplifies male/White tendencies; HPSv2.1 and PickScore reduce male bias but do not achieve demographic parity; ethnicity disparities remain.

Section 7: Man-preferred and woman-preferred datasets, 2.94M pairs each, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. RMM trained on man-preferred data; RMW on woman-preferred data. Table 7 average reward PBSG: CLIP −.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −.7448. Table 8 VCM-VC2 PBSG .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male preference; RMW is counter-biased and shifts toward woman preference, producing more balanced/representative outputs and steering toward gender equilibrium. Mixtures proposed, not reported.

Section 8 conclusion: HPDv2 qualifying verbs: 69.23% (18/26) favor men; Pick-a-Pic: 61.11% (11/18) favor women. Table 4 average PBSG: HPSv2.0 .6039; PickScore −.1157. Limitations cover predefined U.S.-Census-style categories, potentially biased VLM evaluators, limited single-step testing, synthetic gender-preference manipulations, and fixed 42 actions. Broader Impact notes alignment may stabilize/amplify bias and repeats VCM-VC2 .8034→HPSv2.0 .9116, gender TAS .9763→.9967 and perfect stability .8850→.9830; risks are stated without numerical deployment evidence. Acknowledgment lists funding/support and disclaims representing funders’ official views; no substantive result claims.

The paper studies how alignment tuning—post-training optimization toward human preferences—affects social representation in video diffusion models. It introduces VideoBiasEval, an event-based framework separating actor attributes from verbs and contexts. It evaluates ethnicity bias, gender bias within ethnic groups, changes after alignment, and temporal stability of demographic portrayals. It examines human preference datasets, image reward models trained on them, and video models aligned with those rewards. Main reported findings: preference biases can be inherited, amplified, and made more temporally stable; reward-data composition can reinforce or counteract an existing gender bias, including via man-preferred and woman-preferred reward datasets. Limitations include demographic-category choices, automated evaluators, training choices, and a fixed action set.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval uses deterministic event prompts of the form “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” The controlled space includes 42 verbs, seven ethnic groups, and earlier sections define four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person). Prompt conditions here are Person-only (42 prompts, actor fixed as “person”) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts: 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups). No ethnicity-only condition is used. Contexts are fixed and do not alter verb semantics; prompts are reproducible and videos are generated under identical decoding settings. Demographic attributes are inferred post hoc, not imposed during generation. Three VLM judges—Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B—uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Each VLM predicts frame-wise gender and ethnicity, majority voting gives video-level labels, and predictions are fused across models. In this part, however, the VLM gender label set is explicitly only {man, woman}, conflicting with the earlier four-category controlled gender space. Ethnicity labels are White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The method evaluates both frame dynamics and video-level representation/stability, with human–model correlation analyses in Section 4.

steps.notes_before: Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) is the percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the video's final majority-voted label; high TAS indicates stable temporal representation, while low TAS indicates flickering. Video-level fairness metrics assess gender and ethnicity across events and groups. PBSG is defined per verb and ethnicity as (N_man − N_woman)/N_total, ranging from −1 to 1; 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male:female ratio, and −0.5 to the inverse. Section 6 aligns VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Table 5: baseline average PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, Black -.2381, East Asian -.2333, Middle Eastern -.1690, SDI .1433. Table 6 ethnicity TAS means: .8904 baseline, .9305 HPSv2.0, .9632 HPSv2.1, .9406 PickScore; SDs .1673, .1358, .1019, .1302. HPSv2.1 ethnicity perfect stability rises .5670 to .8330. Gender TAS/perfect stability: baseline .9763/.8850; HPSv2.0 .9967/.9830; HPSv2.1 .9895/.9440.

Section 7: man- and woman-preferred datasets each have 2.94M pairs, plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 averages: CLIP -.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW -.7448. Table 8 aligned VCM-VC2: baseline .8034, +RMM .9584, +RMW .3082. Section 8 proposes mixtures as tunable future control, not reported experiments. Figure 6: RMM amplifies exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts bake/sleep/sweep; sleep/stretch/read rank highest in normalized sensitivity under both.

Section 5.1: 69.23% (18/26) qualifying HPDv2 verbs favor men; 61.11% (11/18) qualifying Pick-a-Pic verbs favor women. Table 4 Average PBSG: HPSv2.0 .6039; PickScore -.1157. Conclusion reiterates Tables 5 and 8. Limitations: category constraints, evaluator bias, limited reward models, synthetic manipulations, and 42-action generalization limits. Broader Impact repeats Tables 5–8 and gender values, and notes dual-use risks without numerical deployment evidence for normalization, exclusion, homogenization, or propaganda. Acknowledgment reports funding/support and disclaims that conclusions represent funders; no conflict with paper results.

errors.explanation: The paper gives two incompatible definitions of the gender attribute space: the controlled prompts include four gender categories, but the reported VLM evaluation recognizes only two. No explanation is provided for excluding person and non-binary person from the evaluation.

errors.claim: “We apply our proposed evaluation framework to four state-of-the-art video diffusion models…” and “the aligned models include InstructVideo…, T2V-Turbo-V1…, InternVid2-S2…, and ViCLIP…”

errors.evidence: Table 3 lists 1,176 prompts for the “Ethnicity + Gender” setting. The benchmark is described elsewhere as covering 42 verbs and seven ethnicities, so restricting gender to man and woman would yield 42 × 7 × 2 = 588 prompts, not 1,176.
errors.explanation: The reported prompt count implies four gender variants per verb–ethnicity combination, whereas the figure description specifies only two genders. The paper does not explain this factor-of-two discrepancy.

errors.claim: “PBSG score here can be greater than one.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define PBSG as ranging from −1 to 1.
errors.explanation: The stated possibility of PBSG values greater than 1 contradicts the earlier definition of PBSG’s range. If the standardized-score adaptation changes the metric’s range, the paper must explicitly distinguish this adapted PBSG from the original bounded definition.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 reduces some disparities by improving balance for White and Black groups, but significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”

errors.explanation: The reported RMW bias is opposite in sign but not magnitude-matched to RMM, so the description of an equally strong or magnitude-matched contrast conflicts with the table.

final_notes: TAS: percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the video’s final majority-voted label; high TAS means stable temporal representation, low TAS flickering. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total per verb and ethnicity, bounded −1 to 1; 0.5 means 3:1 male:female and −0.5 inverse. Positive = male bias, negative = female bias, near-zero = balance. An adapted reward-score PBSG can exceed 1, conflicting with the earlier bounded definition. Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e². Image reward results: ethnicity-aware gender PBSG—CLIP −0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, PickScore −0.1157, HPSv2.1 −0.0984. Video VCM-VC2 base PBSG .8034, SDI .1433; HPSv2.0 .9116/.1257; HPSv2.1 .2267/.0976; PickScore .3714/.1467. Base strongly favors White (RDS .6405); PickScore most balanced. Narrative mislabels HPSv2.1 Δ Latino PBSG −.4352 as Latino RDS. Controllable-preference section: Table 7 RMM average PBSG 1.5280 (group range 1.4323–1.6300), RMW −.7448 (range −.6282 to −.8846). Text incorrectly calls them equal/magnitude-matched. Table 8: VCM-VC2 .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. RMM reinforces male bias; RMW shifts toward female bias. Summary says RMW can correct skewed portrayals and suggests continuous tuning via mixtures. Figure 6 analyzes 42 actions; RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals, RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions; sleep, stretch, read are top-sensitive under both. Conclusion says reward alignment inherits/frequently amplifies human-preference biases. Limitations note gender/ethnicity categories, VLM evaluator limitations, single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference controls, and fixed 42-action benchmark. Broader Impact says alignment tuning can stabilize/entrench biases; controllable preference modeling can amplify or suppress social attributes and is dual-use, with fairness and exclusion risks. Acknowledgments report support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving; views are authors’ and not official endorsements. No new contradiction.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference comparisons/datasets to preference or aesthetic reward models and post-training optimization of video diffusion models. “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures; unaligned models are likelihood-trained baselines. The introduction claims alignment improves perceptual quality and temporal coherence but may inherit/reinforce social biases from human preferences, affecting representation and roles. Existing frameworks allegedly lack diverse identity prompts, comprehensive identity coverage/metrics, and methods for before-versus-after alignment distribution shifts. The framework focuses on gender and ethnicity, uses event-based prompting and social-bias taxonomies, and introduces metrics for ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal persistence. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthen biases, and make them temporally stable, producing smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts separating semantic content from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess ethnicity bias, ethnicity-conditioned gender bias, model distribution shifts, and temporal stability/persistence of social attributes. The paper analyzes a pipeline from human preference datasets (HPDv2, Pick-a-Pic), through image reward models (HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore), to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. It fine-tunes a VideoCrafter-2-derived video consistency model using different image reward models and compares outputs before and after alignment. The paper claims human preference datasets show non-neutral gender preferences and a strong imbalance favoring White representations; reward models inherit and amplify these biases, which propagate through alignment-tuned video models. Male- or female-preferred reward models shift gender portrayals, while ethnic representation remains uneven. Alignment improves perceptual quality, temporal coherence, and temporal consistency of attributes, but may reinforce and stabilize biased representations. Section 7 examines intentionally curated reward datasets with manipulated social-attribute distributions and whether they enable controllable bias representations; targeted data composition and counter-biased reward modeling are proposed as mitigation strategies. The paper also analyzes reward-model preference changes across 42 events and corresponding pre/post-alignment video bias shifts. No internal contradictions identified so far.

VideoBiasEval evaluates social bias in video generation using event-based prompts that separate semantic content from actor attributes. Events are tuples <p,a,c> (actor, verb, context). The controlled attribute space includes four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person), seven ethnic groups (White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino), and 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. steps.notes_before: VideoBiasEval uses deterministic event prompts of the form “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” The controlled space includes 42 verbs, seven ethnic groups, and earlier sections define four gender categories (man, woman, person, non-binary person). Prompt conditions here are Person-only (42 prompts, actor fixed as “person”) and Ethnicity+Person (294 prompts: 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups). No ethnicity-only condition is used. Contexts are fixed and do not alter verb semantics; prompts are reproducible and videos are generated under identical decoding settings. Demographic attributes are inferred post hoc, not imposed during generation. Three VLM judges—Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2.5-8B—uniformly sample 16 frames per video. Each VLM predicts frame-wise gender and ethnicity, majority voting gives video-level labels, and predictions are fused across models. In this part, however, the VLM gender label set is explicitly only {man, woman}, conflicting with the earlier four-category controlled gender space. Ethnicity labels are White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. The method evaluates both frame dynamics and video-level representation/stability, with human–model correlation analyses in Section 4.

steps.notes_before: Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) is the percentage of frames whose classified attributes match the video's final majority-voted label; high TAS indicates stable temporal representation, while low TAS indicates flickering. Video-level fairness metrics assess gender and ethnicity across events and groups. PBSG is defined per verb and ethnicity as (N_man − N_woman)/N_total, ranging from −1 to 1; 0.5 corresponds to a 3:1 male:female ratio, and −0.5 to the inverse. Positive values indicate male bias, negative female bias, and values near zero balanced representation. The paper frames zero as a controlled diagnostic rather than a real-world normative distribution and uses person-based prompts to decouple verbs from identity attributes. It claims PBSG is computed under an “ethnicity+gender condition,” but earlier notes define only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person conditions, with no ethnicity+gender condition. The section also says gender bias is excluded when ethnicity is unspecified because outputs are predominantly White, while then introducing ethnicity-aware gender analysis.

Ethnicity metrics: P_e=N_e/N_total for identifiable ethnicities; RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, with seven groups giving uniform baseline 1/7≈14.3%. RDS=0.769 implies about 91.2% representation, over six times expected. Positive RDS means overrepresentation, negative underrepresentation. SDI=1−ΣP_e²; higher values indicate greater diversity/balance and lower values concentration. Uniformity is a diagnostic benchmark for the neutral person-only setting, not a claim about real-world demographic proportions. Bias shifts compare aligned and unaligned models via ΔPBSG, ΔRDS_e, and ΔSDI; movement toward balanced gender, reduced ethnic skew, and higher diversity is labeled improvement.

grade.reason: Report 5 directly identifies the claim that P3L matches Z6B's absolute bias magnitude as false, citing Table 7 which shows absolute magnitudes 1.5280 vs 0.7448.

errors.claim: “We use two conditions: 1. Person-only ... 2. Ethnicity+Person ...” and “Because ethnicity+person already specifies ethnicity, an additional ethnicity-only setting is unnecessary for isolating ethnicity effects.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the evaluation conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only.
errors.explanation: The paper’s stated evaluation design elsewhere includes Ethnicity+Gender and ethnicity-only conditions, contradicting this section’s claim that there are only two conditions and that ethnicity-only is unnecessary.

errors.claim: Each judge independently assigns a gender label \(g\in G=\{\text{man, woman}\}\).
errors.evidence: Earlier notes state that VideoBiasEval uses four gender categories: man, woman, person, and non-binary person.
errors.explanation: The paper’s evaluation is defined over four gender categories, but this section restricts extracted gender labels to only two. No explanation reconciles the omission of the person and non-binary-person categories.

errors.claim: “ModelScope has the strongest imbalance: RDSWhite = 0.769 and SDI = 0.0538.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports InstructVideo with a higher White RDS of 0.7833 and a lower Overall SDI of 0.0267, compared with ModelScope’s 0.7690 and 0.0538.
errors.explanation: By both stated imbalance indicators—greater White overrepresentation (RDSWhite) and lower ethnic diversity (SDI)—InstructVideo shows a stronger imbalance than ModelScope, contradicting the claim that ModelScope has the strongest imbalance.

errors.claim: "Alignment increases average male skew... The prose reports the first increase as 0.04."
errors.evidence: The same bullet states that Table 2 gives the first alignment increase as "+0.0480" for Average PBSG.
errors.explanation: The prose value 0.04 does not match the table value 0.0480; if rounded to two decimal places, 0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “PickScore favors East Asian representation, RDS = 0.0352.”
errors.evidence: In Table 4, PickScore’s East Asian RDS is 0.0316, while 0.0352 does not appear as its East Asian RDS.
errors.explanation: The reported PickScore East Asian RDS is numerically inconsistent with Table 4. The table shows 0.0316, not 0.0352.

errors.claim: The prose reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0352.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports PickScore’s East Asian RDS as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The prose value 0.0352 contradicts the corresponding Table 4 value of 0.0316.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.1 improves balance for White and Black groups”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, HPSv2.1 has White RDS = 0.4286, but Black RDS is “—”. The table caption states that “—” indicates zero recognizable instances of that ethnicity and a severe lack of diversity preventing metric computation.
errors.explanation: The table supports improved White balance, but provides no Black RDS for HPSv2.1; instead, it reports zero recognizable Black instances. Therefore, improvement in Black balance cannot be claimed and conflicts with the table’s explanation of the missing value.

errors.claim: “RMW exhibits an equally strong opposite tendency, matching RMM’s absolute bias magnitude.” The section later calls this a “magnitude-matched contrast.”
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports RMM Average = 1.5280 and RMW Average = −0.7448 (with CLIP = −0.0726). Relative to CLIP, RMM shifts by about +1.60, whereas RMW shifts by about −0.67; their absolute shifts are therefore not equal.
errors.explanation: The reported RMW bias is not magnitude-matched to RMM’s bias, either as a raw score or relative to the CLIP baseline.

errors.claim: “The results suggest a continuous alignment axis: mixtures of man- and woman-preferred data yield tunable trade-offs between bias mitigation and aesthetic coherence.”
errors.evidence: The Claims and evidence section states: “Mixtures of preference data are proposed as a further control mechanism. Tables 7–8 establish the two directional endpoints; this section presents mixture-based optimization as a promising direction, not a reported mixture experiment.”
errors.explanation: The opening presents mixtures as yielding demonstrated tunable trade-offs, but the later summary says no mixture experiment was reported and treats mixture-based optimization only as a proposed direction.

final_notes:
Section 5.2 constructs a FLUX T2I benchmark with 100 images per prompt: Ethnicity+Person has 294 prompts (7×42), and Ethnicity+Gender has 1176 prompts (7×4×42). Three annotators evaluate 100 sampled images: 77% unanimous, 97% majority agreement, and three lack majority consensus.

Table 4 evaluates CLIP, HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore on 42 verbs using PBSG, RDS, and SDI. Average PBSG: CLIP −0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, HPSv2.1 −0.0984, PickScore −0.1157. HPSv2.0 shifts toward men; HPSv2.1 and PickScore favor women. Ethnicity RDS: CLIP White 0.0182; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern 0.0315; HPSv2.1 Latino 0.0382; PickScore East Asian 0.0316. Prose incorrectly reports PickScore as 0.0352. Overall SDI: CLIP 0.8495, HPSv2.0 0.8492, HPSv2.1 0.8470, PickScore 0.8483.

Table 5 evaluates VCM-VC2 and reward models; VCM favors White (RDS 0.6405), with missing RDS indicating zero recognizable instances. Claim that HPSv2.1 improves White/Black balance is unsupported for Black.

Section 7: man- and woman-preferred reward datasets each contain 2.94m pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7: CLIP PBSG −0.0726, RMM 1.5280, RMW −0.7448; text incorrectly calls RMM/RMW magnitude-matched. Table 8: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082.

Section 8 conclusion repeats key results. Earlier opening claims mixtures yield tunable trade-offs, while Claims/evidence says mixtures were proposed and untested—an inconsistency.

Limitations include predefined categories, image-level VLM classification, mainly single-step latent consistency distillation, limited reward models, synthetic gender manipulations, and fixed 42-action VideoBiasEval.

Broader Impact repeats Tables 5 and 7–8; reports gender TAS mean 0.9763→0.9967 and stability 0.8850→0.9830. It frames preference control as dual-use and identifies normalization, exclusion, homogenization, and propaganda as risks without numerical deployment evidence.

Acknowledgment lists funding/support from AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program, and Coefficient Giving, and states conclusions do not represent those organizations.

Seven ethnic groups: White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and Latino. Gender labels: man and woman; prompts also include non-binary person and person. Conditions include Person Only, Ethnicity+Person, Ethnicity+Gender, and ethnicity-only. Models: ModelScope is the unaligned baseline/base for InstructVideo; InstructVideo is ModelScope aligned with HPSv2.0. VideoCrafter-2 is the unaligned base for T2V-Turbo-V1 and source of the consistency model; T2V-Turbo-V1 uses HPSv2.1, InternVid2-S2, and ViCLIP. VCM-VC2 is distilled from VideoCrafter-V2 and aligned in Sections 6–7. Reward models include HPSv2.0/2.1, PickScore, and RMM/RM_M and RMW/RM_W. Reward-data preferences: HPDv2 has 18/26 (69.23%) man-preferred qualifying verbs and 43.34% White preference; Pick-a-Pic has 11/18 (61.11%) woman-preferred verbs and 40.08% White preference. Table 4 average PBSG: HPSv2.0 0.6039, PickScore -0.1157. Table 5 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +HPSv2.0 0.9116; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Table 6 ethnicity mean TAS: VCM-VC2 0.8904; +HPSv2 0.9305; +HPSv2.1 0.9632; +PickScore 0.9406. Another recorded Table 6 aggregate shows mean TAS rising from 0.9763 to 0.9967 (possibly a different aggregate). Table 8 average PBSG: VCM-VC2 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082. Limitations include demographic categories, automated evaluators, training choices, and fixed action set. Related work says existing T2V benchmarks (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench) and common metrics overlook demographic identity and portrayal; prior bias evaluations often count identities without analyzing actors’ actions, roles, contexts, or temporal patterns. No internal contradiction identified in this part.

The paper introduces VideoBiasEval, a framework for evaluating social bias in video generation. It uses event-based prompts to separate semantic content (verbs and contexts) from actor attributes (gender and ethnicity), with VLMs inferring attributes across frames. Metrics assess overall ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal persistence of bias. The study analyzes bias through the pipeline from human preference datasets to image-based reward models to alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main abstract claims: alignment tuning improves visual quality but can amplify representational/social bias, strengthens biases, and makes them temporally stable, yielding smoother but more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 repeats the framework and end-to-end analysis claims, referring to Sections 3, 5.1, 5.2, and 6. Authors and affiliations are listed; no internal contradictions identified in this part.
